speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This has been the crisis of a generation – a battle against one of the most disruptive viruses the world has encountered in recent history.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The crisis upended our lives in ways we never could have imagined.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In the most acute phase of the pandemic, our economy ground to a halt and workers lost their jobs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Many key life events were put on hold.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Some of us suffered the pain of losing loved ones during this difficult time.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Others were separated from family members who were based overseas.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The whole experience has fundamentally challenged and shaped who we are as a people and as a nation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Today, we have fully transitioned to living with COVID-19 as an endemic disease.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The virus is still among us and no one can tell how it will continue to evolve.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But, for now, the evolution seems to be plodding, with minor tweaks to its genetic code, rather than major changes that require another Greek-letter name.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, it is timely to take stock of our response so that we can start preparing for the next battle, whenever it comes.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: On the whole, compared to other countries, we have done well in protecting both lives and livelihoods throughout this pandemic.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our healthcare system, though strained, was never overwhelmed.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our case fatality rate is one of the lowest globally.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The actual amount was less than budgeted partly because we had been prudent in our spending and also because we avoided some of the worst-case outcomes we had prepared for.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our financial resources enabled us to mount a strong public health response and to secure early access to vaccines.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: A large proportion of the spending – over 80% – went towards supporting workers, businesses and individuals, so as to cushion them from the worst impact of the crisis.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Crucially, we augmented the direct Government measures with a series of COVID-19 legislation that provided small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) relief from their contractual obligations and protected them from financial distress and insolvency.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These resources were crucial to our COVID-19 fight.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, all in all, this was money well spent to tackle the extreme downsides of COVID-19, to protect lives and to avoid mass unemployment.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our comprehensive and swift economic schemes enabled our resident employment and incomes to recover quickly to pre-COVID-19 levels while keeping COVID-19 deaths low.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our policies and actions to respond to the pandemic have also distinguished us from other countries.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We kept our air and sea ports open and ensured an uninterrupted flow of critical supplies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We enhanced our reputation as a trusted node that can be relied upon even when other parts of the world shut down.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We also stand out in the world because of how our population rallied together in this crisis.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Through all the trials and tribulations, we held together as a society and pulled through as one united people.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We kept faith with our fellow Singaporeans, took care of the non-Singaporeans in our midst and everyone did our part in the interest of the common good.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Another recent survey – this one by the Edelman Trust Institute – found that trust in the Government remains high in Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, it is at a record high.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Singaporeans, generally, trusted the Government's advice and cooperated with the measures.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is unlike many other countries where people railed against the public health measures and trust in government went down.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We supported and looked out for one another throughout this crisis.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As a result, many Singaporeans felt that their relationships with their neighbours, family and friends were maintained or have become stronger.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have deepened the reservoir of trust and strengthened our social capital.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Indeed, there have been many bright spots amid the dark clouds – many stories of personal sacrifices and selfless dedication, instances where we came together as a community and as a nation to fight this crisis of a generation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: On behalf of the Government, I would like to put on record our appreciation to everyone who contributed to our COVID-19 fight.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our workers and unions, as well as tripartite partners who marshalled resources, rolled out support and helped countless businesses and workers through difficult times.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our companies and trade associations, non-governmental organisations (NGOs) as well as community groups who came together to contribute their time and know-how to fortify our response and support the vulnerable.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our public officers who went beyond the call of duty.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Many toiled selflessly behind the scenes to plan and roll out a multitude of programmes and policies, working shoulder-to-shoulder with the people and private sectors.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our dauntless healthcare workers and many others who operated on the frontlines of the crisis.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Whether it was at our borders or in the foreign worker dormitories, in our clinics and hospitals or in quarantine facilities, they willingly assumed personal risks, over and over again, just so that the rest of us could be safe.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They rose to the occasion when the going got tough, even in the darkest of times.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are, therefore, honoured to have a small contingent of our frontline warriors join us in Parliament today.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They represent a cross-section of the wider community of individuals who fought bravely on the COVID-19 frontlines: nurses and doctors and other healthcare professionals in the hospitals and in the community; educators and social service professionals and workers who served our students and vulnerable groups right through the crisis; transport workers, supermarket and warehouse managers and other frontline workers who kept essential services going, including our ports and land links; staff in both the public and private sectors who ran critical backroom operations to maintain supply chains, care facilities and many other services; Safe Distancing Ambassadors, SAF officers and soldiers, and Home Team responders who mounted large-scale responses in support of various policies and programmes.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is just a sampling of all our frontline fighters.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We express a grateful nation's deepest appreciation for your contributions and courage.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Your dedication helped Singapore to keep going through unprecedented and uncertain times.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Your acts of duty, sacrifice and care for fellow Singaporeans uplifted our spirits, boosted our confidence and kept all of us safe.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, once again, we would like to say a very big "thank you" to all of you.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Today, we ask ourselves – what lessons can we draw from this crisis?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: How can we improve our strategies and be better prepared for the next pandemic or even the next wave, if it should come?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There are no straightforward answers to these questions because COVID-19 was a very complex and wicked problem on a grand scale.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our battle with the virus was a journey with many twists and turns and with repeated surprises and disruptions along the way.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The situation was dynamic and fluid, with new information and developments unfolding daily.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We had to operate in the fog of war.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It was often not clear what our next course of action should be.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We had many intense debates among ourselves – political officeholders as well as civil servants – and, in the end, we had to take decisions based on our best judgement and manage the consequences as well as we could.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Even today, as we look back, there will be different perspectives on what had transpired or how certain aspects of the pandemic could have been differently managed.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Indeed, our response to COVID-19 was by no means perfect.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: There were areas that we could have done better.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have highlighted them in the White Paper.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have been forthright and transparent about this so that we can learn from our experiences.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The point is not to look back and critique the past with 20/20 hindsight but to unpack how and why certain decisions were made at those points, what assumptions were held then, which considerations should have been weighed differently and how we can do better the next time.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In particular, some of our initial responses fell short because we knew so little about the virus at the start of the outbreak.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We operated on the basis of the best scientific assessments then, as well as the protocols from our SARS experience.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, while SARS helped us to avoid a cold start, it also in some ways contributed to us making some wrong initial assumptions.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is an important point – that while we learn from this and past experiences, we must also have the flexibility of mind to adjust to new situations and not be trapped by fixed views of how a crisis might unfold.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, the initial prevailing view was that one needed to show symptoms before the virus could spread, which was the case with SARS.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, this turned out to be wrong with COVID-19.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The virus was also spread by individuals with no symptoms.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This wrong assumption contributed to several shortcomings in our initial response.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We never wavered from our commitment to take care of our migrant workers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We acted as quicky as possible and activated every resource we had available to control the situation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have also learnt from this episode and taken steps to plug the shortcomings in our system – something that Minister Tan See Leng will share later in this debate.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Likewise, we started out advising the public to only wear masks when unwell.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We changed this later to mandate the use of masks in public spaces when we realised that asymptomatic transmission was possible.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This would have given people psychological reassurance that they could do something to protect themselves and would also have helped to slow down transmission and spread of the virus, even though the improvised masks only provided partial protection.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In some other areas, like the implementation of safe management measures (SMMs), we did the right thing.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We designed measures that took into account the risk that was inherent in different settings and activities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But we allowed the perfect to become the enemy of the good.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our rules were, at times, too finely calibrated, too complicated to follow and too difficult to implement – the varying group sizes, which I am sure everyone remembers; different rules for adults and children; different sets of rules for physical activity in different settings are some examples of this.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Aggravating the problem, the rules had to be adjusted as circumstances changed, sometimes at short notice.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Again, looking back, we should have tried much harder to simplify things, and gone for more broad-brush measures that would have reduced the implementation cost and burden.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: One of the most difficult judgement calls we had to make was on managing our borders.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Border restrictions are an important defence against the virus, but we also know that such measures only help to buy time; they cannot completely stop the virus from coming in.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The question is how far do we go in tightening our borders, recognising that this will also impose a huge cost on livelihoods and on Singapore’s reliance on the world for a living.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This would have bought us time to understand the virus and build up our hospital capacity.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Furthermore, having decided that we would allow Singaporeans living abroad to return home, we should have acted sooner to ramp up the provision of quarantine and isolation facilities for the returning residents.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At the same time, border measures can only do so much.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Once the virus took hold within the community, we could have eased our border restrictions more responsively, as the main danger would no longer be from cases coming from abroad.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In particular, we took some time to resume the entry of Long-Term Pass (LTP) holders into Singapore because we had found that even with pre-departure testing, a high percentage of travellers from some countries were still testing COVID-19-positive on arrival.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our concern was that the large number of infected persons could easily overwhelm our isolation facilities and healthcare capacity.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It was a judgement call we had to make at that time, and not without reason.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But we also know that the restrictions created significant difficulties for some groups of LTP holders, such as Employment Pass holders with families here but who were abroad, or vice versa.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Some of them endured prolonged family separation and disruption to their work.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Singapore did incur reputational cost and lost some goodwill from this segment of the community who also had their homes here.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We subsequently learnt from these experiences and adjusted our border responses when we dealt with the Omicron variant in late-2021.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Members will remember we swiftly implemented a not-to-land policy to travellers from certain countries and we applied a combination of hotel and home quarantine for other travellers, depending on where they came from.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The quick tightening of rules created a lot of inconvenience for those returning from their vacations then, because this was in December 2021.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And once we learnt more about Omicron and determined that it was less severe and not of significant concern, we eased the measures quickly as well.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That was one example of how we learnt from the experiences with border restrictions.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Another example came up in December last year, when China moved away from its zero COVID-19 policy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At that time, China experienced a significant surge in cases.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Several countries like the US, Japan and South Korea imposed tighter restrictions on arrivals from China.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But we did not do so – and the reason is because we assessed that there were no new variants of concern detected in China, and the viral strains there were already circulating around the world and in our community.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We regret the inconveniences and frustrations caused to Singaporeans and everyone in Singapore when this happened.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At the same time, we are grateful for the fortitude and forbearance that everyone had shown, when we had to put in place tough measures and also when there were shortcomings and errors in our policies and implementations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is the nature of dealing with a crisis.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will always be faced with incomplete information.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have to judge what is the best way forward based on what we know and respond quickly, rather than wait for all the facts to come in, by which time it might be too late to act.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Indeed, there will never be a “perfect response” in a crisis that is as complex, unpredictable and fast-moving as COVID-19.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In such a crisis, no policy can cater for every eventuality; no plan can be implemented perfectly, because there will always be time pressure and resource constraints.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: What is more important is to be honest in our appraisal of our own actions and to keep on learning and improving, and striving to do better.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is the spirit behind this White Paper and that is how we have distilled the key lessons that Singapore should take away to be better prepared for the next pandemic.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For this debate, let me focus on three broad lessons.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: First, fortifying our public health system to better respond to the next pandemic.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: On several occasions over the last three years, our healthcare system came under immense pressure.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We had to activate the entire healthcare ecosystem to cope with surges.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We called on the private and community hospitals to augment our capacity.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Testing had to be ramped up nationally, at an unprecedented scale and pace.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We had to tap on both public and private sector laboratories to expand our testing capacities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Throughout, the Ministry of Health (MOH) and the National Centre for Infectious Diseases (NCID) worked closely with research laboratories and infectious disease experts outside of the Government to understand the changing nature of the virus, perform epidemiological modelling and accelerate the development of diagnostics and therapeutics.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Through these collective efforts, we protected our healthcare system from being overwhelmed and averted many deaths.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But this was not without significant strain on the system and on our healthcare workers, who shouldered the massive responsibility of treating and caring for infected persons.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: To be better prepared for the next pandemic, we must strengthen the resilience of our healthcare system.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will need to build on our plans to strengthen the primary care system, which we are now pursuing through Healthier SG.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will also strengthen the relationships we have established with the private sector through our COVID-19 response, so that in a future pandemic, we can support more flexible responses and faster mobilisation of resources.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And while we have done well in our vaccination efforts, our vaccine resilience can be fortified further with local manufacturing capability.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At the same time, we must grow our expertise in public health and pandemic management.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In particular, we need to be able to detect the spread of novel pathogens quickly through effective surveillance and develop swift response measures to control the spread of the disease.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We already have some of these capabilities, especially in the area of communicable disease control and management, which we had beefed up after SARS.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These currently reside in various parts of our healthcare system, for example in the NCID, the National Public Health Laboratory and within MOH itself.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This will enable us to develop stronger competence in public health and grow these capabilities over time.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Later in this debate, Minister Ong Ye Kung will elaborate on these plans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our planning parameters for the pandemic were largely based on the SARS experience.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But it quickly became clear that these parameters were not adequate.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: SARS was a short, regional outbreak, largely confined to hospital settings.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: COVID-19 turned out to be more transmissible, though less severe than SARS, and the pandemic continued for several years and not just a few months.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This greatly strained our healthcare capacity and manpower.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Just as COVID-19 was different from SARS, the next novel pathogen will be different from COVID-19.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: With SARS, we had a pathogen that was highly severe but with low risk of spread.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: With COVID-19, we have a pathogen that is only moderately severe, but with higher risk of spread.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Being prepared and making investments early can yield immense dividends, especially during a crisis.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But at the same time, realistically, we cannot plan for every possibility.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Every new pathogen we meet will involve a degree of dealing with the unknown and it would be prohibitively expensive to cater for a wide range of “worst cases”.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Some scrambling is inevitable and inherent in the process, as we discover more information and consider the need to adjust our posture along the way.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is why we must dedicate resources and equip our crisis management structures with better forward planning capabilities – so we better anticipate and imagine what might happen next, be prepared for the unexpected and be ready to adapt to changing circumstances as they unfold.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: By doing so, we do not have to front-load all of the investments to cater for all contingencies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But we must create a dynamic, forward-oriented organisation and process whose main mission is to anticipate and monitor risks, to keep buying insurance where needed.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, as the crisis develops, we can continue to buy more insurance and options for the future.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: To be clear, we did set aside some capacity to do such forward planning during the last three years.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But it was very hard to do this well, because our officers were already fully stretched, fighting the immediate fire.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This will help us better anticipate the next bound, develop our next course of action and pivot more effectively as the situation evolves.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Related to all this is the third lesson – how we can strengthen our resilience as a nation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our COVID-19 experience has been a stark reminder of our vulnerability.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As a small and open economy, we were more badly hit than others by a global disruption that was outside of our control.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We found ourselves in situations where it was uncertain whether we could secure critical supplies, even when we were willing to pay a premium for them.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In the early months of the pandemic, we witnessed how other countries had started hoarding essential medical and food supplies, and we grew increasingly concerned about whether we could replenish our own stock.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Significant work had to be undertaken to activate emergency procurement measures and to tap on long-standing networks to secure what we needed.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We also had to design new processes to keep our port and land links open, but in a safe way.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The pandemic has underscored the importance of building up additional redundancies and buffers that we can fall back upon during a crisis.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Besides having additional buffers, resilience is also about being more adaptable.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We must be able to marshal our existing assets and resources quickly, and be nimble enough to move fast when the unexpected happens.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, when we first managed to bring protein and meat supplies into Singapore, which we had to do, there was an issue of where to store these goods.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) scrambled, this was under then Minister Chan when he was at MTI, and we eventually solved this by sourcing and bringing in refrigerated containers, what they call "reefers", to provide sufficient cold storage capacity and we ramped up the capacity of the power supply to support their operations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In particular, we will apply further thought into how we can enhance the resilience of our public infrastructure, especially for new major projects like the Tuas Mega Port and Changi Airport Terminal 5.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We also need to be able to convert and repurpose existing spaces at short notice into facilities that can be used to meet emergency needs in a crisis.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We had faced a steep learning curve trying to do this at the start.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Singapore Expo had to be converted into community isolation and care facilities, hotels into quarantine facilities, Community Centres into vaccination centres, and vacant schools and Singapore Armed Forces camps into temporary housing for migrant workers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Each of these processes took a lot of work and learning from this experience.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will continue to build up our capabilities so that we can pivot and respond more effectively in future.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our private sector partners are a key source of support in these efforts.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Working alongside them over the course of the pandemic has showed us all that there is much more that we can do by coming together, by sharing our resources, capabilities and networks.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we will do more to sustain and strengthen our partnerships with the private sector.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: For example, through cooperation agreements, to shore up our pandemic preparedness plans and to mobilise our national resources more comprehensively in times of need.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Indeed, our Reserves is an integral part of our national resilience.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It shielded our economy and our people from the harshest impact of the pandemic, and it remains our best safeguard in any crisis.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is, therefore, our duty to ensure that the Reserves are used prudently and judiciously, so that future generations can continue to benefit from it.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Ultimately, what lies at the heart of our resilience is our people, because that is our most important defence in a pandemic – to be psychologically prepared, to stay united and to support one another and keep faith with each other.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Throughout this pandemic, Singaporeans were socially responsible and responded to the calls for self-discipline, with admirable fortitude and patience.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We saw a strong communitarian spirit and a high level of volunteerism.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Many ground projects were initiated to rally the community in support of those who needed help.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: COVID-19 brought out the best in all of us, individually and collectively.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Despite the pressures and fears, we did not give in, we did not succumb.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We stood firmly together and left no one behind.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is a mark of our growing maturity and resilience, as a people and as a nation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It has been an emotional journey of ups and downs for all of us, in the same way that our response has had its fair share of setbacks and successes.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In the end, it was the whole nation coming together that made the difference in our fight against COVID-19, allowing us to surmount the odds and face the challenges without fear.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, the aim of this White Paper and this debate is not to rate the Government's or Singapore's performance in this pandemic.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have done our best and that is what matters.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In the final analysis, the long arc of history will judge how well we have responded to this crisis of a generation and how well we have learnt and remembered the lessons of COVID-19.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Today, we are here to give thanks, for we have found our way through the pandemic and emerged from it intact and strengthened.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are here to pay tribute to all who have made countless sacrifices and worked so hard to get us through this crisis.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are here to learn, improve and be better prepared when the next pandemic comes.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I hope that we will not have to go through an episode like COVID-19 again.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Unfortunately, we would have to be very lucky for my hope to be fulfilled.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But if it does happen, we can draw confidence and strength from what we have been through these past three years.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We should not forget our public officers too.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: From civil servants and teachers to those guarding our borders and public spaces namely our men and women in uniform, we must honour them for trying to allow Singaporeans to live our lives as normally as possible while keeping us as safe.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The same goes for every Singaporean involved in this fight.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Reciting this today, I feel – as I felt then – that it simply cannot adequately express the appreciation many Singaporeans continue to have, for our frontliners and public service workers, for seeing us through the last three years.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For some, the challenges took a lot out of them – public health workers, in particular are still reeling from the intensity of the last three years and it is important for us to continually consider the long-term impact of the stresses they faced.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party (WP) Members of Parliament will elaborate further on this and on the findings of the White Paper in their speeches.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Aljunied Group Representation Constituency (GRC) Member of Parliament, Mr Gerald Giam, will speak on healthcare capacity, including Persons with Disabilities (PwDs) in future pandemic response measures, domestic manufacturing during crises and the role of Temasek Holdings.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Sengkang GRC Member of Parliament Ms He Ting Ru will speak on Government communication, the gender wage gap and the underpaying and undervaluing of work traditionally carried out by women, mental health and the implications of "long COVID-19".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For my part, I will speak on the approach the WP as a political Opposition, took on COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, I will speak of the role the party played to bring concerns of the public into Parliament over the last three years through our COVID-19 experience.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Second, I will cover what the WP did and deliberately did not do, so as to support the national effort; and finally, I will speak on the political posture of the WP during a national crisis.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We did not abdicate our role of holding the Government to account, as the design of our political system demands.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even without the full suite of considerations and details that are privy to the Government of the day, we advanced concrete proposals on managing the COVID-19 crisis as part of our General Election 2020 manifesto.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: During my Fortitude Budget speech in June 2020, I reminded the Government that Singaporeans had a right to expect a thorough review and accounting of the Government response to the crisis.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I suggested that a Commission of Inquiry, or some other independent body, be appointed to review specific aspects of the Government's response up to that point.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I emphasised that whatever form such a reckoning might take, our position as a constructive opposition required us to communicate the feelings of Singaporeans in Parliament, which necessarily includes a public expectation of Government accountability.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It incorporates the findings of various reviews by Government agencies as well as the perspectives of the private and people sectors.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The White Paper adds that it attempts to, and I quote, "synthesise and make sense of the breadth of perspectives gathered, weave them together with the known data and facts, and offer as balanced and objective an account as possible” of the Government’s COVID-19 response.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To those familiar with the study of official history, this document would be referred to as a secondary document.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There is an original document from which it draws its findings and conclusions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This original document is not before the House.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While the White Paper acknowledges some shortcomings in the Government response, Singaporeans do not know what has been excluded from the original reports and reviews referenced in this White Paper produced by the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO).

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Are the contents of this White Paper all the findings from the AAR that the Government is prepared to share with the public and Parliament?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Presumably, Mr Peter Ho submitted a more comprehensive AAR report to the Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can that report be made public to Parliament so that Members of Parliament and Singaporeans can better understand the breadth of perspectives gathered, the known data and facts, and draw their own conclusions?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If there is confidential information within the AAR report that could harm national security if revealed, that could be redacted from the report.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In some countries, government approaches to COVID-19 were routinely attacked by parties outside of government in order to gain political mileage.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We did not ride on misinformation or contribute to misunderstandings over national policies which were either intentionally or unintentionally conveyed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On the contrary, we encouraged Singaporeans to be mindful of rumours or unverified information and to clarify their doubts through the proper channels.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, in the middle of 2021, Member of Parliament for Sengkang Assoc Prof Jamus Lim came out to clarify that the tragic death of a young resident was not due to COVID-19, as was being openly propagated by some individuals online, ostensibly to sow doubts about vaccine safety.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Clearly, a unity of purpose was the need of the hour.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A most worrisome medical reality of COVID-19 was that it struck hard at our seniors and elderly.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We needed to protect them against the much higher risk of severe illness and even death.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: During our engagement with residents, WP Members of Parliament encouraged our seniors to get vaccinated.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Whenever they were undecided or unsure, we encouraged them to clarify their doubts on existing medical conditions with their doctors for peace of mind.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Former Member of Parliament, Mr Png Eng Huat, did the same, speaking in Hokkien and sharing his experience, convincing his 92-year-old father to get vaccinated.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Sengkang GRC Member of Parliament Ms He Ting Ru shared with the public that she took her vaccination while she was still breastfeeding as there was a concern and confusion that nursing mothers could be passing something dangerous to their babies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Hougang Single Member Constituency (SMC) Member of Parliament Mr Dennis Tan and Aljunied GRC Member of Parliament Mr Gerald Giam visited residents in clusters of blocks in Aljunied-Hougang town, where residents in entire blocks were identified for mandatory swabbing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When the news suddenly broke out of such mass swabbing, Mr Giam went door-to-door with words of support for residents while working with the Aljunied-Hougang Town Council to assist in the wipe-down and cleaning of the affected blocks, something our cleaners – predominantly migrant workers – did so many times over the last three years to keep our community safe.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We were determined to support, and not undermine, the national effort.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As a political party that is not in Government, the WP will continue to lead with this approach in times of national crisis.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In WP Town Councils, we implemented the necessary protocols effectively.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When some residents expressed frustration at some safe management measures in common areas that came under our responsibility, such as hawker centres, playgrounds and void decks, we dealt with them with empathy and open-mindedness, but without compromising the national measures or the safety of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We realised that some rules could prove problematic when operationalised on the ground, and our Town Council officers diligently submitted their feedback to the agencies concerned.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We took the view that any feedback would be taken seriously by civil servants and we endeavoured to work as one Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As has come to be expected of our public officers, they did not let us down.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, there are many outside this House who played an equal part in saving livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As COVID-19 brought our economy to a near halt, many individuals saw their incomes evaporate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will never forget my engagement with a group of private-hire bus drivers at the start of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These drivers had mouths to feed and vehicle loans to repay, but no business to generate income.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These drivers, and others like them, were helped by the diligence of public officers who engaged with financial institutions to withhold the repossession of vehicles.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I wish to restate my acknowledgement of these efforts.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My appreciation also goes out to the many volunteer lawyers, assessors and SMEs and all businesses that exercised compassion by providing temporary relief to Singaporeans from their contractual obligations and potential enforcement actions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It seeks to internalise the lessons learnt from our COVID-19 journey and to improve preparedness for the next health pandemic.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Doing so would honour the sacrifices made by Singaporeans and the community in our fight against COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: COVID-19 has resulted in the loss of lives and livelihoods worldwide, including in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The workers in the aviation, aerospace and tourism sectors were especially affected when the borders closed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our self-employed persons (SEPs) were hit especially hard by the sudden loss of income during the circuit breaker.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: On the other hand, workers in essential services, such as healthcare and supermarkets, had to work significantly harder to keep the country going.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have endured much pain as a nation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It had not been easy to get to where we are today.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They are the vanguard in winning this battle against COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our Public Service officers also deserve no less praise for developing new policies and dispensing assistance at breakneck speed to Singaporeans during the darkest of times.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They discharged their duties with honour, passion and fortitude.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In the battle to save livelihoods, the rock of tripartism has also allowed us, as a nation, to stand strong against the crashing waves COVID-19 brought before our shores.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Tripartite partners worked together to save businesses, jobs and livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our focus during the crisis was to cut costs to save jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With neither vaccine nor cure in sight, businesses and workers faced a most daunting future.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Businesses needed to conserve cash but also needed to retain capabilities if and when the situation changed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I witnessed how unity prevailed where we could have succumbed easily to self-interests.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) worked with our tripartite partners and recommended reducing non-wage costs and guided businesses to manage excess manpower to save jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We also guided workers and businesses on the efficient use of Government support measures to train and reskill our workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: When the economic problems deepened, union leaders acted swiftly to ensure that retrenchments were minimised to the greatest extent possible.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Though painful, workers took pay freezes and cuts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Labour Movement stood in solidarity with the nation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We provided guidelines to ensure temporary wage cuts were implemented in a reasonable manner.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our union leaders also sought to minimise the overall impact to workers’ take-home pay.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They worked with companies to manage wage costs equitably and gradually.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our tripartite partners never took our minds off our vulnerable workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We worked with companies to prioritise non-wage cost-cutting measures.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: By having higher-wage earners take deeper and faster cuts, we protected lower-wage workers as much as possible.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We were able to do so because of the strong trust built over the many years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Central to protecting workers was also in placing displaced workers to areas of need.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Managed by NTUC’s e2i, it is a placement ecosystem with a network of employers that are hiring and releasing workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: At its core, the JSC aims to support businesses in coping with fluctuating manpower needs across the economic cycle while providing support to workers in need.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In particular, JSC focused on engaging with at-risk or displaced workers to pre-emptively shorten the unemployment period by helping them find jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This proved vital in the aviation, aerospace and hospitality sectors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our union leaders worked hard to encourage workers to switch jobs during the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: An example of such an initiative is the JSC’s Lift-and-Place programme in partnership with trade associations and Government agencies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, Looi Jia Wen had been flying with Singapore Airlines as a cabin crew for only one and a half months before COVID-19 struck.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: JSC assisted cabin crew like her to be redeployed as Care Ambassadors at Khoo Teck Puat Hospital.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They supported hospital care teams to carry out basic caregiving procedures for patients, like oral feeding, positioning and turning, and moving patients.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Jia Wen was able to make good use of the skills she had learnt as a cabin crew and contributed to the healthcare sector.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Those in the hospitality sector were deployed to supermarkets, including NTUC FairPrice and other essential services sectors, performing roles like contact tracers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Workers under this programme would remain employees of their company.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This initiative has allowed companies to ensure that skilled manpower would be readily available in the upturn.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, Gina Ng, back then, she was 59 years old and she had worked for 34 years at Fairmont Singapore and Swissôtel The Stamford as a senior administrative assistant in the hotel’s culinary department.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Gina is one of the many workers who benefited from JSC’s efforts to support at-risk workers and match them to new jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Workers in these affected companies were also able to retain some pay during the height of the pandemic and return to their jobs after the crisis.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: NTUC's e2i has also helped to move displaced workers from affected sectors to new contract jobs arising from the pandemic, such as Safe Distancing Ambassadors and swabbers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Unions and employers also could not have helped as many workers without important Government measures.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, the Jobs Support Scheme (JSS) provided wage support for employers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For the Self-Employed Persons (SEPs), things were not as straightforward.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, during the circuit breaker, taxi drivers and private hire drivers saw their income drop rapidly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Sports coaches, art instructors and tour guides saw their income drop near to zero or zero, during the lockdown.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Unlike the employees with their companies receiving support from the Government, SEPs were not afforded such support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The mechanism used to provide support to the employees just could not work for them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Labour Movement quickly took up their cause with the Government.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Government responded strongly with the Self-Employed Income Relief Scheme (SIRS).

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With the Government stretched immeasurably on many different fronts, the Labour Movement had to step up to administer SIRS.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The circuit breaker would leave almost all of our SEPs with no income.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our priority was to get these monies into the affected SEPs' hands as soon as possible to provide them with a lifeline during such unprecedented times.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Because a sizeable proportion of our SEPs had not previously filed their income, it was operationally challenging to swiftly identify SEPs in need.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With the very short lead time, the bulk of the processing of the SIRS had to be done manually.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Application systems and forms had to be fine-tuned several times to better serve our SEPs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We also recognised that some of our older ones struggled with navigating online forms and faced difficulties in collating the requisite documentation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: NTUC staff stepped up and helped members through every step of the process.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Labour Movement's involvement in implementing SIRS provided us with valuable lessons.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The greatest of which was the precarious financial situations faced by many SEPs, especially the lower-income ones.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need to strengthen their financial and career resilience for SEPs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is especially when the next pandemic is inevitable.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We need to support SEPs to improve their career resilience and flexibility through training to deepen their skills and diversify their work portfolios.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Labour Movement, through our Freelancers and Self-Employed Unit (U FSE), will be focusing our efforts on representing the collective interests of the growing pool of SEPs in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We are starting with the platform drivers and riders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: NTUC has also stepped up working with associations to strengthen the income security, welfare and work prospects of our SEPs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We will actively work alongside them with relevant resources and networking opportunities vital to enhancing their career pathways.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They will also enjoy access to NTUC benefits and privileges such as access to seminars, training grants and insurance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In the intensity and fog of battling the pandemic, mistakes must be expected.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The lessons from COVID-19 will be key to building resilience in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: New capabilities such as the JSC were also developed, showing the there are opportunities in every crisis.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our deepest appreciation goes to our workers who continued to work despite understandable COVID-19 health worries.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They made sacrifices by taking pay cuts and freezes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They made sacrifices by working non-stop because the country needed them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We also appreciate our employers who stuck with workers during the trying times.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This crisis has further strengthened the trust between workers and employers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Government, especially our Ministry of Manpower (MOM) officers, they work hand-in-hand with tripartite partners to care for workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must continue to strengthen this cornerstone of tripartism to prepare for the inevitable next pandemic.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With this, Mr Speaker, I support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Our frontliners, including nurses, doctors, cleaners and drivers, responded heroically in the face of an enemy that we knew little about before 2020.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Words cannot repay the debt of gratitude we owe each of them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I extend my deepest condolences to their families for their immeasurable loss.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While I acknowledge that the Government has performed well in many aspects of its response to this pandemic, it is important that we do not get carried away, patting ourselves on the back to the exclusion of implementing the important lessons we learnt during the crisis.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We need to better prepare ourselves for future pandemics, which are likely to be more frequent and severe, not least because of increasing globalisation and urbanisation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Healthcare capacity was stretched even before COVID-19 hit.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many healthcare workers reported working long hours overtime, being recalled for duty on their days off and even having no time for toilet breaks.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The White Paper highlighted challenges in staffing hospitals with healthcare workers, resulting in existing workers feeling fatigued and burnt out from the prolonged crisis.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We are now no longer fighting COVID-19 like before, yet the shortage of healthcare facilities and manpower still persists.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This can spike to 50 hours during infection waves.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In October 2016, then-Minister for Health Gan Kim Yong launched the Healthcare Manpower Plan 2020, which highlighted the need for 30,000 more healthcare workers from 2015 to 2020 to look after Singapore's fast-ageing population.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: How many of these 30,000 additional healthcare positions have been filled?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: During the debate on the Healthier SG motion last October, Minister Ong Ye Kung said that another 24,000 nurses, allied health professionals and support care staff are needed to operate hospitals, clinics and eldercare centres by 2030.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There needs to be a corresponding transformation in the remuneration of healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The group that bore the heaviest burden of caring for COVID-19 patients were nurses.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Their long working hours and lower starting pay compared to territories like Australia, Hong Kong and Canada, could have contributed to their high attrition in recent years.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Why are so many nurses leaving the healthcare sector?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: A study on healthcare workers conducted by researchers Celene Ting and others from the Saw Swee Hock School for Public Health, Tan Tock Seng Hospital and the NCID highlighted that healthcare workers reported burnout from being overworked, emotional exhaustion and at times feeling a lack of appreciation or support at work.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This was exacerbated by having to care for difficult and sometimes abusive patients.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Nearly a third of healthcare workers witness or experience abuse each week, according to a tripartite workgroup's findings, which the Senior Parliamentary Secretary for Health, Rahayu Mazam, shared earlier this month during the Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Additionally, some healthcare workers are also drawn to work opportunities overseas, where they can receive higher remuneration and more societal recognition.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, a nurse that CNA interviewed mentioned that after moving from Singapore to the US, he felt more highly esteemed by the public, citing an example of how his car loan was approved immediately after he said he was a nurse, despite having no credit history.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Urgent changes are needed if we are to reverse the departure of nurses and boost their numbers in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Nurses' basic pay should be benchmarked to that of their contemporaries in other essential public services.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is a point made by Assoc Prof Jeremy Lim from the Saw Swee Hock School of Public Health during a recent CNA interview.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Such services could include the Police, army and the education service.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The salaries of nurses in other jurisdictions like Australia, Hong Kong and Canada should also be considered in the benchmarking.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It should take into account the longer hours that nurses have to work compared to many other professions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is to ensure that the opportunity cost of taking up nursing instead of another profession would be minimised.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We also need to make the nursing profession more highly esteemed by the general public.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Another way to attract more Singaporeans to take up nursing and increase retention would be to enhance their professional development opportunities.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Nurses in Singapore are often still seen as the assistants to doctors instead of being professionals in their own right.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They should instead be granted more autonomy and entrusted with higher level responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Beyond pay, management culture, work recognition and working hours are also areas that need to be examined for a holistic improvement of the profession.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Next, during the pandemic, many persons with disabilities (PwDs) experienced difficulties coping with measures such as the blocking off of regular exits and entrances, shifting access points for PwDs and having to locate and scan SafeEntry codes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Measures such as COVID-19 swabbing and mask-wearing were difficult for some people.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I recall a resident of mine who was very worried that her son, who had a mental disability, would struggle and hurt himself when made to undergo mandatory swabbing at his block when an outbreak occurred there.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While support for PwDs was eventually introduced, much of this was reactive.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This could be due to an absence of meaningful participation by PwDs when safe management measures were implemented.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Moving forward, it would be advisable to have at least one member of the disability community on emergency task forces so that the community's views can be adequately represented.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: More importantly, all policies rolled out need to take into account the unique needs of PwDs, to ensure that they are not excluded.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The next section of my speech deals with the public communication on pandemic mitigation measures.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Prime Minister rightly pointed out though, that the "Wuhan virus" – as it was then called – was "probably more infectious than SARS, and possibly infectious even before people have symptoms." This was on 31 January 2020.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The fact that the Government knew in those early days that asymptomatic transmission of the virus could occur should have prompted them to advise everyone to wear masks when in contact with other people.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: On 10 February 2020, four local doctors did just that by issuing a statement urging Singaporeans to wear masks always when leaving home, even if they were well.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Dr Colleen Thomas, Dr Judy Chen, Dr Tham Hoe Meng and Dr Lim Pin Pin acknowledged the difficulties in obtaining new surgical masks every day and urged the use of creative solutions like washable cloth masks or scarves.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They pointed out that these measures were better than no mask at all.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In response to the four doctors a few days later, the Director of Medical Services at MOH said that "it is not wearing masks that's most important, it's hand washing" – even though the two actions were not a binary choice.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Straits Times ran an article to "educate" the public on questions like "Is it really true that you do not need to wear a mask if you are not sick?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Is hand washing better protection against viruses than a mask?" These statements were incongruous and did not seem to be consistent with common sense.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: People intuitively knew that any layer preventing the spread of droplets would be better than not having one.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It took a leaked recording of a Minister at a closed-door meeting in February 2020 to reveal that Singapore was rationing masks to save them for healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It took another three months for the Government to stop discouraging people from wearing masks by updating the guidance on 3 April 2020.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans saw through the Government's initial statements – that the real reason why they were discouraging those who were well from wearing masks was because there were insufficient supplies of surgical masks, not because mask wearing was less effective than hand washing.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While concerns over panic buying and hoarding by the public were not unfounded, the Government had stockpiles of surgical masks for healthcare workers and should have had the power to requisition more masks from the commercial market.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This brings me to my next point – why did Singapore not have the sufficient domestic capacity to manufacture items as basic as face masks?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Was the Government not able to marshal local companies to accept and prioritise contracts for the manufacture of materials deemed essential for our defence against COVID-19, including face masks and ventilators?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The White Paper mentioned that the COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) Act gave the Government the option of mobilising civilian resources, using the Requisition of Resources Act (RORA), but it chose not to use those powers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Instead, the Government said it will leverage alternative structures, for example, through strategic partnerships or cooperation agreements, to effectively harness civilian resources for crises.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I agree that it would not have been appropriate to use RORA for the COVID-19 pandemic, given that the Act is a rather blunt tool which is meant more for wartime scenarios than a public health crisis.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In any case, RORA does not appear to give the Government the authority to ask the private sector to prioritise orders from the Government, short of requisitioning the entire line of services.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, it is not clear the Government can ask a company to prioritise orders from the Government for the manufacturing of masks without requisitioning and running the entire mask production facility on its own.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I now turn to the role, during the pandemic, played by one major local company – Temasek Holdings.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Temasek-linked companies played an outsized role during the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Almost all the private sector partners named in the White Paper are Temasek-linked companies.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The White Paper stated that private sector companies like Temasek were indispensable sources of support during COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This may point to an over-dependence on the Temasek ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Would it be better to diversify the base of private sector partners that can support the national effort in times of crises?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The White Paper stated that while Temasek's main goal remains to deliver long-term returns on its assets, it plays a unique role in supporting a robust portfolio of local companies that can anchor important capabilities for Singapore in a crisis.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Does Temasek have goals other than to deliver long-term returns on its assets?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Is this unique role part of the Government's mandate for this Fifth Schedule company?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Notwithstanding the absence of a Committee of Inquiry, which the Workers' Party had called for, we still have many lessons to learn from in the White Paper and this debate.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
