text: For the sake of our future generations who may have to go through catastrophic pandemics like these, we have to both learn and implement these lessons.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In this spirit, Sir, I support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A silver lining of this difficult period is that it shone the spotlight on the invisible in our community.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One such group is our low-wage migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I received desperate messages from workers confined in their dormitories, photos of poor living conditions and photos of poor quality of food.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But COVID-19 also showed how the community came together to help our migrant friends and to address many of these problems that existed for many years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: During the pandemic, we made great strides in improving dormitory conditions and enforcing electronic payment of salaries.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Government and the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) have worked very hard to make these changes a reality with the support from civil society.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The pandemic showed us that many things which we previously thought were impossible could in fact be done with willpower and collaboration between the Government and civil society.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But many of the problems that our migrant workers face will not.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I want to celebrate our wins in my speech today in improving dormitory conditions and enforcing electronic payment and partnership between the Government and civil society.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But I also hope that we do not take this progress for granted.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The pandemic was a painful lesson that the fight for good living conditions and electronic payments are not just issues that are good for our migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They are also good for the Government, for employers and for public health.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope we do not unlearn these lessons and use the momentum from COVID-19 to continue our fight for a more inclusive and fairer Singapore for our migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The first win I hope to celebrate is the progress that we have made in improving dormitory conditions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I first spoke up in 2017 about the living conditions of migrant workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our migrant friends leave their homes to build and clean ours.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The least we can do is give them proper homes in Singapore while they are here.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Before COVID-19, there were an average of 12 to 16 residents per room.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Their beds, which were usually double-decker beds, could be crammed together without any minimum spacing between beds.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Each resident usually had less than 3.5 square metres of living space.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Sleeping spaces and communal facilities for cooking, dining and laundry did not have to be separated.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Up to 15 residents could share one set of common toilets.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Imagine being confined in this space with nowhere to go for months.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad this has now changed for some workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After a comprehensive review of existing dormitory standards, we have now improved standards for new dormitories.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These are improvements that civil society has been calling for.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Today, they are a reality – but only for some workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While new dormitories after September 2021 must comply with the new dormitory standards, existing dormitories or those before September 2021 can operate based on past standards.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We reviewed dormitory conditions and decided 3.5 square metres per person and 15 residents to a common toilet is unacceptable.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We cannot say these standards are unacceptable for some but continue to live with these standards for others.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that MOM is looking into how existing infrastructure can be converted to meet the updated standards.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope we can set a concrete timeline for all dormitories to meet these minimum standards.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Again, I hope it does not take another pandemic for living conditions to improve further.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The second win is increased enforcement of electronic payment of salaries.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Electronic payment protects low-wage migrant workers against underpayment or illegal kickbacks by creating a paper trail.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I first spoke up in 2016 for electronic payment for Work Permit holders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At that point of time, MOM's response was that electronic payments could not be made mandatory.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This was because of difficulties in maintaining minimum bank balances.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We were stuck at only about two-thirds of all workers receiving salaries electronically for years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When COVID-19 struck, electronic payment was made mandatory for workers in dormitories because employers had no other way of accessing workers who were in lockdown.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It took a pandemic for us to achieve the last mile in electronic payment for workers in dormitories.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While we celebrate this win, let us not forget that we are only talking about workers in dormitories.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What about other workers not living in dormitories?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MOM has said that electronic payments help prevent salary disputes as there are digital records for each transaction.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This benefit applies workers whether or not they live in dormitories.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have proven that it is possible for virtually all workers living in dormitories to be electronically paid.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Last, the final win that I hope to celebrate is the strong partnership that we have forged between the Government and civil society through this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many, many NGOs and ground-up initiatives sprung up to support our workers on all fronts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In times of need, we saw how the Government and civil society can work as one and complement each other's efforts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It was a win-win partnership and can continue to be.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As our work for migrant workers continue beyond COVID-19, so should this partnership.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope we maintain the channels of communication and continue the collaboration between the Government and civil society for migrant workers issues – in fact, for all other issues as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I also hope that we ride on the momentum of the progress we have made and continue to improve conditions for our migrant friends.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I declare that I am a council member of the Singapore Business Federation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Before proceeding with my speech, I will ask us to remember for a second all who have succumbed to COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The business community is glad to see that we did not waste the crisis and that the Government chose to professionally and honestly reflect and learn from the events and the actions taken, including the U-turns that had to be made along the way.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The frank analysis on what we did well and what could have been done better provides valuable takeaways for us as a country to handle the next pandemic.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Overall, Singapore has done well in protecting both lives and livelihoods.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In an August 2022 Pew Research Center Survey involving 19 countries, including Singapore, it was found that many countries believed the pandemic has revealed weaknesses or strengths in their political systems.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In the US, the Netherlands, Greece, Germany, Japan, Australia and South Korea, the majority of their people see their countries struggling to handle the COVID-19 outbreak in ways that reveal political weakness.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Only in Singapore, Hungary, Israel and Sweden does the majority feel the opposite, that the way their country has handled the COVID-19 virus outbreak highlights their country's political strengths.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: At the end of the day, it is the high trust and confidence that Singaporeans have in one another and in our leaders that have gotten us through the crisis of a generation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And having our reserves was a real blessing.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For the rest of my speech, I will speak on the key impressions of the White Paper from the various trade associations and chambers (TAC) leaders I engaged with.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Consistently, the business community has brought up the Jobs Support Scheme (JSS) as the lifesaver for many companies, especially the SMEs.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: To quote Mr Farid Khan, President of the Singapore Malay Chamber of Commerce and Industry: "The swift action taken by the Government in implementing this scheme has undoubtedly saved jobs and businesses." In parallel, businesses, especially SMEs, are grateful to the Government for the quick rollout of the temporary relief measures, including rental rebates, bridging loan programmes, deferment of loan repayments, access to credit and so on.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: All these measures, which were urgently needed, were passed into legislation in record time.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Looking back, Mr Kurt Wee, President of the Association of Small and Medium Enterprises (ASME), said: "COVID-19 brought unprecedented collaboration and cooperation between SMEs and Government.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Coordination with ESG was almost on a daily basis, at times, with two to three advisories being disseminated to the business ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: TACs played a critical information bridge hand-in-hand with Government to usher the whole ecosystem throughout the crisis.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It was also an event that demonstrated the strength of the 4G team, which businesses highly recognise and appreciate." Add to that, Government support to help businesses to pivot to e-payment to e-commerce and to reach customers online was transformational for many businesses, but, for many others, it was a lifesaver.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: There were several industries that were particularly hard-hit during COVID-19 and I asked three of them for their perspectives.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Given that, in general, 90% of hotel business comes from international travel, with the closure of our borders and subsequent border restriction measures, this industry was severely impacted.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This, in turn, ensured that the industry had talents to restart effectively when recovery eventually came.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, the rollout of the Enhanced Training Support package by the Government worked really well for the industry as hotels could optimise the downtime to upskill and reskill their employees to cater to a post-COVID-19 tourism landscape.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Ms Kwee shared how all the hotels stepped forward swiftly to repurpose their properties into isolation facilities to help our nation fight against COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I am sure all of us in this Chamber will join the Singapore Hotel Association (SHA) to express our gratitude to all hotel employees, especially the frontliners, who very quickly adapted to their service delivery to offer compassion and care to guests who had to undergo isolation, quarantine or SHN.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Ms Kwee said: "Hotels have made good use of the crisis by enhancing manpower capabilities and adopting technology solutions to accelerate their transformation journey.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: With the support from the Government, the industry has emerged stronger from this crisis of a generation." The next industry that was badly affected by COVID-19 was the construction industry.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The President of Real Estate Developers' Association of Singapore (REDAS), Mr Chia Ngiang Hong, recalled the chaotic condition at the beginning of COVID-19 breakout due to the lack of direction and coordination among the various Government agencies.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I quote Mr Chia Ngiang Hong: "We agree with the finding in the White Paper that the handling of migrant workers was rather disappointing.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: As migrant workers are a lifeline to the construction industry, the impact to the industry and consequences were quite significant, as evidenced by the long delays in many construction projects and the collapse of a few big contractors.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The reopening of worksites after the stabilisation of the migrant worker situation was rather painful, with volumes of new rules and requirements resulting in painfully slow progress on sites.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Fortunately, Minister Desmond Lee stepped in to personally supervise the situation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: With his very regular meetings with relevant stakeholders and agencies and very frank exchanges of views and feedback, the situation recovered well and inched towards normalcy.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In partnership with MOM, the Singapore Business Federation (SBF) foundation, with the support of our SBF members, set up MigrantWell, an IPC charity, to establish one of the centres, St Andrew's Migrant Worker Medical Centre, at Penjuru Walk.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: MigrantWell is also providing care gaps, for example, in dental care for pain management, rehab physiotherapy and mental wellness for our migrant workers.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Govindaraj Mathiyalagan, a migrant worker with BJ Harvest Services, joined us at the launch of MigrantWell and shared that he and his fellow migrant workers are thankful to Singapore for doing this for them.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The silver lining of COVID-19 is that, through the dormitory saga, Singaporeans are now more aware of the contributions of our 600,000 to 700,000 migrant workers whose lives are just as precious as our own.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: These are people who are here in Singapore to earn an honest living to support their families back home.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: During COVID-19, when the plight of migrant workers came to the forefront, Singaporeans and residents opened their hearts and their wallets with generous donations with care packs and warm meals for our migrant workers.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Third, I would like to speak about the public transport industry.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: During COVID-19, among the heroes of our frontline workers include our 21,000 public transport workers.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding that I am involved with the Public Transport Council, I submit to you that our public transport workers, as do our healthcare workers and all the other frontline workers, deserve our heartfelt appreciation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The Land Transport Authority (LTA) and the public transport operators kept our buses and trains running so that our healthcare workers and essential workforce can get to where they need to get to, to save lives, to connect Singaporeans to their families even during the phases when it was only two per household allowed, to keep Singapore humming in spite of the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Our public transport workers put our commuters before self and worked tirelessly with a smile.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: When Malaysia announced the closing of borders, our public transport operators (PTOs) worked around the clock to find accommodation to house our Malaysian bus captains and engineers.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: When the vaccination programme was launched, our public transport workers were given priority access to vaccines.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And when there were concerns with the mental well-being of the public transport workers, especially the foreign workforce having to be away from their family and loved ones for prolonged periods, the PTOs leaned in.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The CEO of SMRT, Mr Ngien Hoon Ping, shared how SMRT stepped up their engagement with the staff and provided strong support to the team throughout to maintain high staff morale.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: During the pandemic, it became also more important than ever to promote a caring and inclusive public transport experience and the PTOs leaned in.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The CEO of SBS Transit, Mr Jeffrey Sim, shared how SBS Transit staff partnered Dementia Singapore and rolled out the "Find Your Way" initiative to make bus interchanges and MRT stations frequented by seniors more friendly for them.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It was a judgement call not without reason.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: However, the implication is that many of our EP holders had to endure prolonged family separation and disruption to their work or schooling for the children.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Per Magnusson, Immediate Past President of the Singapore International Chambers of Commerce, shared with me that the White Paper, having included this issue and suggested improvements to better handle this segment of the community who also had their homes here, makes the already excellent report an outstanding one.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: He said, and I quote: "Singapore did a great job at handling the difficult situation during COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The international community was especially impressed with the equal approach, whether Singaporean or not, to vaccinations during COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Even more importantly, it shows an open and eager attitude towards learning from what went well and what could be improved." Last but not least, I would like to speak to what I believe has saved jobs and livelihoods and prevented lost cohorts of young people who graduated during the COVID-19 years and, that is, the SGUnited Jobs and Skills programme.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It was a good thing that the National Jobs Council was already in place, pre-COVID-19, to help workers acquire new skills and competencies necessary for adapting to the changing business landscape.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Amid the COVID-19 situation, MOM very quickly was able to roll out the SGUnited Jobs and Skills Package, which helped local jobseekers access jobs, company-hosted traineeships and attachments, as well as training opportunities.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The common feedback which SBF received from companies is that both the SGUnited traineeships for fresh graduates in 2020 and 2021 and the current SGUnited Mid-Career Pathways for mature individuals are useful in two ways: (1) helping companies lower their risk in taking near-fit on non-fit individuals through the six to nine months of attachment before offering them permanent jobs and (2) helping fresh graduates and mature individuals secure opportunities to get permanent jobs.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: SGUnited skills have also provided very good support for Singaporeans who were displaced due to the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This is not just because of the allowance that the Government gave to the trainees who signed up for the courses, but the skills that they picked up and the employment opportunities that they secured after the course.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The SGUnited skills trainees hired by SP, in fact, contributed to SP scaling up and accelerating the transition to a more digitalised pedagogical model and ready for the post-COVID-19 hybrid model where 20% of class time in lectures are conducted online increasingly, while tutorials are still face-to-face on campus.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And while we did not track where the rest of them went to, the anecdotal feedback from employers is that the SGUT experience is appreciated.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Over the past three years, I am sure most of us would have come across graduates or mid-career professionals who benefited from the SGUnited Jobs and Skills Programme and, even if not said, all are grateful in one way or another.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: SGUnited Jobs and Skills, in my opinion, has become a brand unto itself.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that it is a programme which can have a long tail, even as we are now operating in DORSCON Green.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: One, what is the Government's assessment of the impact of SGUnited Jobs and Skills Package and tripartite efforts in mitigating unemployment and supporting the recovery of the labour market and whether we will continue to do so?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Two, how has the setting up of SGUnited Jobs and Skills Centres in every HDB town been helpful to jobseekers and do we see this as a permanent support for our workforce?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Three, the Job Growth Incentive (JGI) supported businesses and local jobseekers during COVID-19 and was very helpful for a wide pool of jobseekers, especially the unemployed and mature workers.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It can be helpful even in post COVID-19 to motivate and encourage workers to enter certain industries which traditionally may not be attractive or to incentivise employers to invest in certain persons for jobs in their organisation.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How does the Government plan to use tools like JGI and SGUnited Jobs and Skills to correct some of the structural employment misalignment in our industries for our Singaporean workers and also for persons with disabilities and vulnerable jobseekers?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Moving forward, the strengths of our tripartite partnerships must be further leveraged.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: With Budget 2023, business community is assured that the Government will continue to support businesses and workers in their efforts to recover and rebuild from the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It is crucial for the Government to continue to work closely with industry stakeholders, including TACs to develop targeted measures that address the specific needs of businesses and workers in different sectors and industries.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We are blessed to have survived COVID-19 relatively well and have emerged from the pandemic, ready to take on the opportunities ahead of us.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: What is before us unfortunately is not yet clear skies as we grapple with rapid inflation, supply shocks and energy price hikes from the Russian's invasion of Ukraine and the threat of global growth slowdown.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The scares of a financial system meltdown sparked by the Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) and Signature Bank in the US being brought down in the past weeks and quickly spiralling related or otherwise to the near failure of Credit Suisse Bank add further dark clouds looming ahead of us.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I will speak today on our pandemic defence and our national capabilities – our frontliners and our healthcare workers.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In a crisis, we learn something about the world around us and we learn something about ourselves too.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And from the crisis of a generation, we need to learn the lessons of a generation.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because the next pandemic may be Disease X, more severe, more contagious and less forgiving.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The fight against a pandemic does not begin when the virus lands on Singapore soil.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It starts in the preparation – 10 years, 20 years ahead.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And that is what we must do for the road ahead as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We must strengthen our national capabilities ahead of time, across multiple sectors.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We saw what happened in some other parts of the world, when the healthcare system and its supply chains broke down elsewhere, and cost lives and livelihoods and cost hope for many people in other countries.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, can I ask the Minister, what are we doing to strengthen our supply chains internationally?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What is the Ministry of Health (MOH) doing, to work with the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) on this?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Are we mapping our supply chains carefully, not just the superficial layer, but the dependencies?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Are we identifying the acupressure points, the points whereby if the supply chain comes under stress, there is disproportionate impact?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Are we searching for the shatter points – the vulnerable points in our supply chains, so that we can strengthen, defend and protect ourselves better in a crisis?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because you can have three suppliers providing a tender to supply eggs to Singapore, but if the eggs all come from the same upstream source, from the same basket upstream, it is still a concentration risk for us and we need to learn from this.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: On our legal capabilities, in a crisis, our ability to assess the legal situation and the rule of law around the world – that is also how we protect ourselves.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For certain essential goods which Singapore needs to survive in a crisis, can we look better at the legal process of procurement?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I am sure there are international lawyers with experience in the Ministry, our agencies should be able to study this.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And I encourage the Ministry to look at this as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: On our vaccine capabilities, we saw first-hand how important vaccines are; saving Singaporean lives, saving patients, changing what could have been a fatal outcome to a severe disease, a severe disease to a mild illness and protecting fellow Singaporeans and people throughout our island.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There has been talk of "fill-and-finish" production of COVID-19 vaccines. "Fill-and-finish" means filling the containers and vials with vaccine and then finishing the packaging and process for distribution.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But we must ask ourselves, is this good enough or can we aspire to more?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I called for this two years ago, during the debate on the 2021 Budget.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because this capability would be good for Singaporeans, good for Singapore and good for the region and the world.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: On our scientific capabilities, how might we get better at understanding new pandemics, better understanding to make better policy?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For example, in testing for COVID-19, what tests and how often?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: One key early decision was whether to go with ART or PCR tests and in what situations?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Whether a frequent ART swab with instant results, compared to a PCR test that is harder to do which may need a healthcare facility and which cannot be done as often as frequent ART tests at home.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is an important difference – a test which is less sensitive but done very often at high frequency, compared to a more sensitive test which can only be done one at a time, less frequently.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The concept of frequent rapid ART tests at home to supplement PCR tests in healthcare institutions was already being discussed in expert journals such as the New England Journal of Medicine as early as September 2020.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Could Singapore, with hindsight – and hindsight is always 20/20 – have moved earlier on this?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: How could we have opened our assessments and minds more in advance?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Or for that matter, studying how a new virus is transmitted – is it by droplets or airborne?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Is it something we can detect in the surfaces we touch or the air that we breathe?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: International organisations like the World Health Organization (WHO) play an important role.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: They advise countries on whether masks are needed and other such safety measures.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But we must still develop our own capability, in-house, in Singapore, to research and understand new diseases, test the evidence and draw our own conclusions as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: On pandemic surveillance, we need to get better at detecting new germs in the environment.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Not just what we know but what we do not know.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And importantly, to learn about what we do not know and about what we do not yet know.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The Minister in his 2021 reply mentioned technical challenges, such as the complex mix of germs in the environment, complex microbiome.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But we should keep on exploring these new technologies.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This kind of hard work on sewage – I do not think Speaker will allow me to use the Hokkien phrase – this kind of hard work on sewage research can help save Singaporean lives.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is 20 years since Biopolis opened – big investment, biomedical research.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But the investments created jobs and helped Singaporeans to build up skills and knowledge so that when a new virus came, we could understand it faster, sequence the genome faster, and develop our own tests, kits and equipment faster.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Safe and conventional; everyone agrees it should done, the market already thinks it should be done.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We know this, especially when planning for what is over the horizon, beyond a five-year plan, but looking at 10 or 20 years into the future.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We need to make sure that our R&D, our research projects include a diversity of approaches, including research which might not bear fruit straightaway, but which might be useful in 10 to 20 years' time.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Research that can build skills or act as an insurance policy if we face new and unusual challenges in the future.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We also need to strengthen Singapore's artificial intelligence (AI) capability.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It will change how we work, how we analyse data, even how we do research and shape public policy.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Five years ago, during the 2018 Budget debate, I called for Singapore to make a big push towards AI because, for certain key capabilities and skills, it is not good enough to depend on the private sector or outsourcing.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We want to build in-house capabilities, suited for Singapore's needs and to build these skills in-house as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In the five years since then, the world of AI changed as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We now have ChatGPT and GPT-4 has come out.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Computing power has increased with lower energy cost.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We must continue investing in AI to see how it can help us prepare for the next pandemic and strengthen our healthcare system.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our frontliners made many sacrifices during the pandemic.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I remember a young healthcare worker, a young mother, married to another healthcare worker.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: She had has just given birth, newborn baby, born during the pandemic.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But because of concerns about COVID-19 transmission between the husband's healthcare workplace and the wife's healthcare workplace, the husband had to move out of the home right after his wife had given birth, in order to keep her and her colleagues safe.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There were nurses who were kicked out of their homes, evicted at short notice by landlords who were consumed by fear about this new and unusual virus.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And some frontliners were outsourced workers, worried about falling between the cracks because they were not sure who would take responsibility for their care and support, because although they work in a frontline role, their job contract was with an outsourced company and not the frontline organisation.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, we must learn from our people's stories.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: See through the eyes of our people and prepare ourselves better to support our people through the next pandemic.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I want to speak on outsourced workers in hospitals.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our hospital cleaners and healthcare attendants are part of the frontline, together with our medical, nursing, allied health staff, facing COVID-19 together.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our hospital cleaners helped clean the COVID-19 ward, the toilets of a COVID-19 patient in the ward.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our healthcare Ah Mahs – the uncles and aunties, the attendants – they helped transport COVID-19 patients' samples during the pandemic.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In years gone by, these brothers and sisters were hired directly by the public hospitals.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In the era before outsourcing, these workers would have been direct hires and qualified for the bonuses and support which in-house staff received.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This was an important step forward, but the deeper lessons from COVID-19 remain.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In a pandemic, nobody is safe till everybody is safe.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Migrant workers, outsourced workers, gig economy platform workers, informal workers – no one is safe till everyone is safe.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And, importantly, every worker matters, including outsourced workers, because the COVID-19 virus, a pandemic virus, does not ask to read the terms and conditions of your job contract before infecting you, and we need to learn from these lessons of COVID-19.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: As I highlighted during the MOH Budget debate in 2021, the policy reasons for outsourcing hospital cleaners and hospital attendants are not compelling policy reasons.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The demand for hospital cleaners and attendants is not seasonal.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It does not fluctuate that much throughout the year.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Outsourced cleaners already receive protective gear from public hospitals, recognising they are part of the same workplace.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And it also sends a message when our cleaners and hospital attendants are in-house staff.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Your courage, contributions and sacrifice made the difference, got us through this, saved so many lives.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: (In Mandarin):   Many thanks to our frontliners, healthcare workers, public officers.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Through your contributions and sacrifices, we have today’s reopening and sunny skies after the storm.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):   Thank you so much to our public officers, healthcare workers and frontline workers.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: As a community caring for one another, as a community united, as a community of friends from multiple races, languages and religions, we were able to overcome the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: (In English): In Tamil. எங்கள் மனமார்ந்த நன்றி or thank you very much.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Our sincere thanks for all that you have done and all that you continue to do.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, we must continue exercising our imagination, having the imagination to see what challenges may come ahead from over the horizon.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, we must imagine the unthinkable and prepare to confront the unexpected, preparing not in fear, but with imagination, resolve and togetherness, so that no matter what happens in a dangerous world for small countries, nothing and no one will ever knock Singapore down.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Without them, we would not have been able to pull through this crisis.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope we will not forget that and will recognise their contribution by improving their remunerations and working conditions.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The White Paper has laid out a self-appraisal of our handling of the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I wish to add on in areas that I felt had not been addressed or insufficiently addressed.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Based on what is written in the White Paper and the two occasional papers from the Ministry of Finance (MOF) on the COVID-19 Budget measures, what is missing is an assessment on whether each of the different measures was a good use of funds.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In future crises, should they be deployed and, if so, should they be modified?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In particular, I feel that the support given to businesses should have been more discriminate.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As this was a broad-based measure, even companies that continued to be highly profitable throughout the pandemic were included.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is difficult to understand why companies who can afford to continue paying millions of dollars in executive pay should be receiving wage support from taxpayers.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think greater scrutiny is merited on whether we had spent our Reserves prudently.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can learn from the experience of other countries in past crises when banks had to be bailed out, when assistance was given in the form of equity purchase which, subsequently, recovered in share prices, and restrictions were placed on executive pay.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the need for swiftness is paramount, we can, nonetheless, incorporate clawback provisions that will allow us to recover payments made to non-qualifying companies after the crisis is over.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Companies that remained profitable throughout the pandemic, those that turned profitable after the crisis and those who paid excessive executive remuneration should return the grants given.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second point I wish to bring up is inclusivity.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Being an inclusive society means that we need to respect decisions that may be different from ours and protect the freedom of choice, especially medical choices.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There remains a significant segment of our population sceptical about vaccinations and, in particular, the mRNA ones.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the interest of inclusivity and unity, we should respect the choices and decisions made by individuals and continue to engage them.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, some of the policy decisions have instead alienated a segment of our population and caused a division.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, a definite preference for mRNA vaccines was seen when traditional vaccines were approved later and not given the same financial support initially.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I recognise that the Government had good intentions in pushing for the mRNA vaccines.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Initial clinical data showed that mRNA vaccines are more efficacious than traditional vaccines, so, it was justifiably a better use of public funds to use them in the national vaccination campaign.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, since mRNA vaccines are new to many people and not without health risks, especially myocarditis, there are understandable concerns, and adopting a forceful approach would instead foster mistrust and make some people more susceptible to fake news and rumours.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some of the vaccination-differentiated safe management measures (VDS) were too harsh and disproportionate, particularly the ban on the unvaccinated from going back to their workplace even if they tested negative, which threatened many livelihoods.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a point I have raised before in an Adjournment Motion in January 2022.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I urge the Government to look into the circumstances of those who had lost their jobs due to their unvaccinated status.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They have paid a heavier price than average in the country's efforts to get the pandemic under control and I think special consideration in the form of employment assistance and financial compensation is in order.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even today, when VDS have been lifted, many unvaccinated Singaporeans still feel discriminated at the workplace.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, a recent recruitment advertisement from the National University of Singapore (NUS) for an Administrative Executive stated that "Applicants are strongly encouraged to have themselves fully COVID-19 vaccinated to secure successful employment with NUS".

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I continue to feel strongly that an individual's medical choice should not jeopardise their livelihoods.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Where there is no occupational requirement for vaccination, it should not factor into the employment decision or even appear in a recruitment advertisement.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This should be addressed as soon as possible.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope we can uphold the principle that any policy or strategy to tackle a national emergency should unite our people and not divide them.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Lastly, I believe that our efforts to engage the public on the response to the pandemic would have benefited from a more visible involvement from a team of medical experts, instead of a panel comprising mostly of politicians.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If policy decisions on vaccination, COVID-19 treatment and quarantine measures were fronted and explained by a team of doctors and medical experts, it would have lent greater credence and depoliticised the situation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Given the serious and uncertain nature of the pandemic, it was a testament to the hard work, dedication and resilience of our nation, especially our frontline workers, that we pulled through.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We have, before us, the Government's internal review of our response being debated today, from which we all hope to be able to better inform our actions and decisions when facing the next public health crisis.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While we have comments about the way the review has been conducted, I do believe the report is helpful in identifying the lessons we can take away to build back stronger.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, I will touch on some comments and observations about the communications surrounding our pandemic response before speaking about where I feel our focus should be as we move forward to build our resilience as a nation and as a people.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The White Paper states that effective communication and high levels of public trust were crucial in handling the crisis.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, many of us remember being glued to our screens each time the Prime Minister spoke or a press conference was held by the task force, wondering what the latest updates would be and what changes were awaiting us.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, I think it is worth reiterating some observations that I made in my speech in this House in July 2021, just after the second Heightened Alert phase was announced.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It may seem like a distant memory today, but it was a time of great difficulty, especially for our businesses.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The spread of the Delta variant from the breach of our barriers at Changi Airport, along with the Jurong Fishery Port and infamous KTV clusters, meant that our businesses and our restaurants, in particular, had to constantly change plans at short and sharp notice, lurching from trying to adapt their operations to cater from one highly complicated set of rules to the next.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It would also be important to share how the authorities weigh up various factors in deciding what restrictions to impose, along with the level of support that will be meted out to individuals.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While we all acknowledge that it is difficult to set these matters in stone, having more information and understanding about how decisions are made would be important for both businesses and individuals to plan forward and be psychologically prepared for the various ups and downs that come with any large-scale pandemic, like the one we have just come through.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: One even told me that an officer turned up at his house to issue a quarantine order the day after he returned to Singapore, after he had spent much time on the phone with and sending documents to various departments and was already cleared from needing to quarantine earlier that same morning due to being a recently recovered patient.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The shift to home-based quarantines, otherwise known as the Home Recovery Programme, rather than quarantine in dedicated facilities, likewise, also resulted in much confusion and jammed hotlines as worried Singaporeans tried to find out more about the new protocols.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: One area which we also feel warranted more attention in the review and also our future plans has been the impact that COVID-19 has had on the mental well-being of our population and the development of our children.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As I mentioned in the recently concluded Budget debate, we appear to be reporting increased feelings of isolation and loneliness and this has a direct impact on our life and healthy life expectancy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Also, many educators have said that they have noticed our younger children appear to be struggling more with mental health and developmental issues and that the Singapore Youth Epidemiology and Resilience Study found high numbers of youth have reported mental health symptoms.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Just yesterday, The Straits Times reported the findings of a Ministry of Communications and Information (MCI) poll that while most Singaporeans believe they emerged from the pandemic in good shape, more households with children and elderly reported drops in quality of life, compared with the general population.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The pandemic led to job losses, business failures, school closures and families spending extraordinary amounts of time together indoors, which have, in turn, led to unprecedented stress and pushed our coping mechanisms to breaking point.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: On top of everyday anxiety over catching an unknown and possibly fatal illness, individuals, families and businesses have had to cope with movement restrictions and ever-changing rules relating to what we can or cannot do.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I hope that the promised protocols and provisions for mental health for Healthier SG will be made available as a matter of urgency and that they will sensitively take into account the after-effects of COVID-19 and the findings of the Mental Wellness Taskforce.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Even as we move forward from COVID-19, we must not forget to pay special attention to the gaps that were exposed by the pandemic.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A 2021 paper by the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies (RSIS) stated that residents in the lower-income groups were more disproportionately hit by lockdown and movement restrictions and that Malay respondents to the study were more likely to report adverse economic effects as a result of the movement restrictions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These areas bear special attention, as such groups may have fallen further behind, particularly in the wake of the high inflation we have been experiencing over the last year.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, as I mentioned in my speech during the Government's White Paper on Singapore Women's Development, I asked about the effect the pandemic has had on the gender wage gap and the effect of the chronic undervaluing and underpaying of work – paid and unpaid – that is traditionally done by women.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is despite this work being deeply important and essential, as all of us learnt first-hand during the lockdown days in particular.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While we have seen some wage adjustments to various sectors from education and care work, this does not address the hard work that needs to be done to ensure that our structures reflect the great value that we must place on the work that these often invisible and overlooked workers do.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These points have also been backed up by studies and data, such as the United Nations' (UN) findings on the disproportionate adverse effects that COVID-19 had on women and girls, including the negative impact on economic, physical and mental well-being.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There was also concern that women and children were being exposed to higher levels of domestic violence and, indeed, in Singapore, there have been findings that family violence has increased from 2020 to 2022.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I also hope that attention can be given to the still little-known phenomenon that we often refer to as "long COVID".

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is what happens when survivors of COVID-19 find themselves being plagued with a variety of effects long after they have recovered from the acute phase of the illness.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These can range from gastrointestinal problems, fatigue, respiratory symptoms like shortness of breath to cognitive impairments, alongside psychological conditions, such as depression and anxiety.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While findings are mixed, some studies have even suggested that women, older people and those of minority ethnicities appear to be more severely affected.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There is natural concern about economic and health impact, adding to the hidden toll of the pandemic that we must not forget.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While I acknowledge that the condition is poorly understood, complex and variable, the Ministry of Health (MOH) stated in April last year that it did not track the incidences of "long COVID".

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is a missed opportunity, not only because it means many recovered patients, particularly those for whom these after-effects may not be severe, may be suffering in silence, and it affects their productivity, both at home and at the workplace.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: They also do not have access to the treatment and care that they need to have a better quality of life.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It also means we are not capturing data about whether certain groups are more adversely affected.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We are, therefore, missing the chance to be able to provide more efficient, targeted measures of support and education for these groups, to be given the timely and adequate levels of help that they need.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This has implications on the physical and mental well-being of our population, with an impact on our recent moves to a different approach to health and the expected increased care cost burden as our population ages.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, many people I speak to would mention that they are not quite the same after coming down with COVID-19 but are either unaware of or do not understand what "long COVID" is.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: How do we ensure that sufferers are seeking both treatment and help, particularly for those whose livelihoods and abilities to either work or study have been affected by poorer or sub-optimal health?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There is also a sense that weakened immunity post-infection, coupled with the removal of social interventions to curb the spread of COVID-19, has also led to the circulation of more cases of infectious illnesses like upper respiratory tract infections (URTIs) and I hope that we can be mindful of this as we track workplace and educational performance for these affected individuals.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I would also like to seek a clarification.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Now that we have fully shifted to living with COVID-19, I understand and appreciate that the full subsidies previously offered to patients suffering from COVID-19 are being stepped down.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After all, the drugs are meant to be prescribed to high-risk patients who are more likely to be seen in hospital settings.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This included my then-one-year-old when he was warded at KKH after suffering from a COVID-19-related emergency just a little over a year ago.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Your compassion, kindness and understanding never wavered towards a bewildered and confused pandemic baby unused to strangers and foreign environments despite him crying through the night at 15-minute intervals.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This COVID-19 After Action Review (AAR) process provides us with an opportunity to learn and improve for the next pandemic.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: My clarifications on the White Paper will focus on the areas of health and manpower, given my roles in the two Government Parliamentary Committees (GPCs).

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But every country has different traits, such as demographics, population density, geography and so on, that require different approaches to managing pandemics.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, our response should be tailored according to Singapore's unique traits.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is, thus, essential to ensure that we have access to independent data and research to make informed decisions that align with our best interests.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We should not blindly follow the advice of international bodies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Such advice can serve as a general guideline but may not apply to individual countries' interests.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Likewise, the recommendations may only be announced after an incident has happened, making it difficult to implement them in a timely manner.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can a Ministry explain how we can develop access to such independent data and research, especially from overseas?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we develop the capability to evaluate global data and guidance critically, with a view to adapt them to our local context?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can we pre-emptively develop our own guidelines to shield our population from the next pandemic?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Another area of concern is vaccine approvals, given there were many types of vaccines to tackle COVID-19, for instance, mRNA versus non-mRNA, each manufactured by different pharmaceutical companies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Next, Mr Speaker, Sir, I would like to raise several manpower-related questions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Looking back, were safe management measures (SMMs) and mandatory mask wearing sufficient in managing the risk of COVID-19 spreading through the workplaces?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I believe that implementing SMMs can help prevent the spread of diseases in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, their effectiveness depends on both employees and employers following them diligently.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It would, certainly, be too intrusive and resource-intensive to monitor workers to ensure that they wear masks at all times and keep the recommended distance between them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: So, how can we strike a balance in future pandemics to ensure that everyone takes responsibility for good personal hygiene and follow SMMs?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What was the assessment of the support given to these employees?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How did the tripartite partners provide guidance to employers through advisories, like the tripartite advisory on managing excess manpower and responsible retrenchment?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, due to the pandemic, numerous businesses had to downsize, shut down entirely or pivot operations, which led to retrenchments.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How did the Government assist workers who were retrenched, particularly older workers, who face challenges in finding new employment?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What were the lessons learnt and how can we apply these lessons as we move ahead to promote senior employability in the workplaces?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: By addressing these issues, we can improve our approach to manpower management in future pandemics.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is already challenging enough to navigate a pandemic and we should strive to prevent additional job losses and financial insecurity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Three years have passed since the COVID-19 pandemic began.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Yet, many aspects of how we should respond should a novel virus emerge and spread remain uncertain and fiercely debated.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we get our population vaccinated as quickly as possible, without knowing the full side effects and safety aspects of new vaccines?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we build stronger supply chains without overspending, in order to improve our resilience?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Most importantly, how does the Government instil trust whilst making hard policy decisions with little details when the next Disease X hits us?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: COVID-19 brought out tremendous resolve, scientific innovation and individual and collective steadfastness.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But, even so, millions across the globe died and economies were set back around the world.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Disease X could be a similar threat like COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: So, the question remains: what if the next pandemic happens tomorrow?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our experience taught us that things happen quickly with little information.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our Government must have the gumption to make hard policy decisions swiftly, as each decision has huge ramifications on our people, Singapore and for the costs of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This was how it was like in the early days of COVID-19; it is also how it will be like for future pandemics.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To me, this boils down to one thing.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must build and maintain the trust that Singaporeans have in our Government to do the right thing and to do things right.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And we must do that by learning from past pandemics and preparing for our pandemic response now.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It tested our healthcare workers, our companies and small businesses, our workers, our Government and politics, our NGOs and, indeed, every citizen.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The costs and sacrifices were borne unequally, as is the case everywhere in the world that this pandemic touched.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, in the business sector, some companies prospered exceptionally while many SMEs struggled or closed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But what we can say today is that all the key stakeholders in our system, on the whole, pulled together and acted in the best interest of all.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: When we were tested, we rose to that call.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If we had not, the losses and the scars would be far worse today.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic, a great deal of public funding was deployed to engage private healthcare companies to administer vaccinations and to conduct telehealth check-ins and surveillance of quarantine orders and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: No doubt, at the time, it may have been problematic for GPs to have played more of a role in this effort, at least at the initial stage, due to the very slender staffing and administrative resources that most GPs have.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But given the enhancements to the role of GPs that will come about due to Healthier SG, which should see GPs enhance their access to IT and data, for example, I wonder if, in case there is a future pandemic, could GPs play more of a role in the initial response, in terms of vaccination and surveillance?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Citizens would have to travel less, be inconvenienced less and interact less with large crowds of people at collective vaccination centres if they obtain vaccinations at GP clinics.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, anecdotally, it would seem that many GPs are not fully utilised throughout the day in terms of doctor consultation time, though, of course, this is uneven.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But I suspect many would have the capacity to take on more of this sort of a role at certain times a day.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It could be argued that GP clinics lack the manpower and equipment to play such a role.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, manpower and equipment could be deployed to these clinics from a central pool, as needed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It could also be argued that GP clinics lack the physical space to handle large crowds.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, could this not be addressed through scheduling systems that could be run off a centralised IT backbone?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Of course, during the COVID-19 pandemic, we did not have the time to put in place all of these systems and processes to enable GPs to play more of a role in the initial phase.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But for future pandemics, and given the changes we will make for Healthier SG, could we give some thought to how our GP clinics could play more of a role vis-à-vis private healthcare companies?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: All Singaporeans ought to recognise the vital role migrant workers play in our society and all of us should be in favour of treating them with the respect and dignity that should be owed to all workers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In fact, I believe many, if not most, Singaporeans these days strongly favour such principles.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Our health protocols for the next pandemic must include protecting the most vulnerable communities among us.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: They must not be an afterthought in the next health crisis.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: On this note, I am glad that the COVID-19 White Paper does recognise some of these issues.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And I quote from the White Paper: "In retrospect, the early precautions we took in the dormitories were insufficient.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Given the communal living environment, the dormitory outbreak had every possibility of becoming a major disaster.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We should have probed deeper and conducted better and earlier ground surveillance, such as by doing dipstick testing on sample populations to make the most of limited testing resources.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We also had to make a difficult judgement call on when and how to relax movement restrictions on migrant workers living in dormitories.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We could have eased some of the restrictions earlier, especially after most of the workers had been vaccinated and boosted… In the end, we decided to act with an abundance of caution to keep the workers and the broader community safe.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But the extended restrictions did take a toll on their well-being." Before I go on, I should acknowledge that it was good that the White Paper recognised the room for improvement on the migrant worker front.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I also acknowledge Prime Minister Lee's video message to migrant workers during the pandemic, which was helpful.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Widespread infection of the workers could have been mitigated if the Government had taken more decisive action earlier.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In its letter to The Straits Times Forum, TWC2 said, "We call on the Government to announce in advance what plans they have to rehouse workers should clusters break out in dorms.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This would give reassurance to the resident and non-resident community." The outbreaks at the migrant worker dormitories exposed the cramped conditions that they lived in to many members of the general public for the first time and many Singaporeans were shocked.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As an example of the cost to migrant workers of these measures, here is an excerpt from The Guardian newspaper, 17 April 2020, relating to migrant workers in Singapore: "The restrictions, an attempt to reduce further transmission, have left the dormitories even more crowded than usual as only essential workers are permitted to leave.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One construction worker, from Bangladesh, told The Guardian there were long queues to use shared bathrooms…" Also, migrant workers lived under prolonged lockdowns when others in the wider Singaporean community could already move freely, despite their vaccination rate already being higher than the average for Singaporeans, affecting their mental health.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is good that the White Paper acknowledges that this could, perhaps, have been done sooner.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A study conducted by Yale-NUS in 2020 concluded that migrant workers under lockdown conditions in dormitories suffered from higher levels of stress and anxiety.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I also hope that the COVID-19 episode with migrant workers serves as a powerful reminder to all of us to take the well-being and dignity of workers seriously.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In particular, enforcement of rules and norms over all kinds of matters like food quality and access to bank accounts and payslips, for example, and hotlines to aid in enforcement, should be in place and be seen to be working properly by the migrant workers themselves.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In this House, I recently called for rewards for migrant worker whistle-blowers who expose genuine safety lapses.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There are, potentially, many such ideas through which we can improve the system.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And the best generators of ideas are those NGOs who have been working tirelessly and fruitfully to bring migrant worker issues to the forefront of public debate – groups like HOME, TWC2, HealthServe and many others.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I hope the Government will lend an active listening ear to such groups, so that, in future, they will not again become like the mythic Greek princess Cassandra, who was fated to utter true prophecies which no one believed and who had to see her prophecies realised.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For at the end of the day, taking care of migrant workers is an urgent question of social justice and fairness.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As Mahatma Gandhi once said, “The true measure of any society can be found in how it treats its most vulnerable members.” But there is more to it than that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: By taking care of our migrant workers, we may be able to attract the more effective workers to come and work in Singapore, those who have more experience and a track record and who are capable of becoming more productive and perhaps innovative workers and supervisors.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: After all, there is competition for migrant workers from other countries, like the Gulf states for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A robust migrant workers’ rights regime will help us attract workers who can become more skilled and productive and thus help us to reduce the size of the migrant worker population in Singapore, thereby lessening overall population pressures.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And, as I have argued a few times in this House, very skilled tradesmen and technicians from among this migrant worker population should be given an accelerated pathway to Permanent Resident (PR) status and eventually citizenship, so as to strengthen the Singaporean Core in such trade fields.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Next, Mr Speaker, Sir, I would like to touch on the role of non-governmental organisations (NGOs).

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I spoke of the migrant worker NGOs who played such a valuable role in the COVID-19 crisis.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A more general point I would like to make here is that in future pandemics, there can be a stronger role for NGOs as partners, working with the Government to execute initiatives, but also to inform and critique policies and decision-making, and to disseminate accurate information to their communities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The COVID-19 White Paper refers to the role played by some food aid charities, migrant worker charities, PEERS as well as organisations under the People’s Association (PA) umbrella.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, these organisations were, for the most part, referred to as partners in the execution of projects and workstreams.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If a future pandemic or other national crisis happens, I hope the Government can assign a more institutional capacity to involving NGOs who are close to their various constituents on the ground, not only in executing projects but also in formulating and refining policy approaches and in making decisions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I had earlier referred to the pertinent advice that TWC2 had publicly aired back in March 2020, and I believe earlier as well, which we would have done well to heed at that point.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One area where NGOs could play an important role is mental health – something my colleague, Sengkang Member of Parliament Ms He Ting Ru referred to.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic took a heavy toll on the mental health of many Singaporeans and people around the world.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Due to the general fear and anxiety level, the economic devastation felt by some groups of people even as others prospered and having to work from home and learn from home for prolonged periods.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I am aware that the Health Promotion Board (HPB) is developing a national portal for mental health resources to be curated by experts and hosted on HealthHub.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In future pandemics and crises, mental health-related NGOs should be empowered, resourced and given information to reach out and persuade those at risk to use the helping resources available, which is not always an easy task and may best be handled by non-state agencies.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One area also where we can boost our mental health care capacity for future crises is in terms of our population of psychologists.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Government scholarships are one tool to increase the number of trained psychologists in the public sector.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Training to be a clinical psychologist takes as long as that for medical doctors.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Currently, the Healthcare Graduate Studies Award is open to post-graduate courses for Clinical Psychology as one of the 10 other courses of study, such as Audiology, Health Economics and Epidemiology.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: By contrast, the PSC Scholarship for Medicine and Dentistry targets applications for study only in Medicine and Dentistry.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, the number of post-graduate scholarships dedicated to clinical psychology is probably not as high as for medicine and dentistry and there is no clearly targeted number for clinical psychology alone, for the reasons I explained.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And lastly, Mr Speaker, Sir, let me conclude with some observations about the COVID-19 response White Paper itself.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The White Paper appears to be a public communication document.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In terms of format, evidence of academic and analytic rigour as well as granularity of detail, it stands in stark contrast to a different paper that was published in 2010 by academics on Singapore’s H1N1 pandemic response.
