speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: That paper was entitled “Influenza A (H1N1-2009) Pandemic in Singapore – Public Health Control Measures Implemented and Lessons Learnt.” The authors were academics Joanne Tay, Ng Yuek Fan, Jeffrey Cutter and Lyn James.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: No doubt that was an academic paper rather than a Government White Paper, but that paper seems, at the very least, more detailed and, if I may, more clinical in how it marshals facts and uses them to build conclusions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: That paper was also authored by independent academics who drew on interviews with MOH and other officials but did not represent the views of MOH.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And it has a much fuller methodological note.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This would serve the purpose of greater transparency and a fuller and better-informed public debate on what should be the lessons we learn.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But Singapore did not fail the test when called upon to exert ourselves and come together for the greater good.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: That should inspire the current and future generations with a true story of what we can do if we put our minds and hearts to it.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.55 pm.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.36 pm until 4.55 pm.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As the dormitories went into lockdown in April 2020, the Inter-Agency Taskforce supported migrant workers and dormitory operators in the large purpose-built dormitories that each housed several thousands of workers.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: They ensured timely access to food and medical services and looked into the hygiene and cleanliness of each dormitory.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Despite the mammoth task of having to secure and distribute food to tens of thousands of workers on extremely short notice, several misses in food quality, cleanliness at the beginning, the gaps were promptly addressed.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: At the same time, our medical workers dived in full on.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Doctors from various specialisations closed ranks all to serve migrant workers in Accident and Emergency (A&E) wards and mobile clinics, risking their own lives for the migrant workers as they fought a then unknown virus.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Concurrently, NGOs came in to support the well-being of those in the smaller Factory Converted Dormitories (FCDs) across Tuas, Jurong, Kranji, Woodlands and Ubi.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: These amazing organisations include HealthServe, Migrant Workers' Centre, COVID-19 Migrant Support Coalition, Alliance of Guest Workers Outreach and Crisis Relief Alliance.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Volunteers took the effort to walk the grounds, talk to migrant workers to identify where the FCDs were and searched out those with limited access to daily essentials.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: NGOs supplied food to these FCDs where employers did not and went the extra mile to cater to early morning food deliveries during Ramadan, which fell during the lockdown period.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Apart from care packs, some provided SIM cards with data plans so that migrant workers could occupy themselves and stay in touch with their families.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The NGO volunteers also unexpectedly served as community mediators.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Under lockdown conditions, tensions rose in some dormitories between workers across different faiths and nationalities.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I understand from one of the NGOs, that without the volunteers' intervention, one of these conflicts would have led to bloodshed as weapons had been involved.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We must also remember individuals such as Ms Sudesna Roy Chowdhury, then a fresh graduate from medical school.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Within eight hours from the breaking news of widespread infection in the dormitories, she produced a website to provide the English-Bengali translations for clinical consultations.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We shall also not forget the many individuals who have stepped forward to serve as interpreters in medical, formal and informal service settings.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The selfless and collaborative spirit between the Government, medical workers, NGOs and members of the public in the early days saved lives.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Over time, we saw MOM move to make further improvements to the well-being of our migrant workers – updates to accommodation standards, quick and prioritised vaccination roll-outs for migrant workers and the quick development of the FWMOMCare app that gave workers access to prompt and accurate information, including medical services.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: MOM also worked with employers to give workers online access to salary accounts and remittance services, a service that is greatly valued by the migrant workers even till now.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Meanwhile, NGOs continued to support the mental well-being of our migrant workers by organising social activities, celebrations, outings and the provision of tele-counseling services.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Mr Samuel Gift from Alliance of Guest Workers Outreach shared that one positive outcome of this crisis response has been a greater trust in the migrant community for our authorities.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This is credit to MOM's Assurance, Care and Engagement (ACE) Team, who showed up meaningfully for the migrant workers when they needed help.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: One migrant worker shared that they used to worry that if they spoke of any regulatory lapses in the dormitories to MOM, they would lose their jobs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: But because the ACE officer attending to their case took time to build trust, they felt safe to freely share their concerns, knowing that their identities would be kept anonymous.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: To the ACE officers who have laboured much on the ground to care for our migrant workers, what a tremendous difference you have made in the lives of our migrant workers.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: However, the call to improve living conditions in FCDs had been made years before the pandemic started.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In response, MOM announced new and improved living conditions that must be met by FCDs, starting from 1 January 2017.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As NGO volunteers have witnessed while supporting the FCDs during the crisis, many FCDs did not fulfil the above conditions stipulated by MOM.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: It appears then that there has been a lapse in the monitoring and enforcement of these new conditions that FCD operators were supposed to have met since 2017.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: MOM had also launched the DormWatch app in 2018, with the intention for it to be used by migrant workers to give feedback to dormitory operators on issues faced at the dorm.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: However, NGOs reflect that few migrant workers used the app as many were concerned that reporting issues would cause trouble to their employers and hence also put their jobs in jeopardy.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As I understand, the DormWatch app was eventually evolved to be used by dorm operators to manage their list of residents for MOM reporting and will be discontinued later this month in March.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I believe the original intention of the DormWatch app remains relevant today and would serve the migrant workers and dorm operators well.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In leveraging the trust the ACE team has built with the migrant workers since then, may I propose that the ACE team conduct a survey with the migrant workers to better understand how feedback on dormitory issues can be received from them in a manner that they feel safe to provide?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: If an app remains the best means for the workers to give feedback, it could be integrated in the FWMOMCare app that the workers already use on a regular basis.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: To summarise, as FEDA kicks in for the FCDs on 1 April 2023 for the safety and long-term resilience of our migrant workers and Singapore, we must learn from the lapses of 2017 and its impact during the pandemic.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: It is encouraging that we have set in place new regulations and standards.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: But as we have observed, what is needful is the ongoing monitoring and enforcement of regulations over the FCDs as they tend to be most prone to lapses in living conditions and require greater support.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Second, accountability by employers of migrant workers residing in FCDs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As mentioned earlier, at the start of the pandemic, NGOs stepped in to serve migrant workers in FCDs that were left by their employers to fend for themselves.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The question begs – why did it take so long for employers to step in to care for the workers?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Some employers reflected, given the pandemic and lack of business income, that they were financially unable to support the costs of providing food for their workers.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: However, employers could have taken ownership to work with MOM or the NGOs to support the migrant workers in other ways, especially in maintaining lines of open communication, updating the workers with key information or providing assurance of income.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This, instead of leaving the task to NGOs or going off the radar, as it was the case in some FCDs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I would also like to ask MOM two further questions relating to our crisis response moving forward.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Second, how will errant employers be held accountable in the event they abandon care for their workers as they did in this last crisis?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: One of the greatest challenges faced at the start of the crisis was communicating with migrant workers who spoke different languages.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Even NGOs struggled with this, as some were not resourced with volunteers that spoke different languages.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Without a crisis communication system that incorporated the workers' native languages, there was much confusion as quarantine measures saw frequent changes and workers moved from one place to another.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Some workers were uncertain if having COVID-19 meant certain death and if they would be left to perish.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: With the dearth of information in their native tongue, workers sought information from alternative news sources from their home country, which may not have provided accurate reflection of the situation here in Singapore.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The missing communications also negatively impacted the migrant workers' health-seeking behaviours during the onset of the pandemic.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Some workers who felt ill would not seek medical help and continued to head to work, out of fear that their income would be affected.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Clear communications in their native language providing assurance of their income and jobs despite contracting COVID-19 would have made a difference.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I am glad to hear that now, through the FWMOMCare app, essential health information and MOM advisories are now disseminated in the various native languages of the migrant workers.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This recent crisis is a reminder that we must include our migrant worker population in crisis communication, especially when it concerns public health.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I trust we will continue to leverage the app to provide centralised and timely communication to our migrant workers in our next crisis.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As workers from different nations do not always enjoy friendly relations with each other, NGOs have found that in migrant workers' communication, it was helpful and important to have a representative from each nationality staying in each dormitory.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Where this was missing, NGOs faced situations where food or resources were not evenly distributed to workers from other nationalities in the same dormitory, leading to even greater tensions.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Moving forward, MOM could consider the nationality profile of each dormitory and then identify representatives for each nationality.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: These representatives can help with the prompt dissemination of information and fair distribution of resources.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This will support the work of dormitory operators in times of crisis.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We all know that infectious diseases are no respecter of persons.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: They do not discriminate between nationalities, social or work pass statuses.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: May we never forget the good you have shown to our people in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There were countless difficult decisions and tradeoffs made in the fog of war.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But right from the start, we had one overriding objective and that is to protect lives, jobs as well as livelihoods.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We were determined to emerge with a strong and resilient economy and to shield our workers from the full economic brunt of the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We also made a concerted effort to safeguard our migrant workers' health and thankfully, despite the scale of the outbreak in the dormitories, the mortality rate among our migrant workers was very low.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The other silver lining in the dark cloud of this pandemic was witnessing the resilience of our people – one people, standing together, as one nation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It has been a profoundly humbling and heartening experience to see the outpouring of support from the private and people sectors and the indomitable spirit of our workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To our local and foreign workers, our employers, the industry associations, tripartite partners and non-governmental organisations (NGOs) such as the Migrant Workers' Centre (MWC), HealthServe and Hope Initiative Alliance (HIA) and the many more on the list whom Senior Minister of State Zaqy Mohammad will mention tomorrow – thank you, from the bottom of all of our hearts.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Bernard Menon from the MWC, Dr Benjamin Kuan from HealthServe and Reverend Ezekiel Tan from HIA also joined us earlier today.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It has been all of your support, your labours, your sacrifices, together with all the rest, that have weathered us through the storm.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Today, I will reflect on the decisions made, the tradeoffs considered, and the lessons learnt in the Ministry of Manpower (MOM)'s journey in the following areas: one, bringing the outbreak in the migrant worker dormitories under control; two, protecting jobs and livelihoods of our workers; and three, building stronger systems and capabilities for the future.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We were thrust into an uncertain and extremely unpredictable environment in early 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There was a paucity of knowledge about the virus regarding its inherent characteristics and transmission modes at the early stage.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The prevailing expert view in early 2020 was that the COVID-19 virus was closely related to SARS and symptomatic transmission was the main mode of spread.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It was also thought that COVID-19 was spread primarily through droplets rather than airborne transmission.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Some experts were even saying that the pandemic itself would be over by the summer season.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The inherent mutagenic potential of the virus however, resulted in rapid mutations from Alpha to Delta and subsequently Omicron.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Even now, it continues to evolve and it continues to mutate.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We had to respond, we had to adapt quickly, learning continuously in real time, given the uncertainties about the virus.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Drawing from the SARS experience and prevailing expert views about symptomatic transmission, we implemented measures like temperature taking at the migrant worker dormitories and isolation of workers who reported sick with acute respiratory infection (ARI) symptoms.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: At every point in time, our measures were guided by science and the latest evidence available at that moment in time.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We did not pick up on the asymptomatic cases and we were under the impression then, that our measures were sufficient.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Of course, looking back now, we were completely mistaken.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It was only in April 2020 that the infectious disease experts began to realise that COVID-19 could spread asymptomatically.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: By then, the virus was already spreading in the dormitories.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We did not have a clear, comprehensive and timely picture of the workers who were sick, because not everyone reported sick.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There were significant gaps in our understanding of the disease, in testing, in surveillance and in the data and information regarding the location of the workers in the dormitories.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We required the resources and organisation to manage the highly complex operations in the dormitories.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: During that period, we worked closely with dormitory operators, employers, the medical community, NGOs and other community groups, to provide care and support for the migrant workers in the dormitories.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This helped to arrest the spread of COVID-19 in the dormitories.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We knew that the dormitory lockdown put the migrant workers under stress and strain, but if we had not done so, the transmission among migrant workers across the dormitories and into the community would have been much more severe and much more widespread.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: If we had allowed transmission to grow out of control, the situation could have become what we saw in other countries – a large number of cases that may have overwhelmed the entire healthcare system with a high consequent number of deaths.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Thermometers and oximeters were given to migrant workers to monitor their health.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We took care of our migrant workers the best we could, based on what we knew, with the resources that we had, and we ensured that all migrant workers had access to good medical care, help and treatment if needed – timely treatment, if needed.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Here, I would like to put on record our appreciation to many of our selfless healthcare workers from both the public and private healthcare institutions who were among the first to step up and provide medical services to our migrant workers living in dormitories at the start of the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: One exemplary individual, who also came earlier on, during the lunch, I think some Members of the House would have met him.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: One exemplary individual was Dr Muntasir Mannan Choudhury, a hand surgeon with Sengkang General Hospital, who was serving at a medical post in the S11 dormitory in early-2020.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: During the early days of the pandemic where communications with migrant workers were challenging due to language barriers, Dr Muntasir took the initiative and spoke in Bengali using a loud hailer to reassure the residents that their medical needs, their safety and their well-being would be attended to.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In the last three years, he has continued to volunteer his medical services and linguistic capabilities and continued to provide free medical advice to Bengali workers living in smaller dormitories.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: He also gave health talks to large groups of migrant workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: At the time, we did not have many large-scale facilities readily available to de-densify the dormitories.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We knew that conveying COVID-19-positive workers away from COVID-19-naive ones and isolating them was key.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To this end, the Government worked with private sector partners to set up quarantine, isolation and recovery facilities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Forward Assurance Support Teams (FAST teams) were formed, they were deployed at the dormitories to provide direct access to workers to assure them, to care for them and to engage them.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mobile remittance services were also set up to make it convenient for workers to remit monies back home to their loved ones.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As mentioned by Miss Rachel Ong, we recognised that some migrant workers, particularly those in the factory-converted dormitories (FCDs) faced difficulties in accessing food as they typically sourced and cooked their own food.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It was a challenging time for everyone, we appreciate the NGOs stepping in and working with MOM to provide food for the workers where needed.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Workers who could not access food could contact MOM for assistance, while MOM concurrently liaised with employers to take over this responsibility when things stabilised.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The number of migrant workers who were severely ill, for example, requiring intensive care in hospital, was fortuitously low.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In spite of that, regrettably, two workers from the dormitories passed away as a result of COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We had not managed to keep transmission in the dormitories low, but we did our level best at that time, to make sure, alongside with the doctors, that the migrant workers received good medical care and attended to their other needs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The situation could have turned out much worse, but through the collective efforts of multiple stakeholders mentioned earlier, we managed to stave off a potentially worse outcome.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: At this juncture, I must also acknowledge the trust and support given by our migrant workers throughout this period.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It was an immensely difficult time for them because they were worried about COVID-19 and they also worried about the uncertainty for their future.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I am gratified that they trusted the Government to do right by them.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: One of the migrant workers, Mr Hassan Mehadi, conveyed his appreciation to us in a piece of feedback.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: He wrote: "In April 2020, I was brought to Tan Tock Seng Hospital and I was confirmed to be COVID-19-positive.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: When I was there, I saw other Singaporeans who were being treated in the same room as me.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: That gave me a lot of assurance that I would be well taken care of and given the same level of treatment as Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: From the bottom of my heart, I want to thank the Singapore Government and the great healthcare team for taking care of migrant workers like us with so much care and concern." His story reflects the trust, cooperation and the incredible resilience of our migrant workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: With their support, we were able to safeguard their health and their livelihoods.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The mission of the ACE Group was to safeguard the well-being of our migrant workers by enhancing support for their healthcare, housing and social needs while keeping the workers safe during the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our priority continued to be to protect the health and well-being of our migrant workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: ACE established ground presence in the dormitories to assure migrant workers of our continued support.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We set up an infection prevention and control programme working with nurses and FAST teams to teach hand washing, personal hygiene and social distancing.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In addition, we implemented routine testing and quarantine processes to keep the migrant workers safe.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The team also looked after their well-being and recreational needs together with NGOs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We worked with private and public laboratories to increase the frequency of collection of swab samples and expanded capacity for processing of test results, so that we could test more workers more quickly.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This enabled our ACE teams on the ground to identify infected workers and their close contacts quickly and to convey them to recovery and quarantine facilities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We undertook all these measures before vaccination was available, so that the situation in the dormitories would remain safe and stable.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This brought a new sense of confidence and optimism in our ability to respond to this virus.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Vaccination was a key lever in our arsenal in the fight against COVID-19 when it arrived.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: MOM and MOH worked closely together to make vaccination available to migrant workers from March 2021, at the same time as the rollout for the local community.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Informational packages in the migrant workers' native languages were distributed to help them understand the benefits of the vaccination.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Leveraging the networks of our migrant worker volunteers, dormitory operators and NGOs, we were able to reach out to all workers and encourage them to come forward to be vaccinated.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Bringing COVID-19 infection under control in the dormitories was only one piece of the picture.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We had to keep it that way, even as new workers entered Singapore to support our economy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For example, MOM set up one-stop onboard centres so that new workers entering Singapore were brought into a dedicated facility to complete their Stay-Home Notices (SHNs), get the necessary medical examinations, COVID-19 testing, vaccination and orientation programme done all under one roof.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: At the onboard centres, imported cases could be screened out, isolated, managed and contained, so that the disease was not brought into the dormitories.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: With the tightening of border measures due to new variants of concern, various industry associations organised a pilot initiative to test workers and safeguard them from infection at dedicated facilities in their home countries before onward travel to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Once the infrastructure was in place, we were subsequently able to reopen safely and earlier, so that the economy could also restart earlier.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We started bringing back the migrant workers in significantly larger numbers from end 2021.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This was important for many sectors, including the restart of Singapore’s construction efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Senior Minister of State Zaqy Mohamad will make further mention of our efforts in the construction sector.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Members of the House, looking back at the way we contained and managed the outbreak in the dormitories, we asked ourselves – could we have done things differently?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: If all of you recall, at the start, testing capacities were very limited, but I think we could have done more.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We could have done more surveillance through sample testing for the different migrant worker population to detect clusters early.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Masks were very scarce at the start, but we could have ensured some form of facial covering, protective covering or some form of mask were worn by migrant workers to reduce the incidence of transmissions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In the fog of war, we could also have communicated better with the dormitory workers at every stage and every step of the way, to better share information and to assure them on the measures we were taking to protect them.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: MOM will learn from these lessons and we will strive to do better in the future.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This brings me to how we will use the lessons learnt from COVID-19 to build resilience in the dormitories against a future pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The three areas of reforms are: (1) housing resilience in the form of new dormitory standards; (2) healthcare resilience in the form of a new primary healthcare system; and (3) focusing on mental well-being and social support resilience by building awareness of mental health issues and support resources.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As we transit to endemicity, we have continued to review measures on the living arrangements of our dormitory residents as part of enhancing liveability in the dormitories and ensuring that Singapore will be better prepared for future health crises.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Leon Perera asked for NGOs to be engaged.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have engaged with a very broad range of NGOs for these improved standards, including Healthserve and HOME.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Some of these standards include enhanced living and public health such as larger living space per resident, in room wifi, en-suite toilets, better ventilation in rooms and dedicated bed spaces for isolation purposes as well as wastewater surveillance.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Louis Ng earlier spoke about minimum standards in the dormitories.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We are also working closely with stakeholders to develop a plan for existing dormitories to transition to the new improved standards.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This will take into consideration what existing infrastructure in the dormitories today that they can support, as well as the potential disruption to dormitory bed supply, and how this will impact the inflow of migrant workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will announce details of this transition plan later on in the year.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Miss Rachel Ong spoke earlier about the conditions in the Factory Converted Dormitories (FCDs).

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Prior to the pandemic, MOM inspected all FCDs in 2016 and took action against a quarter of them.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Six FCDs were also prosecuted for unacceptable living conditions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This was followed up with another round of inspections for those with poor standards.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Since 2017, 175 FCDs were served with warnings and fines.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Another four were also prosecuted for unacceptable accommodation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But we recognise, beyond punitive measures, that more needs to be done to raise the standards of dormitories, including the FCDs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will continue to strengthen our regulatory levers on dormitory operators.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This will also give MOM additional levers to enforce against the dorm operator.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Other than financial penalties, the Commissioner for FEDA can issue compliance directives to the operator to rectify lapses as well as business restrictive orders which will prohibit operators from taking in new tenants until the operator makes good on all its shortcomings.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They will also provide MOM with the opportunity to innovate and pilot new ideas for public health resilience and dormitory living, to improve the lived experience of migrant workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These initiatives to enhance the standards of the living environment of our migrant workers, will transform the features of the entire migrant worker landscape.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our FAST teams, first deployed during the circuit breaker in 2020, and now under ACE, continue to proactively and regularly visit dormitories to engage migrant workers on their overall well-being and work with both workers and dormitory operators to resolve issues on living conditions in a timely manner.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: At the end of 2022, we have also added a new feature on FWMOMCare, where migrant workers can send a request to talk to MOM via the mobile application.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The FAST officer will then contact the workers directly to address any issue or feedback that the workers may have.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This provides an additional avenue for workers to seek assistance when they face a problem.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: ACE is now a permanent capability to support our migrant workers in their everyday lives and will also have the capability to respond quickly in a future pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In addition to housing resilience, learning from the pandemic, we will also need to strengthen healthcare resilience in the migrant worker community.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We took a holistic approach to redesign the way primary care services were delivered to migrant workers and change the way migrant workers sought care when they are unwell.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: First, we organised workers living in dormitories into six geographical zones all over the country and we appointed Anchor Operators to provide integrated primary medical service at designated Medical Centres and affiliated clinics.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To date, there are 10 medical centres and a network of partnered private clinics serving the population of more than 300,000 workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To bridge language and cultural barriers, the Anchor Operators have put in place multilingual translation capabilities and augmented their clinical teams with healthcare workers who can speak the native languages of our migrant workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: With the PCP, workers can now choose to seek medical consultation 24 hours a day via telemedicine or report sick at their designated regional medical centres for a small co-payment fee.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: With these measures, we help employers provide quality primary care at affordable cost and allow workers to develop better health-seeking habits through accessible medical care.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: At the same time, we are also able to leverage on the new primary healthcare system for public heath surveillance.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The healthcare resilience of our migrant worker community is now significantly strengthened.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As the COVID-19 situation improved in Singapore, we took a careful and calibrated approach to progressively ease restrictions in order to safeguard migrant workers’ health.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We started relaxing movement restrictions from as early as September 2020, but we had to roll back because of the emergence of new variants.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We increased the frequency of such visits to recreation centres and the community significantly, in the latter part of 2021 after the Delta wave had passed and we had assessed that it would be much safer to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We had to constantly make judgement calls on when and how quickly to ease movement restrictions on migrant workers living in dormitories.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: New COVID-19 variants were emerging all the time and there were persistent concerns about vaccine breakthrough and re-infections.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There were also concerns that new variants were getting more infectious while time was needed to assess if there were any changes to disease severity and vaccine effectiveness.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, amid the uncertainty, our considerations were always to prioritise our migrant workers’ safety and ensure that they could continue working, receive their salary and send money home.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Nonetheless, this took a toll on the mental well-being of the migrant workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: However, if we had opened up more quickly and it precipitated another series of large outbreaks, it would have put at risk, again, the health of the migrant workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As it turned out, there were no further COVID-19 fatalities beyond the two in the early phase.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The DAWN task force has since developed resources and raised greater awareness of mental health issues and among our migrant worker community and stakeholders.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Suffice to say that they are meant for primary prevention and then, for that, we have mental and social wellness awareness and promotion.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For secondary prevention, we have identification of at-risk patients and the risk factors, screening for mental health issues, surveillance for the mental health and emotional distress and counselling, and the ramping up of training of para-counsellors.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For tertiary prevention, we have developed a plan for timely escalation of care and, when they recover, the provision of post-intervention support to rehabilitate them back, hence, normalisation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These initiatives have been progressively rolled out over the past two-and-a-half years.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our employers and the dormitory operators form an integral part of the support ecosystem for our workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They are regularly reminded by MOM to look out for the well-being of their workers and encourage closer networks and engagement at work and also in the dormitories.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Appropriate access to care services, such as counselling and community support, was also strengthened.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We would not have been able to build resilience in these areas alone.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It was in this pandemic that we saw the best of Singaporeans, and, indeed, our humanity shone through when we demonstrated care for our neighbours.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We saw NGOs, businesses, migrant workers, local communities step up to provide food and gifts, care and contributions for our migrant workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We learnt how important it was to continually foster these partnerships, as each and every one of these partners made a difference in turning the tide.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will remember these lessons as we build a stronger migrant worker ecosystem, as we work collectively with our many partners to care for our migrant workers and ensure that the migrant workforce remains a productive and pandemic-resilient complement to our workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I am going to spend the next few minutes going through and elaborating on what we are doing to support our local jobs and livelihoods.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Even as we safeguarded the well-being of our migrant workers, our abiding concern was the jobs and livelihoods of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To help workers and employers navigate through the storm, MOM and the tripartite partners acted quickly.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We convened the National Wages Council (NWC) soon after the start of the pandemic in March 2020, to guide employers on how they could sustain their businesses and save jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The tripartite partners also issued and updated numerous advisories on matters ranging from leave arrangements during quarantine, managing excess manpower and responsible retrenchment, to workplace vaccination policies.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The NWC guidelines and many of the advisories were negotiated under pressing timelines but they provided fair and balanced guidance for both workers and employers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This was only possible through and with the trust among the tripartite partners that has been painstakingly built up over the past many decades.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Various members of the NJC, including unions and business leaders, mobilised their respective networks, their expertise and their resources to support jobseekers to enter into new opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng also spoke earlier about assistance to workers who were retrenched.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Where retrenchments were inevitable, the Taskforce for Responsible Retrenchment and Employment Facilitation (RTF) reached out to affected local employees to offer employment support, including the provision of information kits on career resources and job fairs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Workers were also supported through matching of excess manpower across industries, skills upgrading efforts and career coaching and advisory initiatives.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Taken together, the collective efforts of the Government, the unions and the employers achieved significant traction and scale in supporting jobs and livelihood.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In addition, to help self-employed persons whose livelihoods were affected by the period of extraordinary economic uncertainty, we introduced the Self-Employed Persons Income Relief Scheme (SIRS) for self-employed persons with less means and family support.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We appreciate NTUC for stepping forward to help with the appeals for SIRS.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Additional support for self-employed individuals, such as taxi and private hire car drivers, also came in the form of other Government schemes like the COVID-19 Driver Relief Fund.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This support was disbursed by taxi and platform operators, who also helped their drivers with rental relief and commission rates.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These efforts contributed to the recovery of the labour market even before the pandemic ended.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The resident unemployment rate stayed below 5% throughout 2020 even when economic conditions were at their worst and, of course, it eventually recovered to pre-pandemic levels in 2022.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have drawn useful takeaways from the experience of COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: First, we found that accessibility is key to the delivery of employment facilitation services.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The establishment of the SGUnited Jobs and Skills Centres in all 24 HDB towns was accompanied by improved sentiments towards Government employment facilitation, which suggested that the increased accessibility and physical presence of these job matching services could have helped to reduce the anxiety of jobseekers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Post-COVID-19, we have maintained the network of Jobs and Skills Centres as readily accessible touchpoints for jobseekers in the heartlands.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Second, we have expanded the diversity of channels available to support the employment of jobseekers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For example, the new SGUnited Mid-Career Pathways Programme introduced during COVID-19 has allowed employers to evaluate job fit through company attachments and facilitated positive employment outcomes for trainees.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Among those who had completed or exited the programme, around eight in 10 found employment within six months.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Among the trainees who found employment, more than half earned the same or higher wages, compared to the last drawn wages prior to onboarding.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have, therefore, regularised the programme from April 2022 to provide more options to mature jobseekers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Ms Janet Ang asked how the Government intends to use the jobs and skills initiatives to correct structural employment misalignment for vulnerable jobseekers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To do more for specific groups that may need greater support to secure employment, the Government had announced enhancements to the Enabling Employment Credit and also introduced a new Uplifting Employment Credit to encourage employers to hire persons with disabilities and ex-offenders respectively.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Third, and importantly, COVID-19 has also demonstrated that we should and must continue to build on the tripartite trust and partnerships as a key competitive advantage for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our ability to navigate to tide over the worst of the crisis was a testament to the importance of the strong tripartite partnership.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Like the ballast of our ship, strong trust and partnerships will allow Singapore to make steady progress, no matter the winds and waves ahead.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: If Members will bear with me for a few more minutes, I am concluding.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Distilling lessons from the pandemic, we have made permanent structural reforms in our migrant worker management capabilities and the ecosystem of support for the local workforce so as to institutionalise lasting change.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Care for our migrant workers has been reinforced in three ways: first, we have improved standards for migrant worker dormitories and we will be expanding the coverage of FEDA; secondly, we have set up a new primary healthcare system and the Primary Care Plan for migrant workers; and third, we have better capabilities to improve migrant worker mental health with Project DAWN.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For the local workforce, we have enhanced the accessibility and diversity of channels to support jobseekers in securing employment and their career transitions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Above all, we have built and strengthened relationships and networks with both public and private stakeholders to help us weather future storms.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: COVID-19, indeed, fell on us like a heavy storm.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But, together, we have weathered the worst and were able to build back stronger.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The mettle of our workforce was put to the test, and we showcased our resilience by facing the challenges with grit and gumption.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I have said it earlier but let me say it again.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: If not for the sacrifices of each and every one of us here in Singapore, we could have come out of the pandemic in far worse shape.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Stefanie Sun's song, "We will get there", was re-sung by Aisyah Aziz with images of various workers struggling through the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The video tells the story of the many sacrifices all of us made.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Many of us would have felt our stories told by the images interspersed through the video.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As the lyrics go, "We've struggled through the darkest storms, with family and friends.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Together, we'll stand and, in the end, hand in hand, we will get there".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I am not sure if there was enough empirical or scientific basis but after three years of the pandemic, we can finally move on and live with COVID-19 as an endemic disease.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Fortunately, since our decisive opening in 2022 and the resumption to normal lives, we have not seen significant stresses in our healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: By and large, we have moved on, with COVID-19 very much like a normal flu.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Singapore and Singaporeans as a whole went through an extraordinary experience, adapting and overcoming the harsh onslaught of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: On our economy, we went through a roller coaster ride.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Among the worst hit sectors were construction, retail trade, F&B, tourism and airline.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Total employment shrank sharply in 2020 while many self-employed were left with no incomes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The nation came to an almost standstill during the two months of circuit breaker.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I still remember feeling eerie, seeing the streets so empty.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Even in this very Chamber, extraordinary things happened too.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In fact, we now use the pandemic as a time reference, referring to life before COVID-19 and life after COVID-19 – "before COVID-19" as in "BC".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As part of the pre-workshop warm up teaser, the workshop moderator asked participants to share what they were most grateful for in the last three years.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I was most heartened that many participants shared they were most grateful for being a Singaporean during the last three years.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: They felt safe, shielded and were assured that we are well-resourced, both financially and in terms of capabilities to cope with the crisis.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many knew that there is no perfect way to manage such a formidable crisis of this magnitude and scale, yet appreciated the balanced approach we took to manage the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The paper detailed areas that we have done well but also crucially self-evaluated the areas that we could have done better.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There was no glossing over of shortcomings and almost every area where we can take issue with are covered in the paper.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Wong's speech as well as Minister Tan See Leng's speech have also elaborated some of these shortcomings.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This honest and reflective approach is important as we take stock of the whole-of-Government response to the pandemic, reaffirm and reinforce what we have done well, but also initiate necessary follow-up actions to address learning points to strengthen our response to future pandemic.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Our healthcare system withstood the stresses of the crisis well, albeit with considerable strain.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Consequently, NPHL had the ability to develop our very own polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test kits early in the pandemic and NCID was able to attend to early serious COVID-19 patients and saved lives.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Our entire healthcare ecosystem, both public and private, were mobilised to respond as an integrated health system to this unprecedented public health crisis.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I read in the media that even retired nurses and medical professionals stepped forward to join the frontline healthcare warriors in the battle to save lives.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Another remarkable area that I wanted to highlight is how we as a small, tiny island ensured that vital supplies were not disrupted despite the lockdowns, the border controls, the intense competition for scarce items and the export restrictions by many countries.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I can imagine the uphill tasks our frontline procurement officers faced securing large amounts of sought after critical items like medical equipment and supplies, test kits, masks and a whole range of food and daily necessities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It must have required the officers to use whatever conventional or unconventional means to secure these supplies, possibly having to deviate from the usual standard operating procedures (SOPs) and instruction manuals (IMs) in such emergency situations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It was mentioned by Deputy Prime Minister Wong as well as Minister Tan.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Allow me to also express my views on the two.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Among the most severe situations or high stress points was the outbreak at the migrant workers' dormitories in this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The White Paper called it a "crisis within a crisis".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Given the communal living arrangements, the dormitories inevitably became a high-risk area in a highly infectious disease outbreak.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Fortunately, as what Minister Tan has said, the morbidity and the mortality rate has been very low, notwithstanding the scale of the outbreak there.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I noted that MOM has since taken significant steps to improve the dormitories' environment, with new standards and continuous efforts to de-risk the exposures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As what Minister Tan said, even with significant improvements in the living environment of these workers, we ought to still continue to institute more defensive measures such as having self-segregating features in the event of a disease outbreak, contingency plans for quarantine arrangements as well as a business continuity plan (BCP) set up.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We must continue to review and weigh the trade-offs of our dependency.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The White Paper highlighted the shortage of masks that we had to contend with.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Given our domestic constraints, both labour as well as costs, as well as our shift towards more high-value-adding advance manufacturing, producing medical masks domestically may not be economically viable.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is difficult to compete with countries with a much lower cost structure.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Hence, our medical masks are almost dependent on imports.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In an ironic way, thanks to the transboundary haze situation that we faced years ago, the Government does stockpile a significant quantity of masks, which helped us meet the initial wave of demand when the outbreak happened.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But the stockpile quantity was never able to meet that sort of daily consumption demand needed for the entire population in a long-drawn pandemic.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We scrambled to assemble our own mask producing capabilities so that we can produce some of our mask needs locally.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Credit goes to the MTI, Enterprise Singapore and the relevant agencies for getting the mask producing factory up in double quick time, just so that we have some additional back-up supplies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: However, for the production to be viable, it would require some domestic anchor orders or offtake from the Government so that there is a base level production volume to work with – very much like how the Public Utilities Board (PUB) undertook the liability to buy a certain quantity of desalinated water from water production companies even though it cost more than treated water.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In this regard, can I suggest two related supportive initiatives?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This would not only create some local demand for masks but also help to reduce the spread of other airborne diseases such as flu, cold, cough and other influenza.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Studies indicated that there was a sharp decline in flu cases during the pandemic, which could be attributed in part to mask wearing.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Just last week, The Straits Times reported that doctors saw a rise of as much as 30% increase in flu cases in the last few months as we unwind almost all our COVID-19 measures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: If less of our population were infected with flu and cold, we could free up demand for primary care clinics like polyclinics for other patients.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There will be more healthy people around, which in turn leads to overall savings on healthcare costs for the population.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This could be a part of the Healthier SG movement.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The grassroots volunteers rose to the occasion in various pandemic operations in the community.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For example, just in Bukit Panjang, we distributed masks and hand sanitisers to more than 50,000 residents, delivered more than 4,000 care packs, groceries and social assistance to residents affected by COVID-19, installed 5,585 bottles of hand sanitisers at lifts and supported the distribution of more 4,000 TraceTogether tokens.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Our volunteers also reached out to 12,566 seniors to urge them to go for their rounds of vaccinations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I am sure Members in each of their constituencies have done similar things.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These and the many other areas are where our grassroots volunteers have selflessly stepped up in this crisis in carrying out some of these duties while at risk of being infected themselves.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: They made a big difference in the overall health outcomes, providing last mile support and care at the neighbourhood level and, in particular, taking care of those that are vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Money is not everything, but not having the financial means is inconceivable.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: When the pandemic landed upon us, the Government had initially drawn on our current Budget surpluses to fund the urgent expenditures in public health defences and the various support measures for businesses and households.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Given the severity and the magnitude of the crisis, I had expected the Government to do more to support and assist, but I must admit the massiveness and the decisiveness in the series of fiscal interventions were more than I expected.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It once again demonstrated that the Government may well be cautious and prudent in managing its finances during peace time, but when hit with a severe crisis, the Government would not hesitate to use our fiscal firepower in an impactful way to protect lives and livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In essence, in 2020, it is the Government's spending that propped up the entire economy.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: When air traffic dropped to almost zero for a prolonged period of time, our national carrier SIA posted huge full year financial losses in 2020.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Fortunately, the company was able to raise massive cash from their rights issue, with its major shareholder Temasek pledging to exercise all its rights to buy the shares.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I am glad that we have shareholders that saw the strong fundamentals and long-term value of SIA as well as its business growth potential beyond the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We have kept Singaporeans safe, safeguarded the economy and taken care of the overall well-being of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the earlier stages of the pandemic, the Prime Minister addressed the nation at each turning point of the pandemic, updating Singaporeans on where we are and what may lie ahead.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In particular, the 4G leadership led by Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong has shown its mettle in leading Singapore through this crisis of a generation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: (In Mandarin):   COVID-19 is the pandemic of the century.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: COVID-19 did not just present a health and economic crisis, it also presented a social crisis.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Given its unclear origins and elusive transmission pathways, the secretive nature of the virus can lead people to guard against others and focus on self-protection.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: These various factors may lead us to become a society driven by fear, where we may turn on each other for the sake of personal survival.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We have seen severe divisions in some countries over whether to wear masks or to get vaccinated, leading to a failure of implementing preventive measures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We have also seen other countries experience strain on their healthcare system and even ethnic conflicts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The reason we have been able to overcome the pandemic and minimise its social impact is due to the strong collective collaboration and a high level of mutual trust in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: COVID-19 is different from ordinary diseases because of its highly contagious nature.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: When one person falls ill, it affects not only their own health but also the health of others.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Everyone may have their own views on COVID-19, whether to wear masks, whether to get vaccinated, whether students should go to school.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: However, if everyone only considers their own views without regard for others or is unwilling to collaborate collectively, it would be challenging to implement preventive measures with success.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The foundation of collective collaboration lies in the trust between individuals.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: They examined various factors such as a country's healthcare system or medical advice, but these were not the decisive factors in reducing mortality rates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The key factor was the level of trust in society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The high level of trust between people in Singapore is the key to our success in fighting the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: People trust that the Government can handle the crisis in a transparent, honest and scientific manner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Businesses and institutions not only focus on their operations but also consider the health and caregiving responsibilities of their employees, providing them with the confidence that they are being taking care of.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Every individual fulfils and stands by their roles, takes care of their families and cares for others.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It is because of the mutual trust between the Government, businesses, institutions and the people of Singapore that Singapore can harness the energies of everyone, unite in mutual assistance and overcome the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The trust of the people in the Government is not inherent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Trust is earned through years of sincere efforts and practical actions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: When Singapore secured high-quality vaccines, the Prime Minister and ministers took the lead in getting vaccinated and recorded videos for everyone to watch.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: These efforts aimed to reassure the public, build mutual confidence and unite everyone in fighting the pandemic. "Caring for the elderly and young children as one’s own parents and children".

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This has been well reflected in our fight against the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The elderly are most at risk from COVID-19; hence, taking care of them is an important part of our work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: During the circuit breaker period, visits to the elderly were temporarily restricted to minimise virus transmission.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: However, essential services for the elderly continued to operate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Community partners also initiated home visits, delivering cooked meals and necessities to elderly individuals without family support under hygienic and safe conditions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Community partners actively persuaded and guided elderly individuals who had concerns about the vaccine.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We would also like to thank the elderly for their willingness to listen to our advice and receive the vaccines and boosters that we have prioritised for them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This is not an easy task in other countries, especially when the elderly may not have the habit of receiving vaccinations regularly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: There were even instances in other countries where people do not follow government guidelines.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: While the elderly and the families trust the Government and community partners to do the best for them, the Government and the community also empowers the elderly to engage in organic and spontaneous activities, supporting their endeavours and promoting their well-being.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For example, during the pandemic, the daily lives of the elderly were affected by strict restrictions and they were unable to engage in group activities such as going to the hawker centres or the markets or gathering at the coffee shops.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: They had to change their daily routine and engage in home-based activities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Government then specially designed television programmes on nutrition, healthcare and home fitness for them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Active Ageing Committees in some of the communities also purchased portable radio sets to distribute to the elderly for free, enabling beneficiary seniors to be kept up-to-date on COVID-19 news.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The interactive talkshows on the radio also helped our seniors keep loneliness at bay.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Although they are not digital natives, they wanted to learn digital technology to stay connected with their families and friends during the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Seniors Go Digital programme played an important role in this regard, working with community partners in equipping our seniors with the skills to go online.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Many seniors also learned to use WhatsApp to send each other text messages and greetings to keep in contact and check in on each other.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Some even participated in group activities such as celebrating Mid-Autumn Festival and Lunar New Year through Zoom.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: These activities promoted connection among seniors and this enabled them to provide each other with emotional support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Kudos to them for seizing the moment and making the best out of a difficult situation!

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: During the pandemic, we paid special attention to vulnerable families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Government assistance packages and active donations from the public provided care for vulnerable families in Singapore in a comprehensive way.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Through various Budgets, we provided financial assistance as part of an enhanced safety net.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: At the same time, around 200,000 individuals found job opportunities through the SGUnited Jobs and Skills programmes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In the private sector, countless kind-hearted individuals donated generously to support vulnerable communities, social service organisations and charities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Community Chest was able to raise over $87 million from April 2020 to March 2021.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: During the pandemic, schools in some countries were closed for extended periods, resulting in children's studies being delayed by half a year to a year, or even longer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: However, in Singapore, while ensuring our children's health, we were able to keep preschools and schools mostly open, allowing them to continue their education with minimal disruption and with virtually no delay in their learning progress.

speaker: The Minister of State for Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I recall being in Ministry of Education (MOE) meetings when it seemed like the most straightforward solution was just to shut our preschools and schools.
