text: Several industries such as aviation, hospitality and the aerospace industry were brought to a literal standstill, threatening people's livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In 2019, 68.3 million passengers passed through Changi Airport.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The impact of COVID-19 was unprecedented in many ways.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Streets, schools and offices were empty during the circuit breaker.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: People were separated from their loved ones during festivities such as Chinese New Year, Hari Raya Puasa, Deepavali and Christmas.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Even places of worship were empty as we all took the collective responsibility to stop the spread of this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It was indeed the crisis of our generation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The crisis tested our values as a society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It laid bare what we would be willing to do to support one another.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Now that the pandemic has passed, it is an opportune moment to reflect on how we perform as a society and what values will we like to shape the future of our society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Three critical values that emerged during the pandemic were trust, care for each other and the resilience of society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Compliance with Safe Management Measures (SMMs) and guidelines was essential, and it became everyone's responsibility to practice basic hygiene for the greater good.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Additionally, when the guidelines changed during the pandemic, such as group size, distancing and mask wearing, we trusted the view of experts and adapted quickly.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At work, new requirements were implemented due to the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Staff had to be split into two teams to minimise contact between employees.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In factories, even during breaks, workers had to be separated from one another.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Additionally, masks had to be worn by those in high-risk jobs, such as those for our delivery workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In many other countries, even basic needs, such as the wearing of masks, became highly contentious and heavily politicised issues.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We trusted the advice of experts and implemented necessary measures without delay.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: By doing so, we were able to move forward without losing valuable time and energy on unnecessary debates.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The pandemic has brought to light the sacrifices that workers make to support society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Among them are healthcare workers who continued to serve tirelessly even during the early days when little was understood about the virus.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As the number of cases increased, healthcare workers put in longer hours to ensure our healthcare facilities were not going to get overwhelmed.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In addition to healthcare workers, our essential workers, driven by a sense of responsibility, have also made numerous sacrifices to continue serving society despite their own reservations and even those of their families.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Workers in industries such as transportation, platform workers, aerospace and ports, and water and electricity industries, have played a crucial role in keeping our infrastructure running amid these challenging times.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Besides the sacrifices of our workers, care for one another also meant helping those in need of financial support due to the financial challenges brought about by COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Government's financial support for businesses, workers and individuals was unprecedented.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As someone from the aerospace industry, I personally witnessed how the JSS assisted companies to retain workers and allowed companies to use the downtime to reskill our workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Individuals who lost their jobs or are self-employed also received support such as through the COVID-19 Support Grant and Self-Employed Person Income Relief, which provided up to $9,000 to support taxi drivers and platform hire workers and their families through the difficult times.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The SGUnited Jobs and Skills Package also helped redeploy manpower to high-demand areas.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For example, I remember how, with the facilitation by MOM and Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) staff, aerospace workers were reskilled and redeployed to the busy electronics industry.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To help deliver this support, grassroots and union leaders like Ms Jobie Lee from Pasir Ris went online to raise awareness for these support measures.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: During the early stages of the COVID-19 outbreak in Pasir Ris, it was the community that stepped up to provide sustenance to those in need.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Grassroots volunteers such as Mdm Uma, Mr Raymond Phua, Mr Rajeev and Mr Charlie Cheong, all volunteers from Pasir Ris East, were among the first to offer food packs and rations to families who were quarantined at home.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The community's efforts evolved into the Pasir Ris East Care Store, which continues to provide monthly assistance to needy residents.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Additionally, SGUnited Buka Puasa delivered over 300,000 food rations to residents to break their Ramadan fast.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Engineering Good provided laptops to children who had no access, so that these children could continue with remote learning.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Together with the Government support, the unity and generosity of the community played a crucial role in providing sustenance during the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Beyond providing physical support, the community also prioritised mental health and digital connectivity during the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Volunteers and staff from the Silver Generation Office and Active Ageing Centres visited seniors who felt isolated to check on their well-being and to allay their fears about vaccination.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Digital ambassadors were deployed to assist seniors in learning how to use technology such as Zoom, digital payments and WhatsApp to stay connected with loved ones.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Proactive steps were taken to ensure that residents had the necessary mental and emotional support during the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Thirdly, our resilience as a society was integral in our ability to overcome the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Unsurprisingly, our journey through COVID-19 was far from smooth.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At times, we had to re-evaluate SMMs just as they were loosened, such as when we combated the Delta and Omicron variants.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Often, it felt as if we were forced to backpedal even as we thought we had forged ahead.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We moved between the circuit breaker, Phase 2, Phase 2 (Heightened Alert) and the Stabilisation Phase.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This required resilience from our society to stay the course.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The entire education sector had to adapt to home-based learning.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Even religious practices had to make significant changes, such as suspending prayers and booking for prayers at mosques.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These examples show the value of resilience and perseverance and how it had helped us to adapt to changing circumstances.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   Mr Speaker, we have witnessed how the transmission of COVID-19 has drastically changed Singapore's environment.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: From the circuit breaker to Phase Three (Heightened Alert), to Phase Two and back to the Stabilisation Phase, we had to carefully shift these stages to ensure public safety is maintained and Singapore's healthcare system is not overburdened.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Despite being faced with a challenging and uncertain situation, I was proud to see our community display resilience in the face of the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One of the best memories that I recall fondly was when our community joined hands to support healthcare workers during the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: From giving words of encouragement to driving them home from the hospital for free, the COVID-19 crisis has shown our ability to come together and help each other in critical times.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our Malay/Muslim community also exhibited commendable qualities during the COVID-19 pandemic crisis.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many cooperated with various parties to help the needy in this challenging environment.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Spiritually, we did not let the COVID-19 crisis hamper our ability to perform religious obligations.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In fact, we used this opportunity to look for innovative solutions such as performing congregational prayers under SMMs or implementing online classes for madrasah education and Quran reading.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We also understood that religious practices can be adapted to safeguard the well-being of the general public.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While this achievement is certainly worth celebrating, we must also look to the future and prepare ourselves for the next pandemic.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As the Malay proverb goes, "Prepare an umbrella before it rains" – we should also learn what works and what can be improved so that we are better prepared to overcome the next pandemic.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am confident that with Singaporeans’ ability to rally together, we will be able to overcome any challenges that may come our way.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, at this juncture, I would like to express our heartfelt gratitude and appreciation to everyone in Singapore who had contributed and sacrificed in one way or another for the common good of all.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Truly, it is only with each and everyone's effort and commitment to the cause were we able to pull through this crisis which, at times, seemed almost insurmountable.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, there is an eighth lesson that is equally important and also mentioned by fellow Member Mr Seah Kian Peng – a lesson that is hard to pen down, that cannot be taught in textbooks but only learnt.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is the need to anchor, strengthen and build upon the values of our society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Therefore, we must use the same values to guide us not only through the next pandemic but also through other challenges in our volatile and uncertain world.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These values will help us to transform our economy and ensure inclusive growth, providing equal opportunities for everyone.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is too easy to forget these values of our society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Left to chance and on its own, it may deteriorate with time.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When the next pandemic comes, we may not be able to rally together as a society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: COVID-19 is often described as the crisis of our generation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, given the volatility of the world today, it may not be the only crisis for our generation.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Many of us do not remember that there was contact tracing then, too.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: When an engineer in another refinery contracted H1N1, the workers that he spoke to the days before had to go into self-isolation.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Then, the workers in that dormitory room who were working in my jobsite, had to go in as well.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Workers who took the same transport from jobsite, also went into isolation and it was tough to plan our work.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The ideal situation would be for the workers in the same dormitory to work in the same jobsite.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But that is not possible as there will be new hires, resignations and change of jobsites due to work the requirements every week.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Human Resources (HR) staff would see which dormitory had spaces and put workers there.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It was not an easy job, as sometimes, there may not be enough man-year entitlement (MYE) and they will send experienced workers back and re-hire them when MYE is available, but that dorm spot would be filled by other new hires.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: There is probably no ideal, practical solution because every situation is unique in its own way and we cannot have systems that can dynamically adjust all the time.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: However, most businesses will try their best to make things work.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They have to, because their businesses depend on it.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Some initiatives work only in theory, but in reality, can impose a lot of friction and we may be better off not having some of these solutions in the first place.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Hence, businesses must speak up in trade and business dialogues.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Because sometimes, not only are the desired outcomes not achieved, there can also be serious unintended consequences.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We needed better conditions for our workers and be prepared for the next virus and even isolation rooms for chicken pox and flu.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We wanted to factor in the possibility of quarantine by building shared toilets between two rooms, but that would end up building a dormitory for lesser than the 804 persons approved.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The sums began not to add up and did not seem to make any business or efficiency sense.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Businesses have to decide how much contingency is needed.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The more we did, the more we managed the risks downwards, the higher the cost.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Is it worth spending $X million for a scenario that may or may not happen?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This is not unlike how we can be under-insured sometimes.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It is when we are hit by a major illness that we wished we had purchased the insurance when we could.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: If we leave it to businesses, their efforts to prepare will be patchy and that is where the Government needs to step in.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But there must be discussions with the businesses in order to realise the real impact of these policies.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: If we are not careful, it can affect our competitiveness vis-à-vis the region.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: With hindsight, it is always easy to critique and say that one should have done this or that.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But the reality is, every crisis is likely to be different.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: And what we learnt and put in place in the aftermath, may not be wholly applicable in a new pandemic.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: When COVID-19 struck, I was no longer in the process industry but was involved in some work on the ground as a volunteer.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I am grateful to the many people who responded to my Facebook call for mask-making in March 2020 and we received thousands per week.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: On the first day of the circuit breaker, I was outside Mustafa Centre.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The streets were empty, except for the hundreds queuing for food handouts by charities, hotels and one hawker even provided fresh fruit juices.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The workers were stranded, as their flights were cancelled and they were staying in units above the shophouses in the area.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They had no masks and they did not know where to get them.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We gave them care packs with handmade masks.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: After that, I volunteered with Crisis Relief Alliance as the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) had given each Non-Government Organisation (NGO) a list of dormitories to visit.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: There are many Purpose-Built Dorms and it is critical to leverage on these NGOs and other volunteer groups to assist MOM and the authorities to visit them, evaluate the conditions, assess the risks and also to ascertain what the needs might be.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: For me, being a volunteer was the fastest way to get the masks to the dormitories and even for the dormitories I could not visit, I used the headcount in the spreadsheet and threw bags of required masks over the gates.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Many workers gave thumbs up and friendly waves from their windows.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I salute the doctors, nurses, MOM officers and volunteers who went into the dorms in the early days.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) and N95s masks were in short supply, the seriousness of COVID-19 was unclear, there was a lot of fear.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Even as we drove from dorm to dorm, PPE and masks could not be taken off for fear of contamination.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But there was a strong sense of duty, as we moved from room to room to check on workers' mental health and hygiene.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I remember pulling open one huge metal door of a shed to see a COVID-19 case sitting on his bed with heavy equipment all around him.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: He was all smiles and said he was okay.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: He said he had to be considerate to the other people in dormitory and he will stay there until there is ambulance available for pick-up.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The workers could watch movies and kept in touch with their friends and loved ones.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I had great empathy for Malaysian workers in dorms as they chose to stay here because of the Movement Control Order (MCO) but were met with circuit breaker.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: So, even simple things like watching YouTube or ordering Grab food and other transactions were not available for them.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I posted on my Facebook and residents donated food rations at my Tampines Town Council office for them.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: In the outreach work, there were so many officials we met on the ground and they were professional in their efforts and tried to do as much and as quickly as possible.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The patience and forbearance of the workers are to be highly commended too.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It was clear that the foreign workers were aware of what was happening back in their homes and were glad that they were working in Singapore where they were largely treated fairly and reasonably looked after.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: At the local level, I am grateful to our Town Council staff and workers who helped with all the additional work that was suddenly required.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Disinfecting blocks when residents were infected, replenishing hand sanitiser bottles in every lift, enhancing the hygiene regime and many more.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Lastly, I want to recognise the People's Association (PA) staff who worked long hours distributing masks, sanitisers, tokens, temporary relief fund applications and many more.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: They facilitated the first masks distribution without wearing masks nor have sanitisers for the pens that everyone was using to acknowledge collection.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Some did not visit their extended families even after circuit breaker because of their exposure to the many relief schemes.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: My own sense is that there is much that our Government can and should do in any pandemic.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We need to be better, faster and to prepare in "peacetime" before the next outbreak occurs.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But having been involved in the work, it is also quite apparent to me that the Government cannot do everything.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It is not possible to cater for the surge needs now in anticipation of future pandemics – it would be prohibitively expensive for everyone.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We, as a society and community, need to stand up and take action.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This is how a whole-of-society effort is mobilised to deal with a crisis.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: To be fair to ourselves, despite the mistakes and inadequacies we see, when you take a few steps back, you would realise that relative to so many other countries, we have done pretty well.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Please give ourselves a pat on the back.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Singapore's handling of the COVID-19 pandemic, while not perfect, is one of the best in the world.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For those of us who have had loved ones suffer or even pass away in other countries due to a lack of access to vaccination and proper healthcare, we can appreciate how well the Singapore Government has fared.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: However, I am glad that the White Paper not only highlighted what we do well, but also where we fall short and how we can improve in the future.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Today, I wish to focus on how we can better support Persons with Disabilities (PwDs) in future pandemics.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: First, on the commendable efforts to support the disabled.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Whilst the pandemic has affected many, PwDs and their families have been hit harder.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Nonetheless, there are commendable sparks of great work being done.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: SG Enable, the main disability hub of Singapore, started a dedicated COVID-19 resource page on its Enabling Guide website.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Together with Mediacorp, it facilitated C.A.R.E. – or the Care initiative – to provide cooked meals, financial assistance, respite and essentials distribution.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The amazing support by Temasek Foundation throughout the pandemic is well-known.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The Ministry of Education (MOE) also worked closely with the Ministry of Health (MOH), Health Promotion Board (HPB) and the special education (SPED) schools, to run school-based vaccination centres for those who are still in schools.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It learned from the Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS) pandemic and actively included students from SPED schools in its suite of measures to protect them.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Dr Lim Hong Huay and her husband, infectious disease specialist Dr Leong Hoe Nam, Eden School, SuperHero Me, an arts movement, and Lien Foundation, developed an educational resource package to empower children and older PwDs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There are many other commendable efforts in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Elsewhere, in other countries, I have been informed by disability volunteers and caregivers about some good practices in the disability space during the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In one country, PwDs were prioritised to be vaccinated with other vulnerables in Phase 2, after the health professionals.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: PwDs were also earlier included in the home vaccination programme.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They can also get vaccination jabs whilst sitting in a familiar car, in car drive-throughs in one country.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: PwDs were also given priority lanes in the bigger vaccination centres.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Those with needs can request for vaccination and the use of private calm rooms to avoid meltdowns.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Such were the best practices I hear from other countries and I think those are some things Singapore can refer to in our future planning.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What can we do to better support PwDs more effectively in future pandemics?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This should happen at the strategic Inter-Ministerial Task Force (MTF)-level and at the highest operations level.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is crucial to recognise that the well-being of the vulnerable cannot be solely delegated to just one Ministry or dependent on the kindness of others – piecemeal stop-gap measures.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The voices of the vulnerable should be designed to be heard at the highest level upstream and not downstream.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Many individuals are unaware of how to access disability hubs, such as SG Enable, and there may also be barriers, such as language and information technology (IT) proficiency.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: During the pandemic, we have heard of desperate parents who were also worried what the quarantine arrangements of their children would be, should the children get infected.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For adults with disabilities above age 18 who need supervision and escort, many of their families do not know where to turn to, to appeal for special needs measures, such as being accompanied by a familiar adult before and during vaccination.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Neither was it clear that they have options to be vaccinated either at a centre or at home – not to mention the car drive-throughs that I talk about in another country.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Whenever such cases come to my attention, I had often approached and relied on the kindness of public servants and office bearers, such as Senior Parliamentary Secretary Rahayu Mahzam to point me in the right direction.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But outreach has to be more systemic and affected parties need to be confident enough to have their needs heard and responded to.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Besides involving Government agencies, such as the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) and SG Enable for the disabled, there must be a platform to actively engage and consult with disability agencies and advocates to ensure that the unique needs and perspectives of the disabled, their caregivers and their community are highlighted.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We need to tap on mainstream practices, wherever possible, and communicate clearly and widely.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For instance, in matters, such as applying for caregiver escort and supervision during vaccination and quarantines; and in offering the younger disabled options, such as public community vaccination centres; mobile home-based vaccinations and even, if possible, vehicle drive-through centres.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, universal design, including the disabled; upstream, not downstream.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Like many others, I feel so blessed to be in Singapore for a time such as this.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Let us all work together to ensure that no one, indeed, is left behind.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Many Members have expressed appreciation to various segments, including our healthcare workers, our private and people sectors, our own citizens doing their part in their own way.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In my speech, Sir, I would like to express gratitude to our public servants.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It has often been mentioned in this debate that, with hindsight, everything is clear.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: And criticism, taken correctly, including self-criticism, lends itself to identifying weaknesses, improving capabilities and doing better in the future.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But as the hon Minister of State Sun Xueling said yesterday, it is the actions of the man in the arena, when he is in the arena with dust, sweat and blood on his face, that determines the outcome of the battle.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, in this battle, the gladiator was blindfolded because we were dealing with an enemy of which little was known.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: So, it should not be unexpected that there was a good amount of shifting and adjusting as we understood more and even some backtracking in some cases.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I thought I should share my experience as a trade associations and chambers (TAC) representative of an essential service during the pandemic, who worked with various Government bodies.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: There were significant measures imposed on these workers as well as their employers, who had to ensure that the proper procedures were implemented on the ground; that PPE was made available; and that they complied with administrative requirements imposed by the Government.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: For example, during the circuit breaker, employers had to seek approval from the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) for quotas for the number of workers who could be deployed on site.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: These had to be sought and updated on a daily basis, with the names of the workers on site provided.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It proved to be an administratively onerous and unwieldy system.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This and other impositions, presented an administrative burden on employers who had to juggle manpower constraints and day-to-day operations that had changed rapidly due to new requirements in access control, like temperature taking, with a genuine desire to protect their workers and to comply with Government regulations.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The agencies I worked with, in particular, were Enterprise Singapore, the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) and MTI, and at varying levels of staff seniority.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I have several observations working with these Government bodies in respect of an essential service industry deploying a large manpower base.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: First, I found that these agencies made considerable effort to reach out to explain the new measures, to provide updates and, where necessary, to carry out Zoom briefings.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: During the circuit breaker, I received updates almost on a daily basis.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: As a result of all the information coming to my TAC, we were empowered to ourselves send daily updates to our members.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: These communications involved not only information on the measures to be taken on the ground but also schemes that were concurrently being rolled out, like the enterprise financing schemes and support for digital solutions by IMDA.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Second, the officers whom I was liaising with were very responsive.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that Enterprise Singapore officers from all departments and at all seniorities were roped in to man the lines.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I will confess, Sir, that probably not an insignificant number of these calls were made by my own TAC staff.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The officers I was liaising with were also easily contactable by phone, WhatsApp messages and Zoom.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, they were also contactable and working day and night, weekday and weekend.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: My third observation was that not only were they contactable, but that they were also working actively to address our concerns and many accommodations were made on the fly.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I mentioned earlier, one of the more administratively onerous requirements during the circuit breaker the employers faced – the need to seek approval from MTI for the headcount quotas of on-site workers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Employers had urgently approached my TAC that they had received approvals for headcounts far less than what they had requested for.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Another employer that was providing services to foreign embassies' data centres and dormitories, requested for a quota of 729 but was granted approval for only 409.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This meant that these companies did not have approval for the headcount they needed to carry out the very measures that had been rolled out and that were required by the Government and what their clients had engaged them for.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, I understood that this portal and the system had been rolled out for all Singapore companies.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But for employers on the ground, receiving such a reduced quota was extremely frustrating and shocking.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: What made it more difficult was that helplines could not give them a definitive solution as to how to increase the allocated headcount, other than to submit an appeal through the GoBusiness platform.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Because these quotas were given on a daily basis, employers had literally no time to react or to wait for appeal results.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Even worse, some of these appeals resulted in less headcount being approved or just a marginal increase.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: To add to these troubles, MOM also rolled out an SGWorkPass app for foreign workers at the same time.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Many workers who were approved on the MTI platform appeared not to be approved in the SGWorkPass app at the same time.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: We raised these issues with MHA and Enterprise Singapore and asked for them to urgently look into it.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Both MHA and Enterprise Singapore also assured us that security officers could still be deployed, while MHA and Enterprise Singapore worked with MTI on the headcount approvals.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: All this, Sir, was done on a Sunday – specifically, 3 May 2020.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Eventually, my TAC worked with MHA and MTI, even down to the headcounts for individual employers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: These, Sir, are examples of precisely the shifting and adjusting that were being done by our public servants as the situation unfolded, as feedback was coming in and as it became apparent that changes had to be made to some of the Government's requirements.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The security industry, because we have seen the successful effects of our feedback, and I, personally, come out of this pandemic experience with a greater appreciation and respect for our public servants.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Public servants, like Mr Dhruv Ang from Enterprise Singapore, who actively reached out and acted as a coordinator for us across various Government agencies.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Jonathan Mark Capel from MHA, who swiftly and tirelessly supported our companies and their operational needs.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Albert Tsui and Mr Robbie Poo from MTI, who worked with us on the headcount quotas.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: But, Sir, it is made up of individuals, many of whom have contributed so much to the pandemic response effort and who have made a real difference.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The hon Member Liang Eng Hwa mentioned yesterday and commended the considerable effort by Government officers to secure vaccines and masks.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: If we look at the sheer scale of Government intervention, including for businesses and jobs, the effort put in by our Public Service must have been herculean.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This would have taken tremendous hard work under trying and urgent conditions.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Let us also not forget our diplomats overseas, many of whom were stationed in countries where the pandemic situation was far worse than in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I would like to express my gratitude to all our public servants who worked hard and were instrumental in getting us through the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This ensures that the Government will be able to focus on dealing with the critical and urgent issues in the crisis, without being distracted by political challenges and considerations.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It will also help to bring our people together instead of sowing division.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The Workers' Party's stance on this is patently responsible and it is the type of politics that we want to see in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This is a position that Mr Pritam Singh had expressed at the start of the pandemic and I am heartened that he has repeated it in this debate.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It gives me confidence, Sir, and it should give all Singaporeans confidence that, in times of crisis, we will unite as a country, as a society and as a polity.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In my speech today, I aim to support the White Paper, while highlighting a few areas – our healthcare workers, teachers, mental health and asatizahs.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Healthcare workers, in particular, have been on the frontline of this battle, working tirelessly to provide care and support to those who need it most.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Their selflessness, dedication, hard work and sacrifice have inspired us all and we owe them a debt of gratitude.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, there were reports of healthcare workers being subjected to verbal and physical abuse, online and offline; harassment and discrimination, due to fear and misinformation surrounding the pandemic.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope that the recommendations can be implemented soon and practised, as we create a new norm.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Let this be a new norm where abuse and harassment have no space in our society.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: To me, they are as good as frontliners.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I applaud the Government's stance to keep schools open and ensure that education continues.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our teachers more than rose to the occasion to ensure that learning continued even under tremendous pressure.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They had to quickly adapt to new teaching methods and find ways to engage their students in a challenging and constantly changing environment.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They have demonstrated resilience and dedication to their students' education, ensuring that the next generation of leaders can thrive in a post-pandemic world.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: During the pandemic, the sudden shift to online learning and the need to adopt new teaching methods became a burden to some teachers, especially when the Singapore Student Learning System (SLS) broke down intermittently.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Parents became anxious and when the system failed, the teachers became anxious and came under pressure too.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In that regard, we should consider setting up multiple online learning platforms, similar to SLS but different.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Much like food resilience, we now want to have education resilience.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Training for both teachers and students should continue and we must encourage the usage of Home-Based Learning (HBL) as a new norm, especially for Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs).

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This will sufficiently prepare our systems and human capabilities, if and when any other pandemic strikes.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Regardless, they understood the importance and went on to do any other additional jobs and duties.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The Government must provide support and resources to teachers to help them navigate the challenges posed by the pandemic.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This is where the parent-school relationship becomes important.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We could enlist parent volunteers to help with the administrative or additional duties during a pandemic.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Thus, it is important that we begin to continually engage and recruit parents beyond the minimal service hours.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Get them more involved in activities, like school games or events, and participate in pandemic scenario exercises.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic led to a surge in mental health issues, such as anxiety, depression and stress, due to factors like social isolation, economic uncertainties and health-related factors.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We must identify ways to ensure such support continues during a high-anxiety period like the pandemic.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In terms of emergency, the mental well-being circles must be able to transform, step up and take on bigger roles.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This peer network must also leverage technology to connect residents online, so that the first level of mental health support is provided and remains accessible during a pandemic.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: (In Malay):   The COVID-19 pandemic has been a challenging time for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We have now left the pandemic behind, and we have progressed safely.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In the national struggle against COVID-19, the Malay/Muslim community made some important adjustments.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our asatizah, led by the Mufti and the Islamic Religious Council of Singapore (MUIS) played an important role in our community.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They calmly and astutely provided much-needed counsel during a difficult and unprecedented period.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I am grateful to the community for being understanding about the challenges at that time, supporting the decisions taken and cooperating with safe management measures to protect Singapore from the COVID-19 outbreak.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In closing, I would like to express my deepest gratitude once again to all the those at the frontline, including our health workers, teachers and asatizah.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The White Paper on the COVID-19 Response is a fair assessment of how Singapore performed in its fight against COVID-19 and candidly stated certain areas to be improved, which I will elaborate upon in my speech today.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, I would like to express my sincere gratitude to the healthcare workers, frontline essential workers and all those who have worked tirelessly to keep our communities safe during these challenging times.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Your dedication, sacrifice and unwavering commitment to the well-being of our society, have not gone unnoticed and we extend our heartfelt appreciation to every one of you.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we reflect on the past few years, it is important to acknowledge the challenges we have faced as a nation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In particular, I would like to address three areas that we could have done more to mitigate the effects of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, the need to build more resilient housing, especially for low-resourced and vulnerable households.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Challenges in our housing structures and capabilities, especially in the case of 1- and 2-room flats, became even more apparent during the implementation of the Home Recovery Programme (HRP).

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some were unable to get through to MOH's hotline for instructions, while others who were not suited for home recovery faced delays in conveyance to recovery facilities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For our resource-low households, particularly those living in 1- and 2-room flats, these challenges were amplified and experienced more acutely because of their space constraints.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: During the Delta wave, our strategy pivoted from "zero-COVID-19" to "living with COVID-19".

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With the re-characterisation of the virus as a disease mild enough to recuperate at home, the directive that followed was for infected individuals to self-isolate within the confines of their homes.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, for those living in 1- and 2-room flats, where there is only one bathroom and multiple dwellers share the same bedroom, self-isolation proved almost inconceivable and this drastically increased the risk of other household members contracting the virus.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Having multiple members of a resource-low household contract COVID-19, leads to greater financial insecurity, as compared to middle- and higher-resource households.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While their ability to work is compromised, resource-low families often do not have access to work-from-home (WFH) alternatives and rely on a smaller pool of savings to tide them through periods of no work.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As a Member of Parliament of Zhenghua, I have first-hand experience of the challenges faced by such families, especially those living in our public rental flats.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I was in constant communication with residents and appealed to the MOH team who did their best, given the situation, to assist them.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The limitations of our present homes in protecting residents in the face of a pandemic, especially in the case of 1- and 2-room flats, justifies a re-think of our minimum housing standards.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Taking into account the challenges faced by households living in 1- and 2-room flats, due to constraints in living space, what must be done to fortify all housing types to ensure that they are resilient in future pandemics?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: During the pandemic, many businesses in Singapore worked with the Government to manage migrant workers' inflows at dormitories.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This helped to ensure that essential services continued to be delivered.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Particularly, associations, such as the Dormitory Association of Singapore Limited (DASL), contributed significantly to managing the unprecedented situation in the dormitories.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Were there useful lessons learned from these partnerships with DASL and the Singapore Contractors Association and has MOM put in place measures to better prepare for the next pandemic?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is crucial to work with the trade associations (TAs) on pandemic response and establish pandemic-related SOPs and communication channels.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This way, TAs will be ready with a pandemic response and there will be a clear line of communication with the Government to ensure the efficient cascading of information, both ways.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To tackle the possibility of such similar pandemics where the speed and scale of virus spread becomes unprecedented, is the Government looking to prepare pre-emptive policy coordination in the present state?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Will these be included as one of the workstreams of the dedicated centre for public health and forward planning?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In particular, Phase 5 of the JGI payout has caused some administrative pain for companies.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Businesses shared that the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) conducts random checks to verify employment numbers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These checks involve specific documents, like employment details of certain employees, hours worked, work schedules and pay slips, and such reviews take up to six months.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This means that the review has taken close to 10 months.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Upon further enquiry, IRAS was not able to provide the status updates and was not clear on whether the company was eligible for payouts or not.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This must certainly be challenging for civil servants involved too, so I do understand the operational constraints.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, I look forward to the review and some proposed pathways to making this better for all.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has been an unprecedented crisis that has impacted the entire world.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Our lives have been upended and we have had to learn to adapt to a new normal.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Today, I would like to pay a special tribute to our workers in the air, sea and land transport sectors.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: They have collectively kept Singapore connected, kept Singaporeans moving and ensured that we continued to have access to essential goods and services – right from the very beginning and throughout the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Our transport workers showed up to work every day, despite the uncertainties surrounding how deadly and contagious the virus could be.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: They set aside their fears and kept our airways open, our sea lanes flowing and our buses and trains moving for all of us.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As a transport unionist at the frontline, I have witnessed first-hand how the Government, the unions and our corporations, come together to overcome crisis after crisis and emerge stronger together.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Amidst the many uncertainties throughout the pandemic – new COVID-19 clusters, new virus variants, travel bubbles forming and popping – what was certain for the tripartite partners was that we knew that we had each other’s back.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But the aviation industry, a vital part of global connectivity, had to keep moving.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Despite having a high risk of contracting the virus, our air crew and those working at our airport worked tirelessly and selflessly to ensure that all flights coming through Singapore remained safe and secure.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: They worked long hours; sacrificed personal comfort, having to don cumbersome PPEs; and put in extra efforts to uphold the highest standards of safety, sanitation and service on board our flights and at the airport.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: They did so to transport essential supplies and to bring back our loved ones stranded far away, when global travel came to a virtual standstill.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Soon after, the magnitude of the impact of the pandemic set in and many aviation workers were faced with the sobering prospect of an uncertain future.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But the tripartite partners were quick to step in.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) worked closely with the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore and SkillsFuture Singapore to launch the Enhanced Training Support Package to help companies retain and reskill their workers instead of retrenching them.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: During the Ministerial Statement on aviation recovery in October 2020, I had asked the Minister for Transport why Singapore Airlines (SIA) was operating flights to countries that Singaporeans were not allowed to travel to.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Minister explained there were some flights, although the load factor is low, that SIA would continue to fly to maintain a minimum connectivity network, to maintain our presence in those markets.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: So, even though the load factor is low, the Government would support SIA to continue these flights and to mount cargo flights so that our supply chain is not affected.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Next, let me extend my appreciation to all the seafarers and port workers who bravely continued their work during the pandemic, often against all odds, to ensure that our supply chains remained operational during the most challenging of times.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: When global air passenger demand evaporated almost overnight, the demand for cargo increased exponentially.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Unseen and unheard, our maritime workers worked around the clock to ensure that essential goods and services continued to flow into Singapore during the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Without our maritime workers, we would not have had the medicine, food, fuel and other vital supplies that we needed to navigate the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Our maritime workers helped to keep our economies running and our communities fed and provisioned, even as the rest of the world was brought to a standstill.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But our seafarers did not have an easy time during the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Many were stuck onboard their ships for months due to travel restrictions and border closures, unable to return home to their families and loved ones.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Yet, they persevered to keep our global supply chains open.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Such efforts were vital in ensuring the safety and welfare of our maritime workers while keeping supply chains open, even during the worst of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Last, but certainly not least, I would like to acknowledge and thank the many land transport workers who have been silently working to keep our country moving during the pandemic, including during the circuit breaker period.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Every time they interact with passengers, they are exposed to the risk of contracting the virus.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Despite taking precautions, such as wearing masks, using sanitisers and maintaining social distancing, they remained at high risk of exposure.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The risk of infection is real, which was evident when the highly transmissible new Delta variant started spreading rapidly at our bus interchanges.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Will they get the virus too and will they pass it to their family members at home?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: But instead of staying away, they worked extra hours and stood in for their quarantined colleagues.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The tripartite partners also came together to enhance infection control measures at all bus interchanges.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The COVID-19 clusters were eventually closed in October that year, slightly less than two months after the first cluster was detected.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Additionally, public transport workers were constantly facing the challenges of enforcing mandatory mask wearing and social distancing policies.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In quick response, the National Transport Workers’ Union rallied the public transport operators and the Land Transport Authority to take a firm stance against abusive passengers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Throughout the pandemic, they were instrumental in ensuring that we could get our food and other basic supplies, even when we were in home quarantine.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Many hawkers, too, relied on their services to stay afloat, especially when dining-in was prohibited.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: To all our delivery riders out there, thank you for bridging the vital last-mile gap, rain or shine.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Many unsung heroes have come together to ensure that we emerge stronger from the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Today, I place on record our sincere appreciation to the many men and women who work in the transport industry, for keeping Singapore connected and keeping all of us moving even during the darkest of times.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: May their contributions be remembered by all of us, always.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: It was slightly more than three years ago when we first heard about a cluster of severe pneumonia cases in Wuhan, China.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: No one could have imagined the prolonged impact that this would have on the world, our society and our economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Being in the Ministry of National Development (MND) and MOM at the onset of the pandemic, I witnessed how sectors, like construction, faced the risk of collapse if we did not intervene early to address disruptions to supply and foreign manpower; and business distress due to the pandemic and global border control measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: I also vividly remember Prime Minister Lee's speech on our commitment to our migrant workers, for their role in building Singapore over the years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: It was a powerful one – our migrant workers will be paid their salaries and that we will provide medical care and treatment that they need.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: It was a bold and inclusive commitment that resonated and was very much appreciated by the workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Members may recall seeing many videos of thanks from our migrant workers on social media then.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: During my rounds visiting the dormitories and in meetings, the High Commissioners and Ambassadors from our migrant workers' home countries conveyed their nations' appreciation for our efforts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Our swift actions and commitment showed Singapore to be a reliable and trusted partner.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Our migrant workers play an important role in building and maintaining Singapore’s infrastructure and I would like to reiterate our appreciation for all their contributions to Singapore and their trust, patience and understanding during the pandemic, as we worked to keep them safe during COVID-19 and manage the evolving situation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Through this journey, we all learnt to be adaptable and resilient in overcoming the challenges before us.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We rallied together – our people, the Public Service, private companies and civil society – to put the interests of our nation and others before our own and came through, as one united people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: In my speech, I will elaborate on managing the impact of COVID-19 on the construction industry; standing up emergency accommodation facilities for migrant workers and supporting their health and well-being; ensuring that the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) maintained a high level of operational readiness; and adapting to adjustments to religious life by the Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Almost all construction work came to a halt during the circuit breaker period.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Even after work resumed and the dormitories declared cleared of COVID-19, companies had to adjust their operations and adapt to new requirements, such as safe management measures (SMMs) at worksites.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Companies faced manpower shortages, as they were unable to bring in new migrant workers, due to travel restrictions and border measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: And these led to project delays and significant cost increases to the sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We also provided companies with multiple rounds of Foreign Worker Levy rebates and waivers, as well as wage subsidies via the JSS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This relieved some of the burden from manpower costs and helped preserve jobs in the sector, including for locals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We recognised that some companies would be unable to meet their contractual obligations and previously committed timelines, with the work stoppages and delays due to COVID-19.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: COTMA also provided a defence against claims for contract breaches, including liquidated damages in such instances.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We also supported developers and end-users, such as home buyers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Developers whose projects faced construction delays could seek relief on the date of delivery of possession.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Home buyers who were affected by extended delivery dates, could similarly seek reimbursement from the developer, for qualifying expenses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Our TAs also played a pivotal role in addressing the acute manpower shortages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The Singapore Contractors Association Limited (SCAL), Association of Singapore Marine Industries (ASMI) and Association of Process Industry (ASPRI) took the lead to pilot a tightened end-to-end process to bring migrant workers into Singapore safely.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This initiative involved integrating the testing of workers at dedicated onboarding facilities in their home countries, with protocols for them to stay safe from infection.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The pilot's success allowed us to scale up further to meet the manpower needs of the construction, marine and process industries, while safeguarding public health and our healthcare capacity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The lessons learnt and experience gained from these initiatives will help to minimise future manpower disruptions in the next pandemic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Firm formation and cessation numbers also point to a stable situation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The strong partnerships that we have forged over the past three years and the can-do spirit to overcome challenges will go a long way in preparing us for the next pandemic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Ultimately, what COVID-19 has taught us is that we need to transform the built environment sector towards greater resilience and productivity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The Minister for Manpower had elaborated on the fight against COVID-19 in the dormitories yesterday and areas where we could do better.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: To protect our migrant workers and reduce COVID-19 transmission within the dormitories, we brought together public agencies, private companies and NGOs to identify and stand up emergency accommodation facilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Put together, they came up with adaptable and innovative solutions, often under tight timelines and resource constraints.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We also used port land and exhibition spaces, such as the Tanjong Pagar Port and Singapore Expo.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We even used a vacant en bloc site, the former Chancery Court condominium, offered by the Far East Organisation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Moving on to another group of partners, I will always be thankful for the support from our NGOs in providing care and support for our migrant workers throughout the pandemic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: I recall our many meetings and dormitory visits during the pandemic, where I felt heartened by their tireless efforts, especially during circuit breaker.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: They came together to forge new partnerships and coordinated efforts on the ground to meet the needs of our migrant workers in different ways.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We also had medical volunteers from NGO HealthServe, who helped to supplement the efforts of our medical teams on the ground.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: As an inter-racial, inter-religious and inter-cultural organisation, Hope Initiative Alliance (HIA) played an important role in ensuring that the spiritual needs of our workers were met.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: They organised congregational prayers and religious services for our workers of different faiths in the dormitories and recreation centres.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: When workers were unable to return home during their festive holidays, HIA helped to spread cheer by distributing festive care packs and meals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Many of their volunteers came from Christian groups and I remembered them coming at 4.00 am in the morning to deliver breakfast during Ramadan and this was at the height of the pandemic in 2020.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: If I had to share all our stories together on the ground, we would be here for quite a while.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: So, just let me just acknowledge our other NGOs who had made a difference in the lives of our migrant workers and helped as sounding boards for some of our policies and these include the development of the improved dormitory standards over the last three years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Miss Rachel Ong spoke about how we should continue our close working relationship with our NGOs to sustain their outreach within the migrant worker community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The Alliance for Migrant Workers Support (AMWS) was initially set-up as an engagement platform with our NGOs during COVID-19.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The Minister for Manpower spoke yesterday on how the Government stood up the Inter-Agency Task Force and brought in the SAF and the Home Team to manage the COVID-19 situation in the dormitories.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Despite the risks involved, we saw the unwavering dedication of these officers, including those deployed as part of the Forward Assurance and Support Teams (FAST).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Singapore Police Force (SPF) officer Station Inspector (SI) Sheik Ismail volunteered as a FAST officer at the S11 dormitory@Punggol, which saw the largest COVID-19 cluster.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: SI Sheik made sure that the workers' needs were met, helping them to talk to their employers about their salaries, ensuring that they stayed connected with their families and assisting them to remit money back home.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: What struck me was that SI Sheik went beyond the call of duty to lend a listening ear, taking the time to understand their fears and encouraging them to focus on their hopes and dreams.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Corporal (NS) Vinod, a Combat Medic with the 2nd Combat Support Hospital, was deployed to the EXPO Community Care Facility.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: He supported the operations to plan, monitor and deliver care to affected migrant workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: He shared that his In-Camp Training (ICT) has been "the most meaningful one" for him.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: He felt a strong commitment to "fight a different kind of war" in a hall filled with thousands of migrant workers with COVID-19.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Against an enemy that threatened to instil fear and destroy our way of life, Singaporeans from all walks of life, the Public Service, private sector, NGOs, volunteers and national servicemen, have indeed come together to "fight a different kind of war", each playing their part through Total Defence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: One of the key lessons from the pandemic is the importance of adaptability and the resilience of our infrastructure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Learning from this experience, public sector agencies are working to identify suitable facilities to meet possible crisis scenarios and better safeguard and operationalise sites for emergency needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This includes exploring developing dual-use facilities to serve both peacetime and crises functions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: One way to do this is by retrofitting available and suitable state properties to be able to pivot from peacetime to crisis use when necessary.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: It is currently used for new migrant workers to undergo residential onboarding and medical examination when they first arrived in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: In the event of a pandemic, the Onboard Centre can be quickly converted into a dedicated facility for newly-arrived workers to serve their Stay-Home Notice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Public sector agencies will also explore with private sector owners to potentially utilise a wide variety of private infrastructure for emergency housing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: These include chalets, hotels, serviced apartments and exhibition spaces.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: One such example was how D'Resort@Downtown East was used as a Government Quarantine Facility.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: For example, there will be larger recreation spaces, such as multi-purpose and sports courts, which can be repurposed as medical facilities.
