speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We are also looking at strengthening the resilience of key food distribution facilities, such as the Jurong Fishery Port and Pasir Panjang Wholesale Centre, against future emergencies and pandemics, as raised by Mr Saktiandi Supaat.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The Singapore Food Agency is carrying out upgrades to enhance the security, surveillance and access control systems of our key food supply facilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This would allow for better contact tracing, in the event of a future disease outbreak and support the enforcement of control measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Businesses should also continue to review and keep their business continuity plans relevant, to ensure supply resiliency at the company level.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Even as we continue to enhance the adaptability of our infrastructure, we need to maintain strong partnerships across the people, the private and the public sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This will be instrumental to enable us to meet demands for quarantine housing and temporary accommodations in the next pandemic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: One concern was on the necessity of Workforce Vaccination Measures (WVM), raised by Ms Hazel Poa and Mr Yip Hon Weng.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: At that time, the virus was mutating and new variants, which were highly transmissible, were emerging; while time was needed to assess whether these new variants also put infected persons at a higher risk of severe disease.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This was when we were still grappling with Omicron, by the way.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Unvaccinated individuals, especially those who are older, would have put themselves at risk of infection at the workplace.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We were concerned that infected, unvaccinated individuals could be at risk of severe illness.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: There could also be significant added strain on our healthcare system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The Government, therefore, decided that there was a need to put in place stronger measures at the workplaces to protect vulnerable and at-risk groups.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: These measures complemented the public health measures in the community, such as the vaccination-differentiated safe management measures (VDS).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: In the Advisory on COVID-19 Vaccination at the Workplace, the tripartite partners made it very clear that dismissal is a last resort and employers should try to allow unvaccinated workers to work from home, including through redeployment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Following the lifting of the Workforce Vaccination Measures, Workforce Singapore (WSG) and NTUC's Employment and Employability Institute (e2i) had reached out to and offered employment assistance to such unvaccinated employees.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Unvaccinated individuals can also approach WSG or e2i, if they require further assistance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The lifting of the Workforce Vaccination Measures followed the relaxation of the VDS in April 2022.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: With the full lifting of the VDS in October 2022, if an individual feels that an employer is making vaccination-differentiated requirements without genuine occupational needs to do so, he or she may approach MOM or the Tripartite Alliance for Fair and Progressive Employment Practices for assistance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Since October 2022, there has only been a handful of complaints.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: For the broader workforce, a key lesson from the pandemic is developing a strong Singapore Core and complementing it with a diverse foreign workforce, to ensure the resilience of our businesses and our economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This was a point that Mr Saktiandi Supaat spoke about as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: However, the number has since recovered to pre-COVID-19 levels, as border restrictions were relaxed and employers tried to catch the upswing of economic recovery.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Even as we strengthen the complementarity of our foreign workforce and continue to attract global talent, international investments and companies, our focus on strengthening the Singapore Core in our workforce will remain.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We have developed Industry Transformation Maps and Jobs Transformation Maps, which include strategies to prepare our workers for higher value-added jobs in each sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We have in place an ecosystem of programmes and schemes to prepare workers for jobs of the future, such as the Career Conversion Programmes and SGUnited Mid-Career Pathways Programme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We have also put in place various programmes to increase the global and regional exposure of locals to enable them to take up leadership positions in global firms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: By combining and complementing local and foreign expertise, we can grow the pie for Singapore and provide more good opportunities for all.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: While our nation grappled with and were fully focused on overcoming COVID-19, Singaporeans can be assured that the SAF kept up our security operations and maintained a high level of operational readiness to keep us safe from external threats.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Critical SAF operations, such as maritime security, air defence, protection of key installations and counter-terrorism, continued round-the-clock even during the pandemic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Our servicemen had to train in challenging conditions arising from pandemic restrictions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: These conditions tested the SAF's grit, tenacity and resilience.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: But our people adapted quickly and quickly rose to the challenge.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: To minimise infection risk, SAF implemented strict health and safety measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: These included vaccination, cohorting, safe distancing, reduction in training group sizes and COVID-19 testing regimes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Some personnel performing critical operations had to isolate themselves in camps and bases for days, to ensure that they were free from infection before they could start their duties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: For many, this also meant sacrificing time away from their family and loved ones.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This made celebrations like Mother's Day during the circuit breaker period slightly different for our servicewomen.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Major Doris Sam, for example, an RSAF Air Warfare Officer, was isolated in base with her unit to ensure they were free from infection and could continue to safeguard Singapore's skies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This was the first time she was apart from her two-year-old toddler, Atlas, over a prolonged period.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Despite the sacrifices required, Doris, like many fellow sons and daughters of Singapore, stayed true to her mission and continued to defend our home.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: With the gradual easing of restrictions, the SAF progressively resumed training, often operating under conditions more strenuous than before the pandemic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: At the height of the pandemic in 2020, the Singapore Navy participated in the SAF's first overseas training since the onset of COVID-19.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This was for the Rim of the Pacific Exercise, a multinational naval exercise.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Vaccines were not available at that time, so they were in a COVID-19-safe bubble and had no interactions with anyone else apart from their fellow crewmates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The ship was reconfigured with Intensive Care Unit (ICU) capabilities in the event that someone turned positive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Fortunately, the entire crew tested negative throughout their deployment and successfully completed the exercise.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: One of them was Weapons Systems Cluster Chief Military Expert 3 (ME3) Suresh Subramaniam, a father of three.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: ME3 Suresh told me that he was thankful for his wife's support and assurance on the home front.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The SAF is grateful for the support from spouses and families of our servicemen and women, who also shared the belief on the need to uphold high standards of training amidst COVID-19 in the defence of Singapore to ensure our sovereignty and our way of life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Throughout the COVID-19 pandemic, there were many groups who also kept Singapore going in different ways.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: One such group is our public transport workers, as mentioned by Mr Melvin Yong earlier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: They braved the virus every day to keep public transport services running.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Some workers also volunteered to come back to work on their rest days to cover colleagues who were sick, especially when COVID-19 clusters were emerging among bus captains.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Public transport operators – SBS Transit, SMRT, Tower Transit Singapore and Go-Ahead Singapore – adjusted shifts to ensure that their workers had sufficient rest while minimising impact on commuters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: At the height of the pandemic, platform operators and their workers also provided much-needed services: point-to-point transport, food and goods delivery.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: I echo Ms Janet Ang and Mr Melvin Yong's tribute and thank our public transport workers and operators, platform workers and operators, workers in the air and sea transport sector and many others in our fight against COVID-19.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This was a whole-of-society effort, one filled with sacrifice, dedication and duty.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Our Malay/Muslim community, too, played an important role.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: The community had to adjust to the closure of mosques and suspension of congregational prayers, which Mr Sharael Taha and Dr Wan Rizal spoke about.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: While in circuit breaker, the community also had to observe Ramadan and Hari Raya away from their loved ones.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: With the month of Ramadan upon us in just two days' time, there is much to be grateful for to be able to observe and pray together without COVID-19 restrictions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: I recognise that it has not been easy for the Malay/Muslim community or the Muslim community in general, including our religious leaders, because of the sacrifices needed over the past three years to battle and to overcome COVID-19.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Speaker, I will deliver the next segment in Malay.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: (In Malay):   For many Muslims, the circuit breaker phase had been a very difficult period.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We could not perform religious practices and obligations, such as our congregational Friday prayers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We also had to suspend prayers and other activities that were typically conducted during Ramadan, such as Terawih prayers at mosques.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: But the community quickly adapted ─ performing their congregational prayers at home with their family.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: In retaining traditions, the community also turned to online means to convey their well-wishes to family and loved ones for Hari Raya.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Singapore was among the first countries to do so, before other countries made similar decisions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This included Saudi Arabia who announced that the Haj would be limited to domestic pilgrims only, in order to curb the spread of COVID-19.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Many pilgrims were saddened by this decision, especially because of the very long waiting time to perform the Haj.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: But the community understood the need to do so as it would not only protect our pilgrims, but those around them as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: These measures would not have been possible without strong religious leadership of the Mufti, the Fatwa Committee and our asatizah, as well as the strong partnerships within the community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Our religious leaders were astute in assessing the health risks and adjusting religious practices to the prevailing COVID-19 situation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: These were difficult decisions that needed courage during our most trying moments to curb the spread of COVID-19 in the community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Our religious leadership benefitted from the close partnership with our Muslim healthcare professionals, through the Malay/Muslim COVID-19 Working Group.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This Group advised MUIS in developing the necessary precautionary measures and communicating the scientific reasons behind them to the general public.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: For example, Dr Norhisham Main, the President of the Muslim Healthcare Professionals Association, alongside the Mufti, explained the closing of mosques and other changes to the community's socio-religious norms from a medical perspective during an interactive online talk show.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Through these adjustments, the community has shown its progressiveness – one that is able to make adjustments to their religious life, without compromising on religious tenets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: I am proud that the community played an impactful role through a strong sense of citizenry, as displayed in our fight against COVID-19.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Such contributions are important, particularly in our multi-cultural, multi-religious society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: I am also heartened that their contributions have been recognised by the international community as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This is more than just an award for Mufti and the Fatwa Committee, but also a recognition to the community who responded well to the adjustments that had to be made.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: I am glad that the community continues to apply the lessons learnt and good practices from the pandemic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This builds our resilience, which will come in handy as we face future challenges.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: This was initially introduced in response to the reduced size for congregational prayers, but now provides more flexibility on the timing for individuals to perform their prayers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: In a few days, the Muslim community will enter the month of Ramadan.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Three years ago, we observed Ramadan during the circuit breaker period.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Since then, the community has overcome many things.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: As we return to normalcy, let us continue to build on the gotong royong spirit that we demonstrated during the pandemic, to build a united and resilient Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, in Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong's national broadcast on 7 June 2020, just as Singapore emerged from the circuit breaker, the Prime Minister addressed Singaporeans that we faced "the crisis of a generation" and also expressed his hope that "an even stronger and better Singapore will emerge from this crisis".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Three years later and on this side of the crisis, I believe that this holds true.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: We can be heartened by how our people have shown resilience, adaptability and unity throughout the pandemic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: I am confident that the lessons we have learnt will put us in good stead for the future and prepare us for the next crisis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: In June 2020, at the start of the pandemic, I began my speech on the Supplementary Budget with a verse from a song by the legendary band, Queen.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: That verse was, "Your every day is full of sunshine.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: But into every life, a little rain must fall." Today, I would like to close this chapter with another verse, this time from another legendary band, The Beatles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: You can also imagine Deputy Prime Minister Wong playing his guitar, strumming in the background. "Little darlin', it's been a long, cold, lonely winter.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Little darlin', it feels like years since it's been here.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence and Manpower (Mr Zaqy Mohamad)
text: Here comes the sun, and I say, it's alright."

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Before I start my speech, I would like to take a moment to reflect on those who were lost to the effects of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: May those close to them find solace and the departed rest in peace.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The world has undoubtedly changed in the past three years.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: We were forced to embrace technology, to connect and transact digitally when we physically could not.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: We, somehow, became familiar with the Greek alphabet.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: And through the pandemic, Singapore faced a formidable challenge and rose to the occasion, displaying a side of the nation that is compassionate and caring for its fellow man.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: First, on support for businesses, workers, and jobs.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The JSS also enabled the sports and fitness industry to press pause, re-evaluate and reimagine how sports and fitness businesses should run.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Through the Enterprise Innovation and Capability Development Grant, SportSG provided the sports and fitness industry with a way to incorporate innovative technology into their businesses to remain resilient during this challenging period.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: It was a necessary step for the industry to take.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The JSS clarified which industries were considered essential and non-essential during the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: It was apparent that in times of crisis, the sports and fitness industry is non-essential.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: However, I do believe that the industry has a significant role in Singapore's journey towards living with COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The pandemic presented the sports and fitness industry with an opportunity to redefine itself, encompassing not just events production companies but also sports academies, social sports and recreation clubs, fitness clubs, boutique gyms and freelancers.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This realisation has been valuable in equipping the industry for success moving forward.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Second, the MTF has responded proactively to the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Their work is commendable and they have consistently kept Singaporeans updated with the situation.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The MTF has taken a data-driven, scientific approach to the ongoing crisis.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I especially appreciate the co-chairs and members for diligently using their "head and heart" strategy to make decisions that affect us all.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: We are incredibly thankful for their hard work and dedication, especially during these trying times.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Third, Singapore strived to ensure that vulnerable groups were supported during the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Numerous initiatives were put into place, with financial assistance, job retraining, counselling services and additional subsidies being provided by both the Government and NGOs.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The collective effort is a testament to our society's dedication to helping those in need during difficult times.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Former national sprinter, UK Shyam and other athletes initiated a cause to donate laptops to students from lower-income families.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: National tennis player, Shaheed Alam, created "Project Love", which provided meals for migrant workers during Hari Raya through fundraising efforts.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Our Silat athletes, Sheik Ferdous, Sheik Farhan and Nurul Suhaila, started an initiative called "Sayang Sayang Fund". "HopeFull" is a project spearheaded by golfer Jen Goh that provides resource kits for children and youths from disadvantaged backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Members of the sporting community took part in monthly engagements with beneficiaries, including virtual interaction sessions and delivery of kits.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: And, of course, Speaker, as President of Singapore National Olympic Council (SNOC) and the SNOC Athletes' Commission participated in the "You'll Never Walk Alone" by ComChest campaign, which raised funds for children at-risk, persons with disabilities, persons with mental conditions, vulnerable seniors and families in need.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, when our athletes could not compete or train, I am proud that they used their platforms to show resilience in a different way, inspire Singapore and used sports as a force for greater good.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Even with the profound economic disruption caused by global lockdowns, Singaporeans took rapid action to contain the virus and protect their fellow citizens.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Despite the daunting challenges brought on by COVID-19, Singaporeans have embraced the circuit breaker and other SMMs with courage, resilience and a collective sense of responsibility.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: From reducing foreign worker density to closing schools and workplaces, citizens across all sectors have come together to prioritise safety for their fellow countrymen and women.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporeans' strength and resilience are remarkable, proving that unity can produce tremendous positive change even amidst a crisis, that people from all walks of life can come together and contribute to the fight against this global crisis.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: In such times, it is an incredible reminder of what we can do – we are united, SG United in solidarity.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: The lessons learned from this pandemic will help prepare our nation for any crisis in the future.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: This is deeply encouraging and underscores our responsibility as Parliamentarians, to work together for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: They volunteered themselves to be on the frontlines, while everyone else stayed in the safety of their homes.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: They persevered through these trying times to save as many lives as possible.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: They put their own safety at risk to protect us and fought tirelessly, going above and beyond what was required of them.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Together with my fellow Parliamentarians, we would like to express our sincere gratitude to all Singaporeans who have stepped forward and done their part to assist Singapore during the crisis.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Our nation's founding father Mr Lee Kuan Yew and his team understood the importance of building up substantial national reserves for rainy days.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Their vision saved Singapore, in more ways than one, during the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: These reserves provided our Government the ability to work fast and speed up purchases of essential supplies and vaccines.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: On top of that, Deputy Prime Minister Wong and his team was able to roll out essential assistance schemes to businesses for employers and the self-employed.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Needless to say, it is now time to replenish our reserves, in order for future generations to have that advantage during their rainy days.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This White Paper captures the lessons to be learnt and as a nation, we know we must always be better prepared for the next crisis.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Singapore cannot be totally dependent only on a task force to resolve problems during a pandemic.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We must look into preparing Singaporeans to manage daily concerns on the ground.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: There were many groups of Singaporeans who made significant contributions during the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The outbreak in the migrant worker dormitories during the early months of the pandemic was at a near-tipping point, as the virus could have spread rapidly into the rest of our society.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Our military and Police services took control, contained and stabilised the situation.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The Joint Task Force (JTF) was quickly set up to contain the cases within the migrant worker dormitories.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: There were no vaccines then and these officers risked their own health and safety to be on ground.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: During the circuit breaker, some officers had to stay in a hotel for fear of passing the virus to their families.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Our nation depends on the SAF and SPF to protect us and to restore order.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Will we still have these well-trained military and Police personnel during the next pandemic?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Attitudes have been more distinct due to the fast-changing times that we live in.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We need to be able to attract good people to join and maintain excellence in our military and Police services.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Not to add fuel to fire, we do have an expedited falling birth rate.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The second group of people will be our grassroots network and volunteers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This network was built-up over the past five decades.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This extensive and close-knitted network was able to help affected residents very quickly.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: They were responsible for distribution of masks, sanitizers, TraceTogether tokens and care packs, and so on.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Again, how do we ensure that we are able to continue having such support?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: How can we strengthen our grassroots networks and volunteerism, especially amongst the younger Singaporeans?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: While no fault of theirs, they have been severely or permanently impacted by the COVID-19 policies and restrictions.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I hope to be able to appeal for more assistance to help these Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The mRNA vaccine is a very new technology and a small number of people developed severe reactions as a result of administering it.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The first group consist of Singaporeans who suffered permanent injuries or deaths after taking the mRNA vaccines.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Within a short span of time, she and her children had to deal with the sudden grief of losing of two loved ones.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Coping with financial difficulties under such sad circumstances is extremely tough.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: There were other examples of Singaporeans who suffered severe reactions, such as strokes, severe rash breakouts and so on.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: They shared their experiences with me during my Meet-the-People Sessions and house visits.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It was also reported that a nurse was hospitalised for five months and was handicapped after recovery.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: There may not be many such cases and there is not anyone to blame.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: However, we have to acknowledge what these innocent Singaporeans had to go through, how their families have been permanently affected and how much they had to suffer.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: They trusted the vaccines to protect themselves from the COVID-19 virus but, unfortunately, instead of being protected, they suffered.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I hope the Government will look into ways to assist Singaporeans who had to go through such a painful experience.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The second group will be the workers and companies in the construction sector.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: During the outbreak, strict SMM were imposed at the worksites.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Workers had to be transported everywhere they went.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Meal breaks were carefully scheduled and migrant worker dormitories had to be drastically reduced in capacity.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: All these regulations changed how construction companies operate and productivity diminished due to the restricted construction work processes.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: As a result, many construction projects, including various Build-To-Orders (BTOs), were severely delayed.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Many workers left the construction industry during the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: There is now a real shortage of workers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The construction companies had to increase the salaries of workers quite significantly to avoid bigger financial losses arising from delays in project completion.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Many local companies are still struggling with the massive financial losses incurred during the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The rising costs of materials, utilities, fuel and high Certificates of Entitlement prices for their vehicles are not helping them to gradually recover.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I do hope the Government will try to provide even more assistance to the local construction companies during this vital recovery phase.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The third group that I would like to mention are workers and companies in the aviation industry.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Changi Airport was a ghost town when the borders were closed.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: There used to be some 50,000 staff employed in Changi Airport pre-COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: During the pandemic, the aircrew suffered significant pay cuts and some had to switch careers – like one airline pilot, Johnny Tan, who had to sell durians instead of being able to fly a plane.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In response to the fluid situation during the pandemic, the border control measures had to change every now and then.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Airport staff working in the transit areas had to don PPEs, as they faced the highest risks of contracting the virus from arriving passengers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Similarly, aircrew risked their own health and safety, serving passengers who could be COVID-19-positive.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We are now almost back to pre-COVID-19 days, but our recovery has a different set of challenges.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Companies are struggling to find staff who can be trained quickly in order to deal with the sudden surge.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: With the opening of the Chinese border, manpower demand will further increase.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In addition, companies operating in Changi Airport will have to deal with the increase in utility cost, fuel cost, salaries, GST, carbon taxes and so on.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Changi is one of our most important strategic assets and being Skytrax's Best Airport comes with a price.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: That only means that we have to deliver and confront the challenges facing the aviation sector.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I hope that Singaporeans who have saved us from COVID-19 are celebrated, that we will continue to have such individuals to serve Singapore; and that the inadvertent impact and hardship suffered by various groups of Singaporeans will be addressed.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These individuals, not recorded in the official death toll for COVID-19, might have died of undiagnosed COVID-19 infections or COVID-19 could have worsened some underlying conditions, leading to their deaths.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will never know the exact number or all the names and the faces of every victim of this pandemic crisis.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Never had Singapore gone through a crisis that inflicted such a heavy toll on the lives of our fellow men and women since Independence.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is, indeed, the crisis of a generation.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And behind every passing, there were family members, loved ones, doctors and healthcare workers doing their best to comfort them, to save them.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At MOH and, I am sure, in this House, we mourn their deaths and extend our deepest condolences to their families.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: COVID-19 placed lives and livelihoods in very stark contrast – or, maybe more aptly put – it put in contrast your desire to survive and live vs what is the purpose of living.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This same challenge was faced by every country, every region, which is: how do you navigate out of this dangerous conundrum, regain your normal lives while protecting the lives of your people as much as possible?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And every one took their own or its own path – some by choice, others forced by circumstances.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I would say how each country or region faired in this COVID-19 common challenge, essentially, boils down to the following three judgement calls.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, whether through our decisions and, in the early stages of the pandemic, we effectively made hospitals the singular defence against the virus.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many countries in Europe or the Western Hemisphere – the Americas – deal routinely with influenza, including very severe winter seasons.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The influenza playbook – they used that and it was proven to be inadequate for COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, the virus spread widely, hospitals effectively became their singular defence, which became overwhelmed, leading to many deaths.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: On the other hand, places like Singapore, South Korea, China, we had seen "ghosts" before.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We had seen SARS and the Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS).

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We had the processes and capabilities in place and then we moved quickly to contain our initial outbreaks with stringent border measures, testing and isolation of cases, tracing and quarantining of individuals.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, we used our entire public health arsenal and we succeeded in preventing our hospitals from being overwhelmed, especially in the initial stages of the pandemic before there were vaccinations.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If there was one thing the Prime Minister constantly reminded the MTF chairs, it was this golden instruction – protect our hospitals' capacity – and we took it all very seriously.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Because when the entire weight of the country's health rests on hospitals, even if that was not the intention, it will not just be COVID-19 patients that die, but everyone who needs urgent medical attention can die.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Doctors had to turn away patients who were very ill and they were all just waiting along the corridors.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When a hospital bed or ventilator became available, the doctor had the heart-wrenching task of deciding – who do I save?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This judgement call – the careful husbandry of our hospital beds before the great majority of our population was vaccinated – is the primary reason why Singapore kept our COVID-19 mortality rate low.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The second judgement call has to deal with vaccination coverage.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Most countries rolled out national vaccination programmes and they achieved varying levels of coverage and then resilience.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Those, if Members remember, were confusing times, because the vaccines were new and anti-vaxxers were out in full force, spreading falsehoods and half-truths to persuade people to avoid vaccinations.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I know of friends who do not want to take the vaccines.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But I think it is one thing to have a personal preference, and quite another to make it into a public campaign because that affects other lives.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I had to exercise my authority under the Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Act (POFMA) when I judged that a circulating falsehood was misleading people into avoiding vaccines.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The law was designed for such occasions, especially when lives are at stake.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is worth stating in this House, again, that the weight of global evidence clearly shows that COVID-19 vaccines are effective and safe.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Dr Lim Wee Kiak, my colleague, always says, if a medicine has effects, it can have side-effects.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A medicine without side effects has no effect.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We were clear and transparent and published the incidence of side effects every quarter.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The incidence of severe adverse effects for the vaccines has been low – typically, five to seven per 100,000 – and a great majority recover on their own, without even going to the hospital.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is our collective judgement, as a people, to achieve high vaccination coverage.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And this is the other big reason why we could minimise the number of deaths due to COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Then came the third judgement call – the tricky one – which is, having achieved high population immunity, when should we open up?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For many countries in Europe and America, after the virus had spread widely, with many people infected and many deaths, their population immunity was actually high and they could afford to open up early.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, in the course of the pandemic, many people also urged MOH and MTF – can you quickly open up like other countries in the West, in Europe, in the Western Hemisphere?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The desire is understandable, but they overlooked the key difference between us and them.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They paid the price in human lives, which we refused to pay.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We, along with a small handful of countries, managed the situation tightly, contained the spread of the virus and used the time to vaccinate as many people as possible.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Then, came a time to open up and you had to switch from one set of rules to another.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: You had to switch playbooks – from Queen to The Beatles, from a zero-COVID-19 policy to something closer to managing a bad influenza season.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This was a major psychological leap for doctors, MOH and the society.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They took the first step, followed by Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Looking back, in all three decisive moments of judgement, I think we, collectively, made the right calls.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Despite this, COVID-19 has been a humbling experience.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have a duty to learn from the crisis and ensure that those whose lives were lost to COVID-19, did not pass in vain.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have translated the trials and tribulations of the pandemic into six areas of improvements, to better prepare Singapore for the next pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The White Paper had mentioned them briefly but I will elaborate.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our healthcare system was severely tested during the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At one point, we were monitoring bed availability, capacity, caseloads almost by the hour, to detect any signs of imminent collapse.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Fortunately, we had the SMMs in place; we had high coverage of vaccinations, which protected our hospitals.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At that time, many questions were asked, including in this House: why did we not plan for more hospital capacity in anticipation of the pandemic crisis?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At that time, I was asked: if we did, we could have relaxed the SMMs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This would not be a realistic course of action.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To illustrate, even with vaccinations and SMMs, at the peak of the Delta wave in 2021, we had almost 1,300 patients hospitalised, 140 in ICU.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If we had relaxed the SMMs, the number, I think, would have easily doubled, probably tripled.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is equivalent to three or four full general hospitals set aside as spare capacity during peacetime, waiting for a surge and then be deployed.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, it is just not realistic to set aside so much spare capacity.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, we should not size the healthcare system to take on the full brunt of the next pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This pandemic has taught us that true resilience must not come from just adequate infrastructure, but also from our social resilience – our collective behaviour.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That said, with delays in our infrastructure development due to COVID-19 and rising hospital workload post-crisis, our healthcare system today is less resilient than ideal.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Dr Wan Rizal and Mr Gerald Giam raised concerns in this area, which I agree with, especially the stress that it is giving our healthcare workers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It has gone up by almost six percentage points.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is largely driven by patients staying longer in hospitals.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, that increase alone explained for all the increases in occupancy.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Because we are seeing more older patients with complex conditions and they need to stay longer in hospitals.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, the percentage of senior patients aged 65 and above has risen from 39% in 2019 to 43% now, that is, 2022.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many of them are frail and with co-morbidities and we also found an increasing number being hospitalised because of other viral infections.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Not COVID-19 but other viral infections, respiratory illnesses, including pneumonia.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We cannot rule out that this could be after-effects of being infected with COVID-19 for some, or it could be a rebound of other forms of infections post-crisis and, during the crisis, suppressed.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Once masks are removed, we go back to the Disease Outbreak Response System Condition (DORSCON) Green, they rebounded.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It may also simply be a result of our population ageing very rapidly.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As I have explained to this House, MOH is doing many things to address this.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I will not repeat them today and this includes the recent announcement to strongly protect our healthcare workers against abuse and harassment.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, a post-crisis initiative, which I have yet to explain, is the Transitional Care Facilities (TCFs).

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: TCFs are for medically-stable patients from public hospitals waiting for long-term care arrangements, such as going to a nursing home or going for home care.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The TCFs have proven to be very useful.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They are very well-utilised and it is as good as adding 500 more beds to our acute hospitals.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, we do not have a TCF in the West and we will start one there in the next few months, in close proximity to the Ng Teng Fong General Hospital.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will also continue to expand the community and step-down care sector, such as community hospitals and nursing homes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Now, let me move to the second area of improvement, which is, we will boost our pandemic preparedness and response.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This means having the capability to quickly understand what this virus or pathogen we are dealing with is, and then what actions to take.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When dealing with any infectious disease, we, generally, need to understand six key characteristics in order to formulate the right response.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: COVID-19 really helped us boil down to these six important characteristics.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One, how it spreads – for example, between persons in close proximity; or is it airborne through aerosol.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Two, the length of its incubation and infection periods.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Three, R0 or reproduction number, which is a measure of its infectiousness.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For example: is it seniors, children, or both?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Spanish flu, for example, affects young children especially.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And six, how to treat and prevent it.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Without good answers to these six basic questions, we will be fighting in the dark and, most likely, end up fighting the last war.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It will also strengthen our international pandemic research partnerships – to build a network of partners and allies to play our part in strengthening global surveillance of emerging pathogens.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will leverage the Global Initiative on Sharing All Influenza Data (GISAID).

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: After we understand the characteristics of a dangerous pathogen, what do we do with the information?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Having gone through SARS, H1N1 and the various phases of COVID-19, we have developed a range of responses.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The characteristics of the pathogen will determine our response.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong mentioned this briefly in his opening speech yesterday, but let me elaborate a little.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In this chart, the horizontal axis measures transmissibility and the vertical axis measures severity.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is a simplified way of measuring the six characteristics that I spoke about.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, Members will notice at the top right-hand corner what looks like a durian or explosion, that is Disease X – the disaster that we dread, where the pathogen has high transmissibility and high severity and is deadly.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And if you move to the left, you will notice the red dot, that is SARS, with high mortality but low transmissibility.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, when you encounter something like that, it favours a strict containment approach – with extensive contact tracing, chase down, isolate every case, until the virus is eventually wiped out, which we did.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As for COVID-19, which is the blue dot, you will notice there is a blue dot near the red dot connoting SARS, called COVID-19 wildtype, that is the initial COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When it first appeared, the wildtype strain is slightly southwest from SARS.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is why in the early phases of the pandemic we treated it like SARS and adopted a zero-COVID-19 policy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As it mutated, it became Delta, became Omicron BA.1, now we have got XBB, XBB1.5, 1.9.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They are constantly moving to the right, meaning they are more transmissible.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But, with vaccination, we do not just let them move to the right, we also make them move down and suppress the severity of these strains.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, you see the blue dots now moving down closer to the green dot where influenza is.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, overall, with vaccinations, later variants are closer to where influenza is on the vertical axis, which is why we are then able to open up and move towards living with the virus.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, using this framework, what happens when a new pathogen of concern emerges in future?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We may have to respond quickly with appropriate border and domestic SMM measures, to minimise infections and to buy time.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Then, with good science and the local and global capabilities I just described, we hope to quickly ascertain key characteristics of the pathogen, where it lies on the graph, and then determine the right responses.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Concerted efforts to develop and secure effective vaccines and therapeutics will proceed in parallel.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The third area of improvement is MOH will restructure to strengthen our organisation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is something we also did in the wake of SARS outbreak in 2003.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MOH put in place a pandemic preparedness plan involving the primary care sector, which evolved into today's Public Health Preparedness Clinics (PHPC) Scheme.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Polyclinics and PHPCs served as our first line of defence – to test and treat COVID-19 cases, they support home recovery, they also administered vaccinations and helped in surveillance efforts.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, contrary to what Mr Leon Perera said, our family doctors actually have been and will continue to make an immense contribution during the pandemic and for healthcare in future.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We set up the National Public Health Laboratory (NPHL).

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It conducts laboratory surveillance of infectious diseases and aids in outbreak investigations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When COVID-19 first emerged in Wuhan, it was the scientists from NPHL who designed the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test for COVID-19, two days after the scientists in China shared the genome sequencing with the world.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We established the National Centre for Infectious Diseases, which opened its facilities in 2019 and it provides high standard of infectious disease clinical management.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These organisational enhancements after SARS, built up capabilities that helped us respond to COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Given what we have learnt from the COVID-19 pandemic, we should, once again, review our organisation structure to better prepare ourselves for the next pandemic.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The one big lesson this time is that we need to rely on a wide repertoire of responses.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As I had explained in the chart earlier, each pathogen has unique characteristics needing different responses.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In fact, COVID-19 shifted around the chart, requiring us to change playbooks along the way.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Specifically, for a severe but less transmissible disease like SARS, we need an individual-centric approach, comprising testing, isolation, tracing, quarantining, that is precise, accurate and as error-free as possible.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For less severe but highly transmissible pathogens like the Delta or Omicron variant, it becomes almost impossible to contact-trace and isolate, especially as the disease increases and spreads exponentially.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is also of no use insisting on gold-standard accuracy and precision.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Instead, we need to manage the exponential growth of infected persons, through population-wide interventions: mask wearing, Antigen Rapid Test tests in the community, self-testing, self-quarantine for those who are exposed and home recovery for those with milder symptoms.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The individual-centric clinical approach versus the population-based public health approach, they are actually not mutually exclusive.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In fact, they complement one another and we adopted both during different phases of the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We should institutionalise both sets of capabilities for the long-term and be able to deploy both with flexibility and dexterity in future pandemics.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Many countries, such as South Korea, UK and US, they have similar set ups.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They, too, after the COVID-19 crisis, are also reviewing their organisational set up.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: CSOG was established during the pandemic and grew steadily as the pandemic progressed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is the machinery behind all the pandemic-related operations that we are familiar with – contact tracing, home quarantine, conveyancing to isolation facilities, testing, vaccinations and home recovery.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: All this, coordinated and implemented by CSOG in MOH.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: CSOG was staffed by officers from various Ministries, contract staff and also staff from industries affected by COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For example, we had quite a number of SIA pilots as well as cabin crew working in CSOG.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Most of these staff have returned to their industries.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As Ms Poh Li San said, it has rebounded from 2% to 80%.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are sad to see them go, but we are happy that they are gone too because they are going back to their industries.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Nevertheless, we will keep a permanent CSOG force to maintain surge readiness for a mid-sized outbreak as well as other health emergencies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This includes preparing healthcare institutions to be crisis-ready.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In peacetime, when there is no emergency, they help us operationalise Healthier SG, as the skillsets turn out to be fairly similar.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is not surprising, because they are both public health-focused.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will train and equip them to reinforce our operations during larger surges and they will complement the existing pool of SG Healthcare Corps volunteers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Instead of DMS, he will be called the Director-General of Health, which more accurately describes his role as the main overseer of both clinical and public health of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This will take place after the changes to the Healthcare Services Act come into effect later this year.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With these changes, MOH will be organised to place greater emphasis on both clinical services and public health.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They require different instincts, considerations, capabilities and skillsets.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Both are important and critical, and will be institutionalised and built-up within MOH.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Gerald Giam suggested that the Government was not forthright with the people, that was what I heard.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That during the initial stages of the pandemic, we did not impose masking requirements, not because of public health reasons, but because we did not have enough mask supplies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In the initial stages of the pandemic, there was no clear understanding of the characteristics of the COVID-19 virus.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We, therefore, aligned our policy to World Health Organization's (WHO's) recommendations, and WHO, even up to March 2020, maintained that: "a medical mask is not required for people who are not sick, as there is no evidence of its usefulness in protecting them." The risk of shortage of masks for healthcare workers would put their lives in danger because they are at the frontline.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It was, but it was not the basis of the prevailing public policy on masking.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We reviewed and changed our masking policy in April 2020 – that was also when WHO changed its guidelines once the evidence on how the virus spreads became clearer.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Particularly, there was now clear evidence that there was asymptomatic transmission via aerosol.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Nevertheless, as acknowledged in the White Paper, the whole issue of masking is one area where our decisions could have been better.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But no question that during this period, the Government was totally forthright with the people and told the people what we knew.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The fourth area of improvement is to update our laws.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Infectious Diseases Act, or IDA, is the principal legislation for the prevention and control of infectious diseases.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It empowers MOH to take various public health actions for disease outbreaks, such as contact tracing, isolation of infected persons, testing of contacts or the disinfection of premises and so on.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The IDA also provides for the Minister for Health to declare a public health emergency in very grave public health situations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That will activate extensive powers for the Minister, such as controlling the movements and gatherings of people and imposing curfews.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: While COVID-19 was a crisis and a serious threat, we did not declare a public health emergency.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We wanted to restrict group sizes, but not to control the movements of people.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We were not planning to impose curfews or invoke the Requisition of Resources Act to marshal resources.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In other words, the emergency powers under IDA were too blunt and heavy, compared to the public health measures and SMMs we needed at that time.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, instead, Parliament enacted Part 7 of the COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) Act, or CTMA, to provide us temporary, complementary powers to IDA.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This ad hoc legislation allowed us to deploy a broad range of tools to tackle COVID-19 at multiple layers, without declaring a public health emergency and this House just extended Part 7 of CTMA for another year.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ideally, we should review and amend the IDA.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: COVID-19 taught us that, in a prolonged pandemic, we can go through different phases.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, IDA must be amended to deal with a wider range of scenarios.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will put forth the full proposal to the House later this year.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The first tier is Baseline, which is a peacetime state.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The second tier is Outbreak Management, where a pathogen of concern is detected and measures may need to be implemented urgently to manage disease outbreaks.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These include contact tracing and quarantine, testing, border controls and masking.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These will buy us time to understand the characteristics of the pathogen, the six characteristics that I mentioned.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The third tier is Public Health Threat, where more stringent, widespread and longer-term control measures and restrictions are needed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These include various SMMs and restrictions, up to and including a circuit breaker-like imposition.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Then, finally, the highest tier is Public Health Emergency, where very stringent measures, such as curfews and requisition of public health assets and manpower, may be effected.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Will this, therefore, prevent the panic buying that we saw during COVID-19, when we changed DORSCON to Yellow and Orange?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You just change colours to descriptors; there is no reason why panic will just disappear.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Whether a people panic during a crisis depends a lot on the information they are getting and whether they know what to do, to protect themselves and then contribute towards societal resilience.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If people listen to rumours and they do not know what to do, then most likely they will rush to supermarkets and stock up on toilet paper and instant noodles – and Mr Seah Kian Peng will have a problem again.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I believe that with the experience of SARS, H1N1 and now COVID-19, the Government knows much better, what measures are necessary and appropriate; and the people of Singapore understand much better, what to do during a pandemic crisis.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With that, there is a lower chance of having a panic.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The fifth area of improvement, we need to ensure that we have early access to efficacious vaccines for future pandemics.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Without sufficient doses of vaccines, our mass vaccination strategy would have been a non-starter.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So what if we are willing to take the vaccines, if there are no supplies?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But securing vaccines is an art in itself, at best, an inexact science.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This is where the judgement I spoke about at the start of the speech, made all the difference.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: How the vaccine procurement decisions were made in the early stages of the pandemic, is an important story to be told in this House and we shall do it today.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Spoiler alert – this story has a happy ending, as noted by Mr Liang Eng Hwa.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Once they were formed, they immediately faced two challenges.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Although several vaccines were concurrently being developed at that time, nobody knew which one would work.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Second, every country was clamouring for vaccines and there was limited manufacturing capacity to meet that demand.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As a small market, we lack negotiating power.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This would normally push us down the priority queue for delivery.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The situation was worsened by supply chain disruptions caused by the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, how to secure assured and early deliveries for vaccines?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Do not put all our bets on one vaccine, but buy a selected number of vaccines across different technological platforms.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: To identify the most promising candidates, the workgroup was advised by a panel of experts from the research institutes, hospitals and industry.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Since we did not know which vaccine candidate would work and we had to buy several types – if one does not work, we must make sure the other one had enough volume to cover our population.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Therefore, we needed to over-procure such that the combined volumes of all the vaccine candidates more than covered the population of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That made them bite and we entered into the agreements.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Then, to ensure quality and safety, all selected vaccine candidates were reviewed by HSA thoroughly before being authorised for emergency use in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Expert Committee on COVID-19 Vaccination provided a second layer of independent review and gave recommendations on how to optimise the use of the vaccines.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The first batch of Pfizer-BioNTech vaccines arrived in late 2020, Singapore being the first country in Asia to receive them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We rolled out the National Vaccination Programme shortly after, from December 2020 – again, one of the first few countries in the world to do so.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think only after the UK, US and maybe, Israel.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Moderna vaccine was added to the National Vaccination Programme in March 2021, and Sinovac and Novavax in October 2021 and February 2022 respectively.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: While the mRNA vaccines were found to be highly-effective in protecting against severe COVID-19 infections, around the middle of 2021, we faced two new concerns.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, there were early indications that vaccine protection could wane over time, especially amongst the elderly.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We, therefore, procured additional vaccine doses to administer boosters to the whole population.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There was a real possibility that one or more might break through vaccine protection and cause new major infection waves, causing many deaths or many cases of severe illnesses.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Moderna and Pfizer-BioNTech therefore developed new bivalent vaccines that provide better coverage against the newer virus strains.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In September 2022, we took the decision to make a clean switch to these new bivalent vaccines.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The monovalent ones had to be stored away.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Looking back, today, if we can go back in time, given the uncertainties, the high stakes, what we knew, what we did not know and the challenges we faced, I think we would have done things the same way.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Because we secured safe and efficacious vaccines, delivered when we needed them most, Singaporeans took them with confidence, even with relief.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When they arrived, I can take the vaccine and we were one of the first in the world.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We built up our population immunity and achieved DORSCON Green today.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But there is a price to be paid.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Because we deliberately over-procured to mitigate the uncertainty of the selected vaccine candidate not working and the possibility of supply chains being disrupted, there would be spare vaccine stock, which will expire.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Some months ago, MOH was asked by the media how many of our vaccines had expired.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We could only reply that about 10% of our stock had expired because of confidentiality agreements that we have entered into with vaccine suppliers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I would have preferred to be more transparent and forthcoming with the information.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have since discussed with the vaccine suppliers and they have agreed we can reveal the total value of the expired vaccines so long as we do not give further breakdowns of quantity that enable people to guesstimate or estimate the cost of each dose, which is what they are sensitive about.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We had tried to donate our spare vaccines, but there have been no takers because there has been an oversupply of vaccines in the world.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Manufacturers have ramped up their production capacity and demand has been going down as the pandemic stabilises.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are reports estimating that expired vaccines globally could range up to 500 million doses or more.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The expiry of unused vaccines was an insurance premium – the price we were prepared to pay to stave off the risk of catastrophic consequences.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Before vaccines were available, we had to resort to a circuit breaker in April 2020 to contain the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We spent close to another $60 billion, over two financial years, to cushion the hardship for businesses and workers, not to mention all the heartaches and difficulties families had to go through.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Without vaccines, we would certainly have to resort to further circuit breakers during the Delta and Omicron waves in late 2021 and throughout 2022.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we did not have to; because the vaccines, we got them early and they protected us.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: More importantly, our approach averted many deaths due to COVID-19 infections and protected Singaporeans against that catastrophic consequence.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ms Hazel Poa thought that MOH favoured mRNA over other non-mRNA vaccines in our regulatory approval.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Several non-mRNA vaccines could not secure HSA's approval because of insufficient data on safety and efficacy, and we cannot compromise on our standards.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
