text: Ms Hazel Poa and Mr Yip Hon Weng also asked if VDS were too harsh on the unvaccinated.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The relevant question is, whether from a public health perspective, the measures are necessary and justified.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We need to be mindful that while everyone should make their own medical choices, in a pandemic, individual actions affect not just yourself but also others around you.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When the vast majority chose to take the vaccine, they not only protected themselves but also their loved ones; they raised our collective resilience.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As for those who did not take the vaccine, they do not just put themselves in danger and at risk, they also put others around them, including their colleagues at their workplaces, at risk.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Hence, VDS was needed as a public health measure.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we understand the hardship some of them have to go through.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Some of them are allergic to the vaccine.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Therefore, the moment we could step down VDS, we did so.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: More importantly, we must continue to be prepared in case a dangerous variant of concern emerges.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, this is our vaccine strategy going into the future.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: First, MOH will maintain and periodically refresh an adequate stock of COVID-19 vaccines, to allow continued protection of the elderly and vulnerable as needed and to facilitate a rapid response should there be a major or more severe pandemic wave.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Second, we will maintain a network of vaccination centres – primary care clinics, polyclinics and a baseline footprint of five to 10 Joint Testing and Vaccination Centres – even during DORSCON Green.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: With this, we will be able to administer a booster to all persons aged 50 and above and the medically vulnerable within three weeks, if necessary.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Third, we are negotiating agreements to secure early access to vaccines against other pathogens with pandemic potential.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: These might include new influenza and other respiratory viruses.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Fourth, we will invest in vaccine research and development like the PREPARE programme I spoke about earlier.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: One of our objectives is to establish how to quickly develop a working vaccine, based on either the mRNA or protein-subunit platform and bring it to clinical trials locally.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In response to Dr Tan Wu Meng, EDB will continue to engage other vaccine manufacturers to invest in Singapore, grow our biomedical sector capabilities and cement our position as a pharmaceutical hub of Asia.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There is now a global effort to develop safe, effective vaccines within 100 days of a Public Health Emergency of International Concern being declared.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: What we thought was not possible to do or would have taken years to implement were accomplished in a matter of months because we were pushed by the crisis.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We were stretched and when released, will not rebound back to the old equilibrium.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For example, today, we are in a new era of flexible work arrangements.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our schools built up strong digital capabilities and all secondary school students today have their own learning devices because of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I am sure Changi Airport will rebound to a new level of capability, post-crisis.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In healthcare, the changes are even more profound.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: During the crisis, public and private healthcare providers became connected by the same IT network.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Everyone downloaded and got familiarised with healthcare apps.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As pointed out by Ms Ng Ling Ling, telehealth became the norm.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We became converts of preventive care as we became conscious of hygiene, got used to diagnostic tests, wearing masks and vaccinating routinely.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is a strategy born out of crisis and will profoundly change the landscape for healthcare in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The chapter on COVID-19 is a thick one in the story of Singapore, one with high drama, dark days, personal tragedy; as well as bright spots and many high points of courage, collective will and resourcefulness.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The story featured so many men and women who fought to keep Singapore safe.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I cannot name everyone but they are reflected today in the stories of some of their brethren.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Dr Annitha Annathurai, who personally oversaw the set-up of medical operations at the S11 dormitory and helped calm and assure the migrant workers there, that they would be taken care of.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Salman Imtiaz, a volunteer with the SG Healthcare Corps, who helped as a vaccinator with Raffles Medical Group while pursuing his undergraduate studies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Dr Wong Jiayi from Minmed Group, who became a father three times over during the pandemic – one pair is a twin.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But he stayed at his post, leading vaccination centres, a regional swab centre, mobile vaccination teams and home recovery operations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Captain Lee Jia Wei, who volunteered to care for migrant workers being isolated at Singapore Expo and, to protect his family, did not go home for 60 days and stayed at Changi Expo.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Ms Sandra Goh, a lead stewardess with Singapore Airlines, who was furloughed when borders closed, switched to become a Care Ambassador at a hospital and now she is a manager at the Specialist Outpatient Clinics at Khoo Teck Puat Hospital.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: She told me she could transfer her skills from cabin to ward.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Mr Toh Guan Ru, one of my community volunteers, who, between the Institute of Technical Education and polytechnic, requested to work for MOH and handle home recovery cases.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When he discovered that he did not qualify for the COVID-19 Resilience Medal because his stint was slightly short, he says, "It's okay.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I am just proud that I was able to help." I sincerely thank all of them and the hundreds of thousands who contributed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We write the story to record suffering and sacrifice, but also the strengths and remarkable commitment on the part of so many to successfully overcome the crisis.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We write to remember, but also to learn.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Members’ support during the COVID-19 pandemic played a critical role in rallying fellow Singaporeans to battle against this crisis of a generation together as a nation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Many Members have also spoken about the unprecedented challenges the pandemic had brought and its impact on the economy and businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: First, they had to implement the various safe management measures, or what we now know as SMMs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Food and beverage (F&B) services, for example, had to observe the dining-in rules, from two to four to zero, to four to two and many changes; and implement the TraceTogether SafeEntry system, or TTSE – many of you have forgotten what they mean.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Coupled with a weaker demand, their revenues fell as a result.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Some businesses were also affected as their workers fell ill or had to be isolated.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Some workers were stranded overseas and could not return to work, because the borders were closed.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: On the other hand, those in our essential services sectors, such as those producing food and water, electricity and operating public transport, had to keep their operations going to meet the daily needs of Singaporeans even during the circuit breaker, braving the risk of COVID-19 infections.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Some businesses had to quickly pivot to new business models and new markets and embark on transformation and training to improve productivity and stay competitive.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Beyond coping with the pandemic, the private sector also contributed to our fight against COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: They worked in the background to secure lifesaving essential supplies, operated the critical facilities or provided services for those infected with COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: People-public-private partnerships played a critical role in helping us overcome the challenges of the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Today, I will elaborate on three key challenges that impacted our businesses, how we worked with industry partners to overcome them together and the lessons we learnt.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: First, securing essential supplies and strengthening our supply chain resilience; second, preserving Singapore’s hub status and safely reopening our borders; and, finally, working with our industries to chart our road to recovery.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: One of the earliest challenges we faced was securing essential supplies and strengthening our supply chain resilience.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: When countries across the world locked down their economies and closed their borders, production and transport lines were severely disrupted during a time when global demand for essential goods actually surged.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Gerald Giam asked why we did not have sufficient stockpiles of masks and local production capacity.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Prior to the pandemic, masks were rarely worn outside of the clinical environment, even during SARS.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our national stockpile of masks was, therefore, maintained at a level that would be sufficient for the healthcare sector's needs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: To supplement our stockpile, Singapore companies produced masks overseas as it is more cost-effective to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Therefore, when we decided to require everyone to wear a mask whenever they left their homes, we had a problem.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We were faced with an unprecedented situation where everyone in Singapore and around the world was suddenly looking for masks for daily use.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: That is 30 times more than our usual consumption.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We worked very quickly with the private sector, such as ST Logistics, to source for additional mask supplies from around the world.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: At the same time, we worked with industry partners, such as ST Engineering, to quickly set up surgical mask production capabilities here.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The first batch of made-in-Singapore surgical masks was produced in February 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: ST Engineering also stood up capabilities to produce the melt-down polypropylene filters in Singapore from January 2021.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This made us less reliant on imports of this critical material and enhanced the resilience of our local mask manufacturing capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Various homegrown textile and apparel companies, such as Ghim Li Group and Ramatex, also stepped forward to help produce reusable masks.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Many of us would remember the masks with a Merlion logo in your 2020 National Day Parade pack, that was from Ramatex.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: A*STAR and the Nanyang Technological University also lent their expertise to develop reusable masks that were more effective at reducing COVID-19 transmission, but also more breathable and comfortable.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Besides ramping up our mask production, we also worked with various partners to distribute masks island-wide.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Government started distributing masks to all Singapore residents from as early as February 2020, with the support of the SAF and grassroots volunteers from the People's Association (PA).

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Temasek Foundation funded and led more of these distributions thereafter.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Besides masks, many Singapore companies also supported our efforts to keep our supplies of food and other essential items flowing by maintaining our supply lines.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We worked with our shipping lines, such as the Pacific International Lines, to deploy ships to ports in the region and beyond, at times at our request, to bring food supplies to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: When Malaysia issued a Movement Control Order in January 2020 and closed the land links with Singapore, we introduced strict "bubble-wrapping" arrangements for Malaysian cross-border delivery workers, to prevent cross-infection with locals when they deliver their supplies to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We also worked with importers to diversify our import sources.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Sixteen local food importers participated in this project and cargo flights by Singapore Airlines and Air New Zealand flew these food supplies to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Once supplies were brought in from abroad, many Singapore companies also played a part in managing our local distribution network from warehousing to retail shops.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: PSA International stepped up warehousing capacity to ensure we had sufficient space for our upsized stockpiles of essential goods.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Supermarkets, such as NTUC Fairprice, Sheng Siong and Dairy Farm International Retail Group, also worked very hard to keep our shelves well-stocked.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For example, frontliners at Sheng Siong, Mr Sivakumar and Mdm Lee Cheng Hui, were involved in these efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: At the height of the pandemic, they worked overtime everyday alongside their colleagues to replenish shelves as fast as possible and patiently explained the SMMs to their anxious customers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Seah Kian Peng, in his capacity as Chief Executive Officer of NTUC Fairprice, also went out of his way to assure Singaporeans that we had enough supplies and that panic buying was not necessary.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Many Members in this House did so, too, including Mr Speaker yourself.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Much work also went on behind-the-scenes to ensure that our shelves are restocked regularly.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Trucks ferrying supplies from warehouses were coming into some supermarkets twice as frequently, at six to eight times a day.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have been doing this since before the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As Dr Tan Wu Meng, Mr Gerald Giam, Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Mr Saktiandi Supaat mentioned, the COVID-19 pandemic has only reinforced the importance of these strategies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Minister for Health, Mr Ong Ye Kung, earlier explained how we worked with commercial players to secure vaccines and how we will review regulatory levers to improve our response to future public health crises.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As mentioned by Mr Saktiandi Supaat, these initiatives do come at a cost.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will work with the industry and our trade partners to find cost-effective solutions.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I would also like to encourage Singaporeans to support our diversification strategy by trying different sources of supplies, different brands when you go about doing your daily shopping.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Strengthening our supply chain resilience not only helps us meet our domestic needs, but also helps Singapore strengthen our status as a business and trading hub.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Instead of resorting to protectionist measures during the pandemic, we continued to allow our manufacturers and distribution centres based locally to export goods to meet their obligations to their customers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I join Mr Melvin Yong in thanking our transport workers, including our maritime workers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Indeed, because of their dedication, our ports remained open 24/7 amidst disruptions at major transport hubs elsewhere.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Singapore played a critical role in ensuring that global supply chains continued to function.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We remained the world's largest transhipment hub and our ports continued to rank first in various international maritime indices and rankings.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This was due to the efforts of the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore, the maritime industry, and tripartite partners who worked closely together to keep our ports open while facilitating crew changes safely.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: PSA Singapore handled record numbers of container throughput in 2021 and 2022.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: However, people flows were significantly disrupted due to border restrictions overseas and here.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These were complex decisions that had to be made urgently and we took a risk-based and calibrated approach to manage our borders.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: At the beginning, we took some time before deciding to close our borders.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This was an unprecedented decision that we did not take lightly.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As a small and open economy, our connectivity is our lifeline.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As the pandemic persisted, we often had to adjust our plans, sometimes at short notice, to respond to new variants of concern and new COVID-19 waves that emerged overseas.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The multiple delays in the launch of the Singapore-Hong Kong air travel bubble, was a notable example.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Thereafter, we decided not to call it a travel bubble anymore, because it kept bursting.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: One key concern we had in mind when we made decisions on border restrictions was ensuring that workers, especially those in essential services, could still enter Singapore while managing the potential risks of COVID-19 transmission.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: When Malaysia introduced their Movement Control Order, a sizeable group of Malaysian workers who normally cross the border daily were faced with the dilemma of either staying in Singapore for work and be separated from their families, or potentially giving up their jobs and returning home.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Businesses were also affected, with many at risk of critical manpower shortages.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We worked with our businesses to introduce several measures, such as the Periodic Commuting Arrangement and Reciprocal Green Lane, to address this problem.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We also coordinated closely with our Malaysian counterparts to ensure that the implementation was as smooth as possible.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: There were also other times when we erred too much on the side of caution, which created disruption and uncertainty for businesses and workers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For example, when we experienced spikes in local infections, we temporarily suspended the entry of foreigners and Long-Term Pass (LTP) holders, including work pass holders, into Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This was to minimise the number of imported cases to avoid overloading our healthcare system.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: But, as highlighted by Ms Janet Ang, these restrictions created significant difficulties for the LTP holders, some of whom endured prolonged family separation and disruption to their work.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This also affected our global reputation as a hub and open economy and strained the manpower situation of our businesses and services.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As we learnt more from experience and understood more about the virus, we were able to strike a better balance and find ways to safely reopen our border.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We unilaterally opened to general travellers in late 2020, but we did so gradually, for a handful of very low-risk countries.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We regularly updated this list of countries, taking into account COVID-19 transmission trends.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This allowed for a larger number of travellers to enter Singapore, as long as they were fully vaccinated.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These reopening efforts were also supported by our home-grown COVID-19 testing capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Diagnostics Development Hub worked closely with local medical technology firms MiRXES and Advanced Medtech Holdings to develop and scale-up FORTITUDE and RESOLUTE 2.0 COVID-19 test kits, which were also used to test incoming travellers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Ms Poh Li San raised the need to support our aviation companies and workers as they continue on the road to recovery.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: With the continued support of our industry partners and workers, I am confident that our status as a hub will grow from strength to strength.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The final challenge I want to touch on today, is how we worked with our industries to chart the road to recovery.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: When the pandemic struck, almost every sector of our economy was affected.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We also provided grant support to businesses, such as the nightlife establishments, to pivot to other business activities.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Emerging Stronger Taskforce was set up to chart out our long-term response to the structural shifts in our economy arising from the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The taskforce worked with partners from businesses, trade associations and chambers (TACs), unions, the Institutes of Higher Learning and the Government to form nine Singapore Together Alliances for Action (AfAs).

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These AfAs prototyped ideas to address industry challenges and the successful ones were then implemented across the industry.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: One of the Singapore Together AfAs focused on Enabling Safe and Innovative Visitor Experiences.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The AfA was co-chaired by Ms Kwee Wei-Lin, President of the Singapore Hotel Association and Mr Lee Seow Hiang, Chief Executive Officer of Changi Airport Group.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It was supported by the Singapore Association of Convention and Exhibition Organisers and the suppliers of the National Association of Travel Agents Singapore, or NATAS.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The AfA's mandate was to pilot prototype arrangements for the safe resumption of large-scale international business events, design of safe itineraries for business and meetings, incentives, conferences and exhibitions (MICE) travellers, and deployment of digital enablers to facilitate a safe and seamless journey for visitors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These prototypes were piloted at TravelRevive in November 2020 and Geo Connect Asia in March 2021 – the first international travel roadshows to take place physically in Asia Pacific during the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Learnings from these pilots were then incorporated into more than 550 events, subsequently, under the Safe Business Events Framework and other strategically important events, such as the Singapore Airshow and the Singapore International Water Week.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Although the tourism sector was hard-hit by the pandemic, the efforts of the AfA and other industry partners helped the sector bounce back quickly from the pandemic when international travelling resumed.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This was the largest turnout since we first hosted the race in 2008.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As earlier mentioned by Ms Janet Ang, another scheme that gave the sector a boost during the COVID-19 pandemic was the SingapoREdiscover Voucher (SRV) scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Many of these merchants seized the opportunity to adapt their products for the domestic market and boosted their revenues amidst this challenging period.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I am sure many Members and your residents have enjoyed the SRVs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Other segments of our economy that were particularly affected by COVID-19 were our heartland enterprises, retail and F&B sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: They were the worst-hit by SMMs imposed on business operations.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As Mr Seah Kian Peng and Ms He Ting Ru mentioned, the multiple changes and granular differentiations in SMMs for business operations caused uncertainty and disruption for their operations.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: During the various phases of restrictions and reopening, some SMMs were overly calibrated.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This made them difficult to operationalise and caused confusion to businesses and members of the public.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As we learnt more from experience and received feedback from industry partners, we simplified our SMMs in the later stages of the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Striking a balance between mitigating the risk of infection and providing certainty and clarity to businesses and consumers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: For example, we simplified our SMMs into five core parameters: group size, mask wearing, workplace requirements, safe distancing and capacity.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This allowed us to calibrate and communicate our SMMs more easily and clearly.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Therefore, one important lesson we learnt – keep it simple, especially during a crisis.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I am glad that despite these disruptions, many of our businesses showed resilience amidst adversity.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Many heartland enterprises accelerated their digitalisation efforts, as their physical storefronts and workplaces were closed.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This helped them overcome the constraints of the SMMs and grow their businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Over two-thirds now have online presence, about 30% more.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I am glad to hear from Mr Shawn Huang and other Members in this House about how digitalisation has benefited heartland enterprises in your constituencies.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We should thank the business advisors from the Heartland Enterprise Centre Singapore and the digital ambassadors from IMDA's SG Digital Office for their hard work.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Together, they conducted over 66,000 ground engagements with heartland enterprises on e-payment and online presence solutions under the Heartlands Go Digital programme.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked how we would sustain the momentum of these digitalisation efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will launch a third phase of the Heartlands Go Digital programme later this year.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This will tap on the expertise of new partners from the private sector and IHLs to help heartland enterprises develop capabilities in digital marketing and visual merchandising.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Even though the worst of the pandemic is behind us, the Government will continue to work with our businesses as you progress along this journey of transformation.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The key lesson we learnt from the pandemic was that there will always be unexpected challenges that will surprise us.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We do not know when the next pandemic will happen, or what future crises may be like.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: But the one thing we can be confident of and rely upon, is the Singapore Spirit – working together, trusting one another and looking out for each other like family.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We witnessed this Singapore Spirit, when staff from Scoot, Raffles Medical Group and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs risked their own personal safety to evacuate Singaporeans from Wuhan when the crisis first emerged.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: When we face the worst crisis, we will see the best in Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It is precisely this Singapore Spirit that will see us through future challenges that may come our way.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Many people also worked tirelessly behind the scenes to contribute towards our COVID-19 efforts, even taking up functions and responsibilities they were unfamiliar with.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Meritorious Service Medal (COVID-19) was also awarded to three individuals whose unwavering commitment and exemplary leadership during the COVID-19 pandemic helped us safeguard lives and livelihoods and chart our road to recovery.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: They are: Prof Kenneth Mak, Director of Medical Services at MOH.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: He is a familiar face to many Singaporeans due to his professional and calming presence at the MTF's press conferences.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: He led the efforts of the professional healthcare team in managing the crisis.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Pang Kin Keong, Permanent Secretary of MHA, who chaired the Homefront Crisis Executive Group to execute our responses to the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: He and his team of dedicated public servants, helped navigate Singapore safely through the storm.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Tan Chong Meng, Lead for the Community Care Facilities (CCF) Taskforce, Temasek COVID-19 Workgroup, co-chairman of the Emerging Stronger Taskforce and Group CEO, PSA International.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: He coordinated many private sector efforts, including the setting-up of the CCFs and keeping our supply lines open.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: However, in the end, it is not just individual efforts, but the whole society coming together that ensured that we would prevail.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The best example that illustrates the importance of such people-public-private partnerships, is the setting up of the CCFs, where different parties came together quickly and worked together under a tight timeline, with very limited resources, to overcome unknown challenges and achieve a common mission.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These companies and volunteers may not have worked with each other before.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: They have not met each other but they came together nonetheless, each offering their expertise and resources to ensure the smooth set-up and operation of our CCFs.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Mr Edward Chia, Ms Janet Ang and Mr Raj Joshua Thomas highlighted the importance of strong collaboration between the TACs and the Government in times of crisis.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Indeed, we have built strong partnerships through regular engagements and collaboration between TACs and Government agencies over the years.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: During the pandemic, this rapport allowed us to come together very quickly, alongside industry partners, to resolve the challenges we faced.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This established industry norms on tenancy practices and terms, which helped resolve rising tensions between landlords and retail tenants regarding Rental Agreements.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our partnership played an important role in a crisis and we need to continue to strengthen this partnership even in the absence of a crisis.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I would also like to join my colleagues in thanking all our frontline workers stationed at our supermarkets and warehouses, at our air- and sea-ports, our care facilities and other essential services, for your dedication and sacrifices, which has helped us overcome this crisis of a generation and put us on a strong foundation for recovery.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.40 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.19 pm until 3.40 pm.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We have also received feedback from the public on the White Paper.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Many Singaporeans agreed with the broad observations and lessons and gave us further ideas on how we can strengthen our defences against future pandemics.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We take all of the feedback and suggestions seriously and we will study them carefully.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In their speeches, my colleagues have shared several specific moves that the Ministry of Manpower (MOM), the Ministry of Health (MOH) and the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) have made and will soon be undertaking.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Our work will not end with this debate.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will continue to consider additional inputs, put our plans into action and adjust them along the way.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is an ongoing, multi-year effort and commitment to learn and to improve.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: First, as I highlighted in my opening remarks yesterday, the purpose of the White Paper and this debate, is for us to learn, improve and be better prepared for the next pandemic.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I am glad that the Leader of the Opposition Mr Pritam Singh agrees with this and supports the Motion.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I do note, though, that Mr Pritam Singh, in supporting the Motion said, "he supports the Motion to the extent it expresses gratitude to all in Singapore who contributed to the fight against COVID-19 and affirms the Government's efforts to learn from the lessons of the last three years." I may be mistaken and, if so, please pardon me.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But this suggests that it is a qualified support; "to the extent" suggests it is a qualified support.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I am not sure why there is a need for such qualification because after all, Mr Pritam Singh himself did highlight the need for us to set aside politics, to close ranks and to uphold unity of purpose in a crisis, which I fully agree with.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, I would urge Mr Pritam Singh and the Workers' Party to give us their full and unreserved support, so that we can truly demonstrate unity of purpose in dealing with and learning from this pandemic.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Perhaps, Mr Pritam Singh had held back his full support because of the questions he asked about the report prepared by Mr Peter Ho.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Government had asked Mr Peter Ho, in late 2021, to undertake a review of our COVID-19 experience from the start of the pandemic until August 2021 and to draw lessons from this.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At that time, we had envisaged it as an interim or mid-term review, because we were not clear when we would be able to fully transition to endemic COVID-19.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In parallel, various Government agencies embarked on their own After-Action Reviews (AARs).

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: These focused on the policy and operational decisions within their respective domains.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Peter Ho knew about these reviews, and he decided to focus his efforts on the key strategic lessons for the Government, so as to minimise duplication and to complement the agency AARs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: By the time Mr Peter Ho's report was completed, we also had further experiences with the fast-changing COVID-19 threat, including the implementation of the Home Recovery Programme and our responses to the Omicron variant in late 2021.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: By then, we were also clearer about the way out of the pandemic.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Some may ask, "if that is the case, why can't you release Mr Ho's findings and if it is deemed sensitive, why not have it redacted, with the non-sensitive portions released?" But that is precisely what we have done.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Whatever is relevant and fit for release, we have incorporated into this White Paper.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The White Paper will not be the final word on our COVID-19 response.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I am sure academics and experts will continue to undertake more detailed studies, like the one mentioned by Mr Leon Perera on our H1N1 pandemic response.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Incidentally, that study was done by MOH's public health officials.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They decided to publish their findings in an academic journal.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We welcome all academics and experts to do their own detailed assessments of our COVID-19 response and to put out their findings.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They may have a different conclusion and view from the Government on specific issues, like wearing of masks, border measures or SMMs, and that is perfectly okay.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In fact, we welcome the diverse perspectives, because this will help us challenge our own assumptions and learn and improve.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Members generally agreed with the broad thrusts of the White Paper and offered many useful suggestions to strengthen our capabilities and support frameworks.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Clearly, there is much work to be done across all domains.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In healthcare, we need to build up our primary care and hospital capacities, our vaccination capabilities, as well as our public health expertise – as several Members highlighted, including Mr Leon Perera, Dr Tan Wu Meng, Mr Mark Chay, amongst others.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I would also like to assure Ms Janet Ang, Mr Raj Joshua Thomas and Mr Desmond Choo, that we will continue to harness the strength of our tripartite model, our trade associations and industry partners in all of these efforts.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We need to do more to improve public communications, including frontline crisis management communications, as suggested by Ms Jessica Tan and Ms He Ting Ru.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We also need to do more to look out for and care for the more vulnerable amongst us, including our migrant workers; and to address mental wellness issues, especially for our youths; something which many Members, including Ms Ng Ling Ling, Mr Edward Chia, Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Gan Thiam Poh, Ms He Ting Ru, Mr Louis Ng and Miss Rachel Ong all made reference to.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We recognise that the Government cannot do all of this work alone.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will need to work more closely with the people and private sectors.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will go beyond the usual corporate and tripartite partners to involve other stakeholders, including community groups and NGOs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We will involve our partners not just in execution and implementation, but also in upstream planning and emergency preparedness.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we will follow-up on all of these systematically, in order to strengthen our crisis management muscles – something that Ms Poh Li San and Miss Cheng Li Hui highlighted in their speeches.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I also agree with all Members that this work is of great urgency.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Around the world, the risk of animal viruses spilling over to humans continues to rise – due to population growth, urbanisation and increasing proximity to animals.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Climate change has exacerbated these problems by generating more habitat loss, forcing wildlife to migrate out of their usual patterns and come into contact with new species and more people.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In other words, disease spillovers and outbreaks are inevitable.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But every now and again, we encounter a pathogen that becomes a pandemic, causing global chaos.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The urgent global task, therefore, is to reduce the spillovers and, importantly, to prevent any such spillovers from turning into pandemics.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is where early detection is of utmost importance.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is why, there is a crucial need for an enhanced global surveillance system, especially in potential hotspots around the world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: With early knowledge of the characteristics of the new pathogen, along with the dimensions that Minister Ong shared just now, if we know this before the virus reaches our shores, we will be able to buy precious time to decide on our posture and measures.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is why Singapore is plugging fully into the global network of international pandemic research and we are working hand-in-hand with the global community to improve our collective pandemic response.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Singapore was one of the founding contributors to the Fund and we continue to shape initiatives through our membership of the G20 Joint Health and Financing Taskforce.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As Minister Ong shared just now, we will continue to leverage GISAID to keep up-to-date with genome sequencing of pathogens with pandemic potential.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We are a part of the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI) to keep up-to-date with vaccine developments.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We also have professionals and specialists from our scientific community, who represent us on technical platforms at the WHO and other international bodies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, we are doing everything we can to be better prepared, not just within Singapore, but also internationally.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Next, let me touch on the overall effectiveness of spending in enabling Singapore to get through this pandemic.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: At the macro level, governments around the world grappled with the twin challenges of lives and livelihoods.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And, Sir, with your permission, may I display some slides on the screens?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We mourn every death and express our deepest condolences to their families and loved ones.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But what we have in Singapore, is much lower compared to other countries with five or even 10 times mortality rate.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The key reason for this, is that we did not allow our hospitals to be overwhelmed, as Minister Ong had explained just now.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That was always our key objective throughout this crisis and so, we made full use of the tools at our disposal – whether it was vaccinations and boosters, border measures and SMMs – to achieve this goal.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is not excess mortality, but just looking at mortality from COVID-19, as one measure.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In terms of livelihoods, our economy recovered quickly to pre-COVID-19 levels by 2021.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Our employment rates, today, are even higher than pre-COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Our recovery – it is very hard to put this out into a picture, so, I do not have a chart for this – but our recovery was faster, compared to many other economies.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: You can use different indicators to track these, but it is quite clear, our recovery was faster compared to many others.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These are, of course, not comprehensive outcome indicators.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But I think most would agree that they are among the more important ones.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: How much did we spend compared to other countries to achieve these outcomes?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is not so easy to get actual data from other countries, but the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has some estimates, so we put out what the IMF has estimated for the different countries.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Clearly, we are not the lowest, in terms of this chart, with the sampling of countries.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But certainly, we are not excessive either, and there are many countries, like the United States, the United Kingdom, Japan and Germany, which put out much larger fiscal packages.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For the amount of public funds spent, we achieved relatively good outcomes compared to other countries.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There were other achievements, beyond those I have highlighted, that were not so easily quantifiable but no less important.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For example, we kept schools physically open and education going for our students.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We minimised disruptions to in-person learning, particularly for younger students, and mitigated the potential loss in learning outcomes due to the switch to home-based learning.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This helped to preserve firm capabilities and allowed businesses to bounce back quickly when the worst of the crisis was over.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Through the SGUnited Jobs and Skills Package, we also helped those who were in-between jobs transit to growth sectors; and fresh graduates maintain their skills and human capital while waiting for the economy to pick up.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We kept supply chains open throughout the crisis, and continued to service the world as a transshipment hub for air and sea cargo.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Even at the height of the pandemic when many countries, including Singapore, were short of supplies, we never imposed export controls.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We had cold chain facilities, so we facilitated the shipment of vaccines to the rest of the region.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This not only enabled supplies to keep flowing to and through Singapore, but also boosted our reputation as a reliable and trusted node in the global network.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, on the whole, when you look at all of these outcomes and what we had spent, on the whole, compared to other countries, we have achieved good value for the monies we spent – to stave off the most severe downsides of COVID-19 and to mitigate long-term economic and social scarring.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The resources we deployed enabled us to buy insurance and options, sometimes at substantial cost, like what we did when we moved quickly to secure advance commitments for the vaccine supplies.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But, in the end we have to judge whether it is worthwhile to pay a bit more, so that we can be in a stronger position to deal with the crisis and head off potentially very costly downside scenarios.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: When you look at what we have achieved overall in this crisis in the last three years, I am convinced that, on the whole, it is money well spent.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Beyond the macro picture, we can, of course, drill down into specific areas of spending.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is being done through the various ongoing reviews and audits and I am sure through these processes, we will pick up areas where we could have done better.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But I should acknowledge and give credit to all our public officers who worked hard round-the-clock to administer and implement the various schemes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There may have been occasional lapses in their work, but I hope Members understand that all our officers were working under crisis and emergency scenarios.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Where there were lapses or mistakes, I have every confidence that our Ministries and agencies will learn from them and will do better the next time.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Ms Poa had asked whether we could have been more discriminating in the support we had extended to businesses or, for example, to recover payments from businesses that were profitable.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We significantly expanded the JSS during the circuit breaker.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: At that time, everyone was worried, businesses were very worried over whether they could survive and how they may retain and pay their workers.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is why the JSS was designed to be across the board and automatically disbursed, so that businesses, especially the small and medium enterprises (SMEs), could receive the much-needed support quickly.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: And, indeed, the timely cashflow enabled firms to retain their local employees and capabilities, and to bounce back from the crisis once demand recovered.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: As soon as we could, we started to tier the JSS support – different levels of support for different industries and, eventually, phase out the JSS support.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Ministry of Finance (MOF) had earlier published a study on the impact of our key COVID-19 measures.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Behind this aggregate number are real Singaporeans and their families.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I am glad we helped these workers to stay employed, earn their keep and support their households through the crisis.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Mr Gerald Giam asked about Temasek's involvement in our efforts to fight COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, talking first about Government spending, this was the breakdown.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Out of the 10% of procurement, most of it, in fact, went to non-Temasek entities.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For example, most of MOH’s partners in the COVID-19 Treatment Facilities and Vaccination Centres were non-Temasek entities.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Temasek's entities were involved in very specific operations, for example, in the swift setting up of the COVID-19 facility, the community care facility at the Expo.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That was invaluable, because it helped us to get through the very difficult situation we faced with the dormitory outbreak.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Then, what about the resources that Temasek itself spent on COVID-19, for example, the distribution of test kits and masks?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The resources for this come from the portion of its positive Wealth Added returns that Temasek would typically set aside for community initiatives in the Temasek Foundation.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is part of Temasek's CSR – to do good and give back to society.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is something which we encourage of all companies in Singapore – to be good corporate citizens.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Temasek's community initiatives do not in any way detract from its mandate, which is to deliver long-term sustainable returns.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Temasek and its portfolio companies operate independently as commercial entities.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But like all commercial entities, we welcome them to do their part in a crisis, where it really should be all hands on deck.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Tapping on Temasek's capabilities, as well as that of the broader private and people sectors, is just one way we have harnessed our whole-of-nation resources to help bring our society and economy back to normality.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is not a form of dependence or over-reliance by the Government, which Mr Giam seems to suggest, but really a manifestation of Singapore's distinct and unique strength.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, many other countries struggled to galvanise their private sector to contribute to pandemic-fighting efforts.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In contrast, we were able to harness public and private resources to fight the crisis.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We worked closely with all stakeholders to ramp-up vital services and to make up for shortfalls.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is about how well we organise ourselves and marshal resources across the public, people and private sectors, and how we mount responses and deliver the best outcomes for Singapore and Singaporeans In the end, dealing with a national crisis requires a whole-of-nation approach.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, we hope that partners from all segments of society can come together again in any future crisis and we welcome the expertise and contributions from all companies and organisations, whether they are Temasek-linked or not.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Singaporeans trusted the Government to make the right decisions, and to act in the best interest of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The Government did not take this trust for granted.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We were open and honest throughout the crisis.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We shared information candidly, even when things did not go well, and even when we did not have complete information.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This was essential so that Singaporeans could continue placing their trust in the Government.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Equally, if not more important, the trust amongst Singaporeans has been strengthened.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This is not the case in many other places, where trust amongst their citizens had been declining, even before COVID-19, and may even be at historic lows today, post-crisis.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Hence, during the pandemic, it was hard for these governments to implement tough COVID-19 measures – after all, if trust is low then people may say: why should I comply with your measures, because if my neighbours or friends are not complying, then why should I do so?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: You can see this is what has happened in many other places where there is little trust, public health becomes politicised and individualised, and the countries' pandemic response is quickly compromised and impaired.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Fortunately, social capital and trust have been high in Singapore over the decades, and the silver lining in this terrible crisis is that social capital and trust have increased.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: A similar proportion of respondents were confident that the Government would know do what to do in a future pandemic and that Singaporeans would help one another tide through the next crisis together.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: This trust is extremely precious and we will work assiduously to preserve and strengthen it, so that Singapore will always remain a high-trust society.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Lessons learnt should never be hardcoded into doctrine.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Lessons should not be blindly applied from one crisis to another, because while there may be similarities, there will also be differences.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: The key is to have the flexibility and wisdom to adapt and devise solutions that are fit for purpose and fit for the situation at hand.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Indeed, through this COVID-19 experience, we have expanded our toolkit to manage disease outbreaks and pandemics.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, just thinking about the kinds of border measures we have from SARS to now, we have really expanded our toolkit considerably.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, hopefully, if we ever have to do this again, it will not be as confusing and complex, as was the case these last three years.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: By tweaking and adjusting these five parameters, we will be able to manage transmission risks, depending on the severity of the threat.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, be it surveillance, border measures, SMMs, testing or vaccine development, we now have a wider range of policy options and measures to tackle the next pandemic.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: With our enhanced capabilities in detection, surveillance, identification of threat which we are doing, not just by ourselves but hand-in-hand with international partners, we will be in a much better position to protect ourselves and deal with the next pandemic, if and when it comes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will continue working hard to expand our toolkit and to build up our capabilities, because, ultimately, that is the best way for us to honour the dedication and sacrifices that everyone had made to fight the pandemic these past three years.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That is why we acknowledge, with humility, the learnings and points of improvement as a country, a people and a Government.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We pledge to keep on doing better and be better prepared, if and when the next pandemic strikes.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: At the same time, we are grateful and thankful for all the positives that we have seen and experienced these past three years: the dedication of our healthcare and other frontline workers, the acts of kindness within our communities and the solidarity and trust of our people.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have focused in this debate on pandemic threats, but there will be other challenges.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Sometimes, it almost feels like the next crisis is just around the corner.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have got uncertainty now in the global economy and financial market, we have got geopolitical tensions, super-power rivalry in Asia, climate change, and the list goes on.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: There is no guaranteed formula to navigate these challenges.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But, if Singapore and Singaporeans take all what we have been through these past three years to heart, we will be able to overcome any challenges that come our way and prevail as one united people.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Just a quick point on the matter I brought up in my speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As I mentioned, COVID-19 was, indeed, an unprecedented crisis and it would not be realistic to expect no mistakes or missteps by the Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That said, I maintain the position that we do not know what we do not know.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We do not know what is stated in Mr Ho's report and the AARs from the respective Ministries.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would be important, in my view, for Singaporeans to consider the details and the breadth of perspectives secured from all who participated in the various AARs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I hope this information can be made available to the public at some point.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But this difference of opinion does not overshadow the Workers' Party's support for the Motion.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It included details, like the internal workings of the Government, our crisis management structures.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: These internal workings and crisis management structures are not just to deal with a pandemic.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Then, there are other parts of his report, which went into commercial sensitivities.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: For example, how we leveraged on different partners, scrambled to get essential supplies and managed our supply chains.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Those had some commercial sensitivities, and we cannot reveal them.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In fact, it will be a subset of the White Paper.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Because as I explained just now, the White Paper goes beyond Mr Ho's report.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It covers the lessons from the agencies' AARs and it also covers the lessons learned after August 2021.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, it is a fuller synthesis of all the lessons that we have learned from the last three years.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, I hope everyone understands and can see that we have been upfront in doing this.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We have maintained this approach in dealing with the crisis throughout the last three years and we continue to do so in the White Paper, which covers the lessons for the Government.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: By all means, there can be debate on the lessons, on the recommendations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: By all means, disagree with the lessons and the recommendations.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We are happy to hear the differences in views and to be better prepared.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But, I think, it is quite uncalled for to suggest that there has been any withholding of information by the Government in putting together this report.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: I hope that Mr Pritam Singh and the Workers' Party will live up to the ideals that he called for, in upholding national unity when we deal with and learn from this pandemic.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In July 2021, I asked if the Government could develop a COVID-19 risk index that aggregates indicators to provide guidance to policy-makers on decisions to ease or tighten SMMs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Will objective thresholds and matrixes be used to decide which situational tier we are in, and how does that differ from a risk index that relies on factors, such as the number of daily infections, hospital capacity and vaccination rates?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think most of our clinicians and public health experts will continue to maintain the view that an index, somehow, you put different ingredients into it, you will come up – viola! – with one number and use that to decide your policy.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As we learned during COVID-19, it is so fluid.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You need the flexibility to decide what best to do.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Having said that, a separate issue is what I mentioned just now, in reviewing the IDA, even with DORSCON today, you have different tiers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In different tiers, you have a range of options, a range of public health options.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, when you have a pathogen that is dangerous, you first decide which tier you are at.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Within that tier, what the range of options are.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Then, from the range of options, you mix and match depending on the characteristics of the pathogen.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If it proves to be insufficient, then, you upgrade and you explain to people why you need to upgrade the situational tier.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I, likewise, have a clarification as well as a question for Minister Ong.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I believe that the Minister shared that we were among the first to pursue vaccines, just after the UK, US and Israel – is what I believe he said.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Of course, not to take away from the hard and undeniably difficult work of the expert group on procurement, I believe our first vaccination occurred on 30 December 2020.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It was a nurse, I believe – a frontliner nurse.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Based on a quick search, at that time, actually, a large number of developed and emerging economies had already commenced their vaccination programmes, many with mRNA vaccines.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Switzerland did so on 23 December; Spain, 27 December; Hungary, 26 December; Canada; 14 December; Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries like Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) on 17, 22 and 14 December, respectively.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You see, in Europe, they have the European Union (EU).

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They are at the front of the queue.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Global South is very far down in the queue.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But due to the reasons and the decisions we made, we leveraged relationships with the pharmaceutical companies, particularly EDB, we were able to be higher-up in the queue, outside of the EU, outside of the Americas.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think we were still very fast, from that perspective.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Member seems to suggest there is a gap between procurement and rollout.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As I mentioned just now, we got our first batch of Pfizer-BioNTech vaccines late in the year – I forgot which month, could be September or so	– and then we rolled out in December.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When we had sufficient volume – during that time, we had to set up a whole new machinery to handle the vaccine.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You have to maintain minus 70°C, all the way to the vaccination centre.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Once you open it, it has a limited lifespan.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, within those days, you accept appointments and jab it into the arms of people.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Which also explains why – one of the questions that Mr Leon Perera raised yesterday – we did not use general practitioners (GPs) at that point.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That is one reason, because of the ultra-cold chain and the logistical challenges.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: At the earliest possible juncture, we delivered the vaccines safely, efficiently, quickly to the arms of our people.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But, I think, here, we are not just comparing with other countries, but we also want to compare with ourselves – how we want to make sure that we deal with this better in the future, as compared to now.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, it is in that spirit that I ask, whether a review on each of the budget measures has been done or are they ongoing.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Specifically, in future responses, does the Government still feel that giving grants to profitable companies is the way to go?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We published, as I mentioned just now, a paper looking at the impact of our COVID-19 measures.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If not, I will encourage her to look at the detailed studies which highlighted the outcomes we have achieved from our measures, including the JSS.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: We will continue to review and we will continue to improve, because we do want to do better.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: On the specific point that Ms Poa raised, which is, can we put in place a criterion to give out help that will not allow for some recovery of payments to profitable companies, I would put it this way.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: First of all, to do it ex-post is not the right thing to do.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: That means, we will only wait until you know the results, later on.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Then, there will be a lot of uncertainty for companies.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: If you want to do that, you have to do it with a priori – upfront.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: Then, later on, if it exceeds a threshold, yes, you can claw back.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: In principle, in theory, yes, you can think of it like that.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But, I think, it is not so straightforward	in practice.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: It is administratively going to be quite complex.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: How do you set the right threshold upfront?

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: All may try to operate below the threshold.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: So, while what she has highlighted is something that can work	in theory, I think there are administrative complexities.

speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
text: But from MOF's perspective, we will continue to study and review because our interest is to continually make sure that we achieve value for money in what we spend.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: A bit of supplementary information for Assoc Prof Jamus Lim.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: He mentioned several countries that rolled out their vaccination programmes earlier than us.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I should point out that many of them used non-mRNA vaccines – AstraZeneca and others.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, we probably need some time to compile the data, then we know where we stand.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But we were one of the first in Asia.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Those countries that I did mention all had mRNA vaccines.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: There were, indeed, other countries that had non-mRNA vaccines, but I did not cite those.
